title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
Chapter             Fifteen

     T
         his chapter is intended for Gamemasters only. It holds
         an extensive Frankish chronology based on both history
         and the chansons de geste, starting with the first year of
      Charlemagne’s reign. It is meant as an inspiration for scenarios
      of all sorts, as well as an illustration of the game’s themes and
      possible background stories and intrigues.
        Information about the harvest (important for the Winter
      Phase) is given at the end of each year.
      The  Passage     of Time

     T
         he Paladin chronology is based on both the historical
         events and the stories described in the epics. As these
         were written mostly in the 12th and the 13th centuries,
      the historical Frankish culture in this game is mixed with later
      medieval customs and technology. To represent the advanced
      Frankish time, the entire feudal era of our time gets telescoped
      into the 46 years of Charlemagne’s reign (768–814). While
      foreign cultures follow their historical path, the Franks have
      an accelerated evolution. For every eleven years of game time,
      they gain an entire century with regards to science, technology,
      equipment, architecture, and social structures.
        This perspective means the nature of the game is contin-
      ually evolving. The rough and tumble world of feudal “might
      makes right” undergoes a radical change when Charlemagne
      becomes the King of the Franks. The essential nature of knight-
      hood — professional warrior — remains, but is tempered by new
      attitudes of virtue and responsibility. Furthermore, many new
      activities emerge, including the elaboration of tournaments, the
      arts of chivalry and the introduction of romance. Many new ob-
      jectives and ideals come out after the establishment of the order
      of paladins, when the best knights of the realm gather to serve
      King Charlemagne.
rightColumn:
en:    The         Future

  Phase   1: Unification (768–778)

  Customs

  F
      eudalism: Charlemagne manages to bind the counts to
      his personal authority. The feudal pyramid is now com-
      plete, with the king at its summit. In return for their loy-
  alty, the counts get a third of all income from the fiscs they ad-
  minister for him, and the king generously redistributes the loot
  taken during the annual campaigns.
     Truce of God: Since Charlemagne decides that its viola-
  tion weighs heavily against the offender in case of a court trial,
  more knights respect this religious imperative.
     Knighthood: Widespread and commonly accepted in
  Frankland, the British Isles, Spain, Byzantium, Babylon and
  Persia.
     Heraldry: Knighthood is recognized as having special priv-
  ileges and rights, and one of those is to have individual coats of
  arms. Personal designs cannot be duplicated by anyone in the
  kingdom, and fights and feuds may occur if nobles discover
  someone else has chosen the same or similar design. Heralds
  make their first appearance, their job being to advise and to keep
  track of the increasingly complex arms.
     Tournaments: At first, Charlemagne organizes mock fights
  and contests of individual challenges at the yearly May Field to
  impress foreign visitors: tournaments including animals fights, a
  bohort, and knightly challenges. Over time tournaments are es-
  tablished as a method for knights to show their prowess, practice
  their skills, and win Glory.
     Women: A woman must give her consent to be wedded. A
  nobleman’s wife has the right to a third of her husband’s posses-
  sions should he die (the Widow’s Portion).

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Chivalry: Part of the creation of the Order of Paladins
      (767) is the active promotion of this new ideal by the king.
      Chivalry is a condition of recruitment for paladins.
        Romance: Inspired by poetry and chivalry, fin’amor starts
      to become popular at the royal court, especially involving
      Charlemagne’s successive wives, concubines and, later, daughters.
        Fashion: Men start wearing both a long-sleeved under-tu-
      nic and an over-tunic (cotte) of fine wool or linen. The over-tu-
      nic is fastened at the waist by a belt. The legs are still covered
      with trousers, but sandals are replaced by leather shoes.
        Women wear long-sleeved under-tunics which fit tightly at
      the waist and flow into a skirt. Belts are worn around the waist,
      and a cloak is attached with a cord.

rightColumn:
Warfare

     Armor: Chain mail armor (10 points) is rapidly adopted by
  those who can afford it.
     Weapons: Knights adopt the use of the famous Frankish
  steel sword, the horse lance and the mace. Lombard militiamen
  use light crossbows.
     Horses: Chargers become widely available, even to
  sergeants.
     Castles: Motte-and-bailey castles remain common because
  they are cheap and quick to raise, but stone begins to replace
  timber. The king himself finances many square keeps and stone
  walls for royal castles and fiscs.

title: Phase 1: Unification
leftColumn:
Levy Troops: The British princes sometimes send archers
      to serve under Charlemagne, or one of his counts, in the defense
      of Christianity.
      aNNo 768
        May Field (Metz): Duke Otxoa of the Basques submits to
      his Frankish overlord. King Pepin receives envoys from Marsile,
      the Moorish Emir of Cordoba.
        Quatre fils Aymon (1): [←767] At Pentecost, Aymon
      presents his four sons to King Pepin. The king sends his cous-
      in Lothair to command Lord Bevis of Aigremont to come to
      court. When Bevis hears he is accused of herisliz (dereliction of
      duty) for not showing up at court, he is outraged. His council-
      ors and his wife try in vain to calm him down. Lothair arrives at
      Aigremont with his message, but Bevis threatens him and a fight
      ensues in which Lothair is killed. Lothair’s squires bring back his
      lifeless body to the royal court. The king swears vengeance.
        Aymon and his sons discreetly return to their home in the
      Ardennes. Bevis decides to travel to the king’s court to make
      peace, but on his way he and his men are ambushed and killed by
      the black-hearted Fulco of Morillon with King Pepin’s consent.
      Immediately, Doon of Nanteuil declares a feud against the king.
      He raises and army and raids the king’s domains in Champagne.
      A royal army led by Richard of Normandy and Salomon of
      Brittany defeats the rebel baron, who is obliged to accept the
      king’s peace proposal.
        Enfances Roland: [←762] Saint Giles receives Charlemagne
      at his monastery. While he is praying for the prince’s soul, an an-
      gel deposits a letter on the altar in which Charlemagne’s sin (in-
      cest) is explained to the saint. Thanks to Saint Giles’ intercession,
      Charlemagne’s sin is forgiven and the prince receives absolution.
      He takes a solemn vow to become a faithful Christian and to de-
      fend the True Faith against the pagans. [→771, Chevalerie Ogier]
        Death of King Pepin: The king is buried in Andenne by
      the monks of Stavelot. Charlemagne and Carloman are both
      crowned as kings of the Franks. After drawing lots, the kingdom
      is divided up between Charlemagne and his brother (see map).
      Most important councilors are on Carloman’s side: their uncles
      Bernard and Thierry, and Abbot Fulrad. Carloman is angry be-
      cause his brother Charlemagne “unlawfully” inherits half “his”
      kingdom. He contends that his elder brother is only a bastard
      child, as he was not born from a legal and anointed union.
        Quatre fils Aymon (2): At his coronation, Charlemagne
      dubs Renaud. Aymon gives his son the enchanted sword
      Froberge, which Maugis had given him.
        Bertolai (the king’s cousin) challenges Renaud to a game of
      chess. He loses and hits his opponent. Renaud demands repa-
      ration before King Charlemagne and reminds him of the mur-
      der on his uncle Bevis, for which he holds the king responsible.
      Charlemagne refuses to hear Renaud’s plea. Furious, Renaud
      kills Bertolai with a chess board and flees from court with his
      brothers. Aymon is forced to renounce his own sons, whom he
      chases from his castle. The banished sons secretly rebuild the
      castle of Montessor in the Ardennes Forest.
rightColumn:
On the magic island of Vulcanus, Maugis vanquishes a huge
  serpent and the demon Ranas in order to capture the magic
  horse Bayard, which he gives to Renaud to help him in his feud
  against Charlemagne. [→769]
     Winter Court (Aachen): News reaches court of Pope Paul
  I’s death. The new Pope, Constantine II, supports the Franks
  against the Lombards. The furious King Desiderius of the
  Lombards mutilates two papal envoys in retaliation.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 769
     May Field (Tours): Duke Hunold II of Aquitaine denies
  Frankish authority over his domains, so Charlemagne prepares
  for war. King Carloman refuses to come to his brother’s aid.
     Aquitaine: Hunold destroys the bridge at Langon-
  Marmande, forcing (he thinks) Charlemagne to cross at Agen,
  where the duke has amassed his troops. But at night the Frankish
  king, with a handful of his loyal followers, swims across the
  Dordogne River and takes the castle of Langon by surprise.
     Duke Lupus of the Gascons pledges fealty and hands over
  noble hostages, including his own son, Sancho. Lupus then be-
  trays Hunold, who had fled to his court. Charlemagne ends the
  Aquitainian revolt by killing Hunold in battle and hanging the
  duke’s uncle, Remistan. The Franks establish a well-garrisoned
  stronghold at Fronsac along the Dordogne River.
     Quatre fils Aymon: [←768] Richard and his men attack
  a group of royal scouts in the Ardennes Forest. Ogier discov-
  ers their castle. Naymo tries to negotiate peace conditions, but
  Renaud refuses, so King Charlemagne decides to lay siege to
  Montessor. Aymon’s sons launch a sortie and almost capture
  their father, who serves in the royal army. The siege continues.
     With the king’s approval, Hervis of Lausanne pretends
  to have been banished from the kingdom and is welcomed at
  Montessor as a fellow outlaw by Aymon’s sons. Hervis opens the
  gates at night; the royal knights enter the castle and set fire to it.
  Before escaping from Montessor on the back of Bayard, Renaud
  and his brothers slay the treacherous Hervis. Aymon pursues his
  sons and almost captures them. Finally he returns home, while
  his children continue to live as poor robber knights hidden in
  the Ardennes Forest. [→770]
     Charlemagne’s Voyage to Jerusalem and Constantinople:
  At court, Charlemagne asks Queen Himiltrude if she thinks he’s
  the most handsome king in the world. He is surprised and in-
  sulted when she answers that she finds that the rich Emperor
  of Byzantium wears his crown with more elegance than he. The
  queen, seeing that her joke has thoroughly vexed her husband,
  tries to calm him down, saying that even if the emperor is richer
  and more handsome, Charlemagne is much braver and a far bet-
  ter knight. But the king is furious and even threatens to kill his
  wife. When he has calmed down a little, he decides to demand
  the judgment of his paladins: they travel with him to his rival’s
  court straight away!

  luggage on mules, the king and his peers cross the Mediterranean

segments.text:
Levy Troops: The British princes sometimes send archers
      to serve under Charlemagne, or one of his counts, in the defense
      of Christianity.
      aNNo 768
        May Field (Metz): Duke Otxoa of the Basques submits to
      his Frankish overlord. King Pepin receives envoys from Marsile,
      the Moorish Emir of Cordoba.
        Quatre fils Aymon (1): [←767] At Pentecost, Aymon
      presents his four sons to King Pepin. The king sends his cous-
      in Lothair to command Lord Bevis of Aigremont to come to
      court. When Bevis hears he is accused of herisliz (dereliction of
      duty) for not showing up at court, he is outraged. His council-
      ors and his wife try in vain to calm him down. Lothair arrives at
      Aigremont with his message, but Bevis threatens him and a fight
      ensues in which Lothair is killed. Lothair’s squires bring back his
      lifeless body to the royal court. The king swears vengeance.
        Aymon and his sons discreetly return to their home in the
      Ardennes. Bevis decides to travel to the king’s court to make
      peace, but on his way he and his men are ambushed and killed by
      the black-hearted Fulco of Morillon with King Pepin’s consent.
      Immediately, Doon of Nanteuil declares a feud against the king.
      He raises and army and raids the king’s domains in Champagne.
      A royal army led by Richard of Normandy and Salomon of
      Brittany defeats the rebel baron, who is obliged to accept the
      king’s peace proposal.
        Enfances Roland: [←762] Saint Giles receives Charlemagne
      at his monastery. While he is praying for the prince’s soul, an an-
      gel deposits a letter on the altar in which Charlemagne’s sin (in-
      cest) is explained to the saint. Thanks to Saint Giles’ intercession,
      Charlemagne’s sin is forgiven and the prince receives absolution.
      He takes a solemn vow to become a faithful Christian and to de-
      fend the True Faith against the pagans. [→771, Chevalerie Ogier]
        Death of King Pepin: The king is buried in Andenne by
      the monks of Stavelot. Charlemagne and Carloman are both
      crowned as kings of the Franks. After drawing lots, the kingdom
      is divided up between Charlemagne and his brother (see map).
      Most important councilors are on Carloman’s side: their uncles
      Bernard and Thierry, and Abbot Fulrad. Carloman is angry be-
      cause his brother Charlemagne “unlawfully” inherits half “his”
      kingdom. He contends that his elder brother is only a bastard
      child, as he was not born from a legal and anointed union.
        Quatre fils Aymon (2): At his coronation, Charlemagne
      dubs Renaud. Aymon gives his son the enchanted sword
      Froberge, which Maugis had given him.
        Bertolai (the king’s cousin) challenges Renaud to a game of
      chess. He loses and hits his opponent. Renaud demands repa-
      ration before King Charlemagne and reminds him of the mur-
      der on his uncle Bevis, for which he holds the king responsible.
      Charlemagne refuses to hear Renaud’s plea. Furious, Renaud
      kills Bertolai with a chess board and flees from court with his
      brothers. Aymon is forced to renounce his own sons, whom he
      chases from his castle. The banished sons secretly rebuild the
      castle of Montessor in the Ardennes Forest.

On the magic island of Vulcanus, Maugis vanquishes a huge
  serpent and the demon Ranas in order to capture the magic
  horse Bayard, which he gives to Renaud to help him in his feud
  against Charlemagne. [→769]
     Winter Court (Aachen): News reaches court of Pope Paul
  I’s death. The new Pope, Constantine II, supports the Franks
  against the Lombards. The furious King Desiderius of the
  Lombards mutilates two papal envoys in retaliation.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 769
     May Field (Tours): Duke Hunold II of Aquitaine denies
  Frankish authority over his domains, so Charlemagne prepares
  for war. King Carloman refuses to come to his brother’s aid.
     Aquitaine: Hunold destroys the bridge at Langon-
  Marmande, forcing (he thinks) Charlemagne to cross at Agen,
  where the duke has amassed his troops. But at night the Frankish
  king, with a handful of his loyal followers, swims across the
  Dordogne River and takes the castle of Langon by surprise.
     Duke Lupus of the Gascons pledges fealty and hands over
  noble hostages, including his own son, Sancho. Lupus then be-
  trays Hunold, who had fled to his court. Charlemagne ends the
  Aquitainian revolt by killing Hunold in battle and hanging the
  duke’s uncle, Remistan. The Franks establish a well-garrisoned
  stronghold at Fronsac along the Dordogne River.
     Quatre fils Aymon: [←768] Richard and his men attack
  a group of royal scouts in the Ardennes Forest. Ogier discov-
  ers their castle. Naymo tries to negotiate peace conditions, but
  Renaud refuses, so King Charlemagne decides to lay siege to
  Montessor. Aymon’s sons launch a sortie and almost capture
  their father, who serves in the royal army. The siege continues.
     With the king’s approval, Hervis of Lausanne pretends
  to have been banished from the kingdom and is welcomed at
  Montessor as a fellow outlaw by Aymon’s sons. Hervis opens the
  gates at night; the royal knights enter the castle and set fire to it.
  Before escaping from Montessor on the back of Bayard, Renaud
  and his brothers slay the treacherous Hervis. Aymon pursues his
  sons and almost captures them. Finally he returns home, while
  his children continue to live as poor robber knights hidden in
  the Ardennes Forest. [→770]
     Charlemagne’s Voyage to Jerusalem and Constantinople:
  At court, Charlemagne asks Queen Himiltrude if she thinks he’s
  the most handsome king in the world. He is surprised and in-
  sulted when she answers that she finds that the rich Emperor
  of Byzantium wears his crown with more elegance than he. The
  queen, seeing that her joke has thoroughly vexed her husband,
  tries to calm him down, saying that even if the emperor is richer
  and more handsome, Charlemagne is much braver and a far bet-
  ter knight. But the king is furious and even threatens to kill his
  wife. When he has calmed down a little, he decides to demand
  the judgment of his paladins: they travel with him to his rival’s
  court straight away!
     As pilgrims, dressed in cloaks with walking staffs and their
  luggage on mules, the king and his peers cross the Mediterranean

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
Sea to visit Jerusalem first. They set up their camp outside the
      walls of the ancient city and make rich gifts at the cathedral. A
      local Jew, impressed by the beauty and splendor of the king and
      his paladins (whom he thinks are Jesus and the apostles), runs
      to the palace of the Patriarch of Jerusalem and demands to be
      baptized immediately. When the patriarch meets Charlemagne,
      who explains the aim of his visit, the holy man gives the king
      some powerful relics to take back to Frankland: Saint Simeon’s
      arm, Saint Lazarus’ head, Saint Stephen’s blood, a piece of Jesus’
      loin cloth, a nail from the Cross, the crown of thorns, the knife
      used for the Last Supper, Saint Mary’s milk and a piece of her
      dress, and Saint Peter’s hairs and beard.
        After some time, Charlemagne continues his voyage to
      Constantinople. On his way, the relics he carries with him work
      several miracles: the blind see, the lame walk and the dumb
      speak again.
        At Constantinople, the Frankish king is welcomed by the
      courteous emperor, who is plowing a field with a golden plow.
      The handsome basileus invites Charlemagne and his friends to
      stay at his court, giving each of his guests magnificent gifts. At
      the emperor’s impressive golden palace with crystal windows, the
      Franks play chess, drink excellent wine, and talk with the court
      maidens. When a storm breaks out, the Franks are surprised to
      see how the palace slowly rotates. At dinner, Oliver falls in love
      with a Byzantine princess, Iakobina.
        The Franks are lodged in a lavishly decorated room.
      Unknown to them, a spy is hidden in a hollow marble column.
      He hears the half-drunken Franks begin a humorous boasting
      contest (gabbing) about what feats they will perform at court to
      impress the emperor.
        The spy takes the gabs seriously and informs the emper-
      or of the Frankish plans to insult and dishonor his court. The
      next day, the furious emperor demands Charlemagne and his
      friends fulfill their outrageous boasts, on pain of death. Unable
      to explain that their boasts were only drunken gabs, the Franks
      retire to their room, ashamed, where they pray and call on the
      power of the relics they brought with them. Charlemagne re-
      ceives a vision in which an angel promises to help them, on the
      condition that they must live as humble and pious Christians
      from now on.
        Charlemagne takes his men back to the emperor’s court,
      where he accuses his host of a breach of hospitality: he spied
      on his guests. But he declares that the Franks will perform their
      exploits at court, if such is the will of their host. Without hes-
      itating, the emperor points at Oliver and commands him to
      publicly repeat his boast and accomplish it. Oliver makes his
      boast about princess Iakobina known to all (“Would the em-
      peror allow his daughter in my room, I would possess her
      a hundred times in a single night!”). The princess and the
      paladin are brought to a bedroom, where Oliver gently asks
      the Iakobina if she allows him to accomplish his boast, which
      she gladly accepts.
rightColumn:
With the help of God, all the other paladins miraculous-
  ly achieve their feats. The emperor is completely shocked and
  believes himself to be the victim of a band of powerful sorcer-
  ers. He agrees to recognize Charlemagne’s superiority and offers
  him his lands. But the noble Frankish king declines the offer and
  proposes a conciliatory banquet instead. In the evening, as the
  emperor and Charlemagne walk as friends through the palace af-
  ter a great feast, everybody agrees that Charlemagne is the most
  glorious and dignified of the two sovereigns.
     When the Franks finally decide it’s time to return to their
  homelands, princess Iakobina begs Oliver to take her with him
  to Frankland, but the young paladin politely refuses. Back home,
  Charlemagne donates the relics he was given to various churches
  and monasteries. He forgives Queen Himiltrude for the sincere
                              n
  but reckless answer she gave him a few months before.
     Lion de Bourges: [←766] After a year in Toledo, Lion returns
  to Frankland. He meets the faerie King Oberon in the Ardennes
  Forest and sojourns in an enchanted castle with Morgan le Fay. The
  White Knight sets him free and Lion finally arrives at Bourges. He
  defies and kills Fouqueret, the cruel count. The bishop brings him
  the ancestral horn which only Lion can blow. [→770]
     The Siege of Milan: Sir Alantyne loses Milan to invading
  Saracens. An angel sends his message to Charlemagne and in-
  structs the prince to help the Lombards. However, Charlemagne
  takes Ganelon’s bad advice and sends only Roland with a small
  force. The paladin and three of his companions are captured, but
  they manage to escape with God’s help.
     When Charlemagne considers shirking his responsibility,
  Turpin threatens to besiege his lord king in Paris, forcing him to
  go to Lombardy. The siege of Milan is a success and the Saracens
  are routed. In return for his help, Charlemagne obtains the hand
                    n
  of the Lombard princess Desideria.
     Girart de Vienne: [←750] Duke Garin of Monglane’s son,
  Milo, becomes the Duke of Apulia and his brother, Ernold of
  Beaulande, is installed as the new Count of Narbonne. Renier
  and Gerard go to King Carloman’s court, but are received with
  scorn because of their poor attire. The two angered brothers kill
  the haughty royal seneschal, but King Carloman forgives them
  when they make themselves known as Garin’s sons, and accepts
  them as his vassals.
     Renier and Gerard help Carloman to restore order in his
  kingdom by killing a bothersome band of robber knights. In re-
  turn, they demand that the king endow them with lands. He agrees
  to give the city of Geneva to Renier, while Gerard is promised the
  hand of the recently-widowed Gerberga, Duchess of Milan.
     But King Carloman falls in love with the Lombard duch-
  ess, and decides to marry her himself. This angers Ogier, who
  wants the lovely princess for himself instead! Meanwhile, the
  duchess anonymously declares her love for the young Gerard,
  who bluntly refuses. The humiliated duchess accepts the king’s
  marriage proposal. When Gerard finds out he won’t marry the
  duchess because he refused her love, he is angry but accepts

        Queen-mother Bertrada arranges the official marriage be-
      tween her son, Charlemagne, and Princess Desideria, daugh-
      ter of the Lombard King Desiderius, whom she personally es-
      corts back from Pavia. The Lombards now virtually surround
      the Papal States, and therefore this marriage worries the Pope.
      Bertrada engages her daughter, Gisela, to Desiderius’ son,
      Adalgis, much to the displeasure of the Frankish princess.
        Lion de Bourges: [←769] Charlemagne wishes to avenge
      Count Fouqueret’s death and comes to besiege Bourges. But
      when Count Basin informs the king that the Saxon warchief
      Widukind plans to invade Austrasia, Ogier is sent to negotiate a
      peace, which Lion accepts. He is reinstated as Count of Bourges.
      [→775]
        Fierabras: Young squire William of Toulouse, Count
      Basin, and Roland’s father, Milo, go out hunting together. When
      they return to the city of Vauclere, which is being besieged by
      the Saxons of Widukind, they meet three Saxon warlords who
      accept a duel on an island in the Rhine. The three victorious
      Frankish knights try to pass through the enemy camp discreetly
      on their way back to the city, but they are spotted and attacked.
      Thanks to Basin’s magic, they manage to escape unharmed and
      enter Vauclere. The Saxons are finally defeated and pushed back
                n
      into their own land.
        Quatre fils Aymon: [←769] Maugis becomes a Magister
      teaching magic in Paris, but refuses to become Charlemagne’s
      court wizard. The king develops a hatred of Maugis when
      he makes the entire court dance naked against their will.
      Charlemagne imprisons him, but with the help of a conjured de-
      mon the wizard escapes from his royal prison. He travels to the
      Ardennes to help his exiled cousins.
        In spring, Aymon’s sons secretly visit their mother at
      Bouillon. When Aymon comes home he quarrels with his sons,
      but does not betray them to the king. In return, Renaud and his
      brothers promise to leave the Ardennes for Gascony.
        Aymon’s sons are welcomed at Bordeaux by Duke Yon of
      Gascony. Soon after, they bring victory to their new lord in a
      small battle against raiding Moors. The duke grants them the
      castle of Montalban as an allod, and offers Renaud the hand of
      his daughter, Clarissa. [→771]

  Oliver and Princess Iakobina of Constantinople. He is raised at
  the Byzantine court. [→788]
     Ami et Amile: [←765] One night an angel announces to
  Count Amile that his friend Ami can be cured of leprosy only if
  he bathes in the blood of his friend’s children. Though horrified,
  Amile beheads his two young sons. Ami is miraculously cured. A
  second miracle restores life to the sacrificed children, who only
  have red scars around their necks when found playing quietly in
  the countess’ room. [→771]
     Girart de Vienne: [←769] Aymeriet visits the court of
  King Carloman, where the queen reveals the trick she played on
  Aymeriet’s uncle, Gerard. Aymeriet is publicly humiliated and
  in anger he tries to kill the queen. He flees from court and goes
  back to Vienne. Gerard musters his troops and takes counsel
  with his relatives. They advise him to demand a financial com-
  pensation for the insult from King Carloman, but Gerard wants
  the queen herself.
     The king summons Gerard to his court. Doon of Laon,
  as the royal envoy, defies Garin of Monglane’s sons, and the
  hot-headed Aymeriet kills Doon. After a short fight at the
  royal court, Gerard and his men flee to Vienne. Carloman and
  Charlemagne lay siege to the city. [→771]

  Desideria and marries the young Princess Hildegarde of Swabia,

  furious, and even some of Charlemagne’s own family members
  and vassals are shocked, including his cousin, Adalhard, and his
  uncles, Bernard and Thierry; Abbot Fulrad, Ogier the Dane,
  and Count Geoffrey of Anjou.

  home. Ami chases away his false wife, installs his son Gerard as
  the new count and dubs his two loyal servants. Then Ami and
  Amile leave on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. [→773]

  knighted. To prove his valor, he rides out and attacks the roy-
  al tents. Aymeriet nearly manages to capture Carloman’s queen,
  who is saved by Charlemagne himself.
     The siege continues. Roland organizes a small tournament
  outside the walls of Vienne. Oliver secretly participates and de-

  and captured. Ogier the Dane tries to rescue him, but is defeated
  by Oliver as well. Oliver accompanies Lanbert back to the king
  with a message of peace.

leftColumn:
insolent knight. When Aimart wants to avenge his uncle’s death,
      Lanbert intervenes in Oliver’s favor. Oliver flees and a small bat-
      tle breaks out near Vienne. Gerard unhorses a knight who turns
      out to be Charlemagne himself, but instead of taking the king
      prisoner, Gerard offers chivalrous apologies. The battle turns
      against Gerard’s men and they retreat into the city.
        Roland declares his love to Aude, although he knows he
      either has to kill her beloved brother or die himself in the up-
      coming duel.
        Charlemagne has a prophetic dream of two hawks fighting
      at first, but finally making peace. During his duel with Roland
      Oliver offers to lay down their arms, but Roland refuses. Oliver’s
      sword breaks, but Roland allows him to fetch a new blade.
      Joachim the Jew, fearful that his city might be sacked and burned
      should Oliver lose, gives Oliver the enchanted sword Halteclere,
      and the duel is resumed. During a break, Oliver’s squire tries to
      kill Roland treacherously, but Oliver prevents this and banish-
      es his squire. Likewise, when Charlemagne learns how a hun-
      dred knights have secretly hidden themselves to ambush Oliver
      should he win, the king is angered and threatens to hang all the
      treacherous knights.
        After a few hours of indecisive combat, an angel inter-
      venes and tells Roland and Oliver to make peace; they should
      fight pagans instead of each other. They return to their re-
      spective lords, informing them that they will no longer fight
      the other. Ganelon is furious, since Charlemagne had prom-
      ised him the fief of Vienne, and he accuses Roland, his son-
      in-law, of interrupting the fight only for the love of Aude.
      Still, a truce is concluded. Charlemagne goes out hunting in
      a wood, but is caught by Gerard and his men. Aymeriet wants
      to kill the king, but Gerard holds him back and instead offers
      Charlemagne unconditional peace. The king accepts. Aude is
      betrothed to Roland.
        News from Duke Yon of Gascony reaches the court that
      Marsile has invaded his lands and is laying siege to Duke Sevin
            n
      at Bordeaux.
        Pseudo-Turpin: After Charlemagne has reconciled himself
      with the rebellious Gerard of Vienne, he defeats the Moorish be-
      siegers of Bordeaux. The king then receives a vision telling him
      to liberate the tomb of St. James at Compostela. He crosses the
      Pyrenees and lays siege to Pamplona, a town held by the Basques,
      allied to the Moors. After God makes the city walls crumble, the
      Franks take the city. All pagans are converted or slain.
        At Compostela, Wali Agolant defies the Franks. The
      night before the confrontation, several Frankish spears planted
      in the soil miraculously sprout leafs. These are the lances of the
      martyrs who will fall in battle. Among them is Count Milo,
      Roland’s father.
        Agolant is defeated in a judicial combat. He promises
      to convert, but changes his mind when he sees how little the
      Franks care for the poor. Finally, Agolant is killed in battle
      and Compostela is liberated. Charlemagne, as the descen-
      dant of Floris and Blancheflour, restores the Visigothic king-
      dom of Asturias by crowning Aurelio as the new king, which
rightColumn:
includes the duchies of Galicia (where Hamon is duke),
  Oviedo and Cantabria.
     Next, a courteous Saracen giant named Ferragut comes
  to challenge all paladins of Charlemagne’s court. He simply
  seizes Ogier and Oliver without a real fight, carries them off,
  and imprisons them inside a deep hole in the ground. Ignoring
  Charlemagne’s objections, Roland rides forth to fight the giant.
  He avoids the giant’s blows and tries to convert him. During a
  break, Ferragut lays himself down to sleep, and the courteous
  Roland gently places a smooth stone under the giant’s head.
  The combat lasts all day, and Roland notices that the giant is
  invulnerable to his sword strokes. The imprudent giant boasts
  that only his belly button is vulnerable. Roland takes aim and
  kills Ferragut.
     On the way back to Frankland, Roland wants to cap-
  ture the city of Saragossa. He receives a message from Queen
  Bramimonde, who secretly invites him to come and visit her.
  Roland leaves Oliver, who accompanied him, and enters the city
  alone. He slips into the palace and meets the admiring queen,
  who gives him her mantle. The guards discover the intruder and
  Roland has to fight his way out of the city. The Moors pursue
  him, and when Roland asks Oliver for help, his vexed compan-
  ion bluntly refuses. Only when Roland is unhorsed does Oliver
  enter the fray. Roland leaves the field and lets his companion and
  Archbishop Turpin defeat the Saracens.
     A few days later, Oliver and his men capture a small Basque
  castle. When Roland learns his friend has left the Frankish camp,
  he is worried. Oliver’s horse tracks lead him to the castle, where
  Oliver’s men pretend to be Saracens. Roland attacks, but soon
  recognizes his fellow Franks. He reconciles with Oliver and both
  return to the king’s army.
     Hearing of Ferragut’s defeat, Otinel comes to challenge
  Roland to a duel. A Frankish princess, Belissent, helps Otinel to
  don his armor and the pagan falls in love with her. During the
  fight with Roland, a white dove tells Otinel to convert, which
  he does. He is baptized “Ferrau,” marries Belissent and receives
  a fief in Lombardy. Then Otinel’s former lord, the Saracen Emir
  Garsie, accuses the convert of treason, invades Otinel’s lands and
  takes his castle. In the ensuing battle, Ogier is captured. Assisted
  by Roland and Oliver, Ferrau sets the Dane free and then kills
                  n
  Emir Garsie. The Saracens flee.
     Aquilon de Bavière: [←756] Anibal, Naymo’s lost son, ral-
  lies the pagan kings who want to avenge Charlemagne’s defeat
  of Agolant. During the first battle, at Valperse, Roland unsuc-
  cessfully tries to convert Anibal. Lucion of Valperse captures
  Charlemagne, but fortunately Roland rescues the king and
  learns Anibal’s true identity.
     Meanwhile, Anibal’s Moors and some Amazons have been
  raiding various parts of Frankland. Finally, Roland and 19 oth-
  ers defeat 20 pagans in a large-scale judicial combat and force
                        n
  Anibal to convert. He is baptized Aquilon.

  the first Spanish campaign. His brother Vivien has been raised
  at the court of the Saracen Emir Yvorin. Unknowingly, the two

insolent knight. When Aimart wants to avenge his uncle’s death,
      Lanbert intervenes in Oliver’s favor. Oliver flees and a small bat-
      tle breaks out near Vienne. Gerard unhorses a knight who turns
      out to be Charlemagne himself, but instead of taking the king
      prisoner, Gerard offers chivalrous apologies. The battle turns
      against Gerard’s men and they retreat into the city.
        Roland declares his love to Aude, although he knows he
      either has to kill her beloved brother or die himself in the up-
      coming duel.
        Charlemagne has a prophetic dream of two hawks fighting
      at first, but finally making peace. During his duel with Roland
      Oliver offers to lay down their arms, but Roland refuses. Oliver’s
      sword breaks, but Roland allows him to fetch a new blade.
      Joachim the Jew, fearful that his city might be sacked and burned
      should Oliver lose, gives Oliver the enchanted sword Halteclere,
      and the duel is resumed. During a break, Oliver’s squire tries to
      kill Roland treacherously, but Oliver prevents this and banish-
      es his squire. Likewise, when Charlemagne learns how a hun-
      dred knights have secretly hidden themselves to ambush Oliver
      should he win, the king is angered and threatens to hang all the
      treacherous knights.
        After a few hours of indecisive combat, an angel inter-
      venes and tells Roland and Oliver to make peace; they should
      fight pagans instead of each other. They return to their re-
      spective lords, informing them that they will no longer fight
      the other. Ganelon is furious, since Charlemagne had prom-
      ised him the fief of Vienne, and he accuses Roland, his son-
      in-law, of interrupting the fight only for the love of Aude.
      Still, a truce is concluded. Charlemagne goes out hunting in
      a wood, but is caught by Gerard and his men. Aymeriet wants
      to kill the king, but Gerard holds him back and instead offers
      Charlemagne unconditional peace. The king accepts. Aude is
      betrothed to Roland.
        News from Duke Yon of Gascony reaches the court that
      Marsile has invaded his lands and is laying siege to Duke Sevin
            n
      at Bordeaux.
        Pseudo-Turpin: After Charlemagne has reconciled himself
      with the rebellious Gerard of Vienne, he defeats the Moorish be-
      siegers of Bordeaux. The king then receives a vision telling him
      to liberate the tomb of St. James at Compostela. He crosses the
      Pyrenees and lays siege to Pamplona, a town held by the Basques,
      allied to the Moors. After God makes the city walls crumble, the
      Franks take the city. All pagans are converted or slain.
        At Compostela, Wali Agolant defies the Franks. The
      night before the confrontation, several Frankish spears planted
      in the soil miraculously sprout leafs. These are the lances of the
      martyrs who will fall in battle. Among them is Count Milo,
      Roland’s father.
        Agolant is defeated in a judicial combat. He promises
      to convert, but changes his mind when he sees how little the
      Franks care for the poor. Finally, Agolant is killed in battle
      and Compostela is liberated. Charlemagne, as the descen-
      dant of Floris and Blancheflour, restores the Visigothic king-
      dom of Asturias by crowning Aurelio as the new king, which

includes the duchies of Galicia (where Hamon is duke),
  Oviedo and Cantabria.
     Next, a courteous Saracen giant named Ferragut comes
  to challenge all paladins of Charlemagne’s court. He simply
  seizes Ogier and Oliver without a real fight, carries them off,
  and imprisons them inside a deep hole in the ground. Ignoring
  Charlemagne’s objections, Roland rides forth to fight the giant.
  He avoids the giant’s blows and tries to convert him. During a
  break, Ferragut lays himself down to sleep, and the courteous
  Roland gently places a smooth stone under the giant’s head.
  The combat lasts all day, and Roland notices that the giant is
  invulnerable to his sword strokes. The imprudent giant boasts
  that only his belly button is vulnerable. Roland takes aim and
  kills Ferragut.
     On the way back to Frankland, Roland wants to cap-
  ture the city of Saragossa. He receives a message from Queen
  Bramimonde, who secretly invites him to come and visit her.
  Roland leaves Oliver, who accompanied him, and enters the city
  alone. He slips into the palace and meets the admiring queen,
  who gives him her mantle. The guards discover the intruder and
  Roland has to fight his way out of the city. The Moors pursue
  him, and when Roland asks Oliver for help, his vexed compan-
  ion bluntly refuses. Only when Roland is unhorsed does Oliver
  enter the fray. Roland leaves the field and lets his companion and
  Archbishop Turpin defeat the Saracens.
     A few days later, Oliver and his men capture a small Basque
  castle. When Roland learns his friend has left the Frankish camp,
  he is worried. Oliver’s horse tracks lead him to the castle, where
  Oliver’s men pretend to be Saracens. Roland attacks, but soon
  recognizes his fellow Franks. He reconciles with Oliver and both
  return to the king’s army.
     Hearing of Ferragut’s defeat, Otinel comes to challenge
  Roland to a duel. A Frankish princess, Belissent, helps Otinel to
  don his armor and the pagan falls in love with her. During the
  fight with Roland, a white dove tells Otinel to convert, which
  he does. He is baptized “Ferrau,” marries Belissent and receives
  a fief in Lombardy. Then Otinel’s former lord, the Saracen Emir
  Garsie, accuses the convert of treason, invades Otinel’s lands and
  takes his castle. In the ensuing battle, Ogier is captured. Assisted
  by Roland and Oliver, Ferrau sets the Dane free and then kills
                  n
  Emir Garsie. The Saracens flee.
     Aquilon de Bavière: [←756] Anibal, Naymo’s lost son, ral-
  lies the pagan kings who want to avenge Charlemagne’s defeat
  of Agolant. During the first battle, at Valperse, Roland unsuc-
  cessfully tries to convert Anibal. Lucion of Valperse captures
  Charlemagne, but fortunately Roland rescues the king and
  learns Anibal’s true identity.
     Meanwhile, Anibal’s Moors and some Amazons have been
  raiding various parts of Frankland. Finally, Roland and 19 oth-
  ers defeat 20 pagans in a large-scale judicial combat and force
                        n
  Anibal to convert. He is baptized Aquilon.

title: Phase 1: Unification
leftColumn:
brothers fight one another in battle, but when they recognize
      each other they reconcile and Vivien converts. The two brothers
      become the opponents of both Charlemagne and the Moors.
        Charlemagne returns from his Spanish campaign and pass-
      es through Gascony. He orders Yon to hand over Renaud, but
      the duke refuses to betray his brother-in-law.
        Charlemagne organizes a noble horse race in Paris in order
      to lure Renaud out of his castle. Maugis puts a spell on himself,
      Renaud and Bayard and they ride north. They arrive in Paris
      where the paladins do not recognize them nor Bayard, who
      feigns to be slightly crippled. Bayard easily wins the horse race
      and Renaud seizes the prize: Charlemagne’s crown. He reveals
      his identity, mocks the king and escapes.
        Charlemagne prepares to besiege Montalban. Some of his
      councilors plead for peace, but the king ignores them. Yon is
      given four days to decide whether he is for or against the king.
      The duke finally agrees to give up Aymon’s sons and force them
      to accept the king’s peace. Ogier and Fulco of Morillon set up
      an ambush along a field near Vaucouleurs, where Yon invites
      Renaud and his brothers. The Duke of Gascony tells them he
      has concluded a favorable treaty with the king, on the condi-
      tion that they accompany him, riding mules and without arms,
      to Vaucouleurs. Clarissa and Richard have little faith in the plan,
      but Renaud refuses to believe Yon could betray him.
        When they arrive at the field near Vaucouleurs, Ogier sees
      them first and attacks. Aymon’s sons escape and rush towards
      Fulco’s men. Richard is seriously injured and Guichard is cap-
      tured, but liberated soon after. The brothers finally retire to
      some ruins on top of a hill. Ogier sends his men to the front,
      but refuses to participate in the battle himself. He sends some
      knights to Montalban “to ambush Maugis, should he come to
      his cousins’ aid,” but in reality he hopes that the wizard takes
      the knights’ presence as an invitation! And indeed, Maugis
      speeds to Vaucouleurs on Bayard, where he charges Ogier and
      wounds him. The Dane returns to Charlemagne’s camp to re-
      port. Roland accuses Ogier of cowardice and proposes to meet
      Renaud in a duel to end the feud. The young paladin rides to
      Bordeaux and seizes Duke Yon before he can enter a monastery,
      where he wanted to be tonsured. When Renaud hears this, he
      decides to come to the aid of his father-in-law, despite his pre-
      vious betrayal.
        Outside Montalban, Renaud meets Roland and both men
      prepare for battle. Ogier and Naymo try to prevent the duel, ar-
      guing for a diplomatic peace, but to no avail. Roland is unhorsed
      at the first pass. Bayard almost kicks the young paladin to death,
      but Roland regains his balance and counters with Durendal.
      Maugis seizes this chance to intervene and urges Renaud to es-
      cape with Yon while he covers their retreat. Now it’s Ogier turn
      to mock Roland for his incompetence.
        Richard comes to court and challenges Roland, who easily
      defeats him. Maugis keeps Renaud from rash action, riding to
      Charlemagne himself instead, disguised as a pilgrim. The king
      hits Roland’s prisoner, Richard, who recognizes Maugis among
      the guests. Charlemagne wishes to hang Richard, but almost
rightColumn:
all his councilors (Naymo, Berenger, Ogier, Turpin, Salomon,
  Roland, Oliver, Estout, Richard of Normandy and Gerard of
  Anjou) are opposed to this idea. Finally, a knight called Ripeus
  agrees to hang Richard and brings him to the gallows. Using his
  magic, Maugis allows Renaud to pass by sleeping guards and res-
  cue his brother, slaying Ripeus. Once more all of Aymon’s son
  escape safe and sound. Richard wishes to thank the paladins for
  their refusal to hang him. He dons Ripeus’ armor and returns
  to the royal court. He is met by Ogier, who immediately attacks
  him, for the Dane thinks Richard is the dishonorable Ripeus.
  Renaud comes to Richard’s aid. Charlemagne himself then joins
  the skirmish of the paladins against Aymon’s sons.
     When Renaud realizes he is fighting his lawful king, he
  demands a truce. He offers Charlemagne peace in return for
  Montalban and Bayard, and promises to leave Frankland on a
  pilgrimage to Jerusalem for pardon for his numerous sins. The
  king refuses, preferring victory by arms, but Aymon’s sons retire
  from the field. The royal troops give pursuit and Oliver captures
  Maugis, whose horse can’t keep up with Bayard. Charlemagne
  orders the wizard to be hanged the next morning. That evening,
  Maugis escapes from his prison and puts the entire court to sleep.
  He steals all the swords from the king and his paladins.
     Charlemagne sends an envoy to Montalban, where Maugis
  agrees to return the stolen swords. Renaud himself accompanies
  the ambassadors back to court, where Naymo and Ogier offer
  themselves as guarantees for his safety. Renaud wishes to finish
  his interrupted duel with Roland. They fight on foot in a field
  near Montalban, but once more they are interrupted: a sudden
  sand storm makes fighting impossible and the two opponents
  take refuge inside Montalban, together with Ogier and Naymo.
     Charlemagne has had enough and once more besieges the
  castle. One night, Maugis rides out on Bayard, abducts the king
  himself and takes him to Montalban. He then leaves the castle
  and retires to a monastery to pray for his tarnished soul. Renaud
  demands that the king, his prisoner, make peace. Roland, Ogier
  and Naymo beg Charlemagne to accept, but the king stubbornly
  refuses unless Renaud agrees to deliver Maugis into his hands.
  Renaud, who could never betray his cousin, is furious and almost
  slays the king, but Roland and Ogier restrain him. Aymon’s sons
  finally agree to release the king unconditionally.
     The feud and the siege continue. Renaud leads a sortie in
  which they receive the aid of many Gascons, who bear a grudge
  against the king for pillaging their lands some years earlier.
  Aymon’s sons capture some loot, but not as much provender as
  they had hoped for.
     After a few weeks, Montalban runs out of supplies and
  Aymon’s sons are obliged to butcher all the horses except
  Bayard, whose blood they drink. In secret, Aymon bombards
  Montalban with meat instead of stones. He is betrayed to the
  king, but Naymo defends the loving father and leaves the roy-
  al camp in Aymon’s company. Bayard almost dies of blood loss.
  Then Renaud discovers a secret tunnel, by which the brothers
  can escape out of their empty castle. They take the hidden forest
  roads to the north, to Tremoigne. [→772]

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future

Chevalerie Ogier: [←768, Enfances Ogier] One winter day,
      while Ogier is out hunting, the angry King Carloman accidental-
      ly kills Ogier’s son, Baldwin, who defeated his royal liege at chess.
      Charlemagne and Carloman personally bring Ogier the news of
      the tragedy. The furious Dane demands blood vengeance and
      wants to kill both of Carloman’s sons, but Charlemagne refuses.
      Ogier goes berserk. He attacks both Frankish kings, wounding
      Charlemagne and slaying Carloman with a dagger. He then flees
      into the woods (in the royal annals it is written that Carloman
      died of an unfortunate hunting accident). [→773]
        Death of King Carloman: At Carloman’s death,
      Charlemagne and some of his paladins immediately ride out
      to meet Fulrad and Carloman’s barons (including his uncles
      Bernard and Thierry); he claims Carloman’s lands, while his
      armed men stand outside. Charlemagne becomes the sole lead-
      er of his father’s kingdom. Dissident nobles like Count Aymon
      oppose Charlemagne’s usurpation of Carloman’s title and lands.
      Princess Gerberga, Carloman’s widow, flees to her father’s court
      at Pavia with her two young sons, Pepin and Lothair, and oth-
      er Frankish nobles, such as Duke Bero. She is accompanied by
      Ogier the Dane, who is in love with the princess he himself
      widowed.
        Winter Court (Attigny).
        Harvests: Mediocre; Stewardship –2.
      aNNo 772
        May Field (Worms).
        Saxony: Hesse is raided heavily by Saxons. Constable
      Geilon and Count Theodore are killed, many monasteries
      (Erfurt, Lippenheim, Fulda) are burned and their abbots cru-
      cified. In retaliation, Charlemagne marches deep into the Saxon
      forest. He captures the fortress of Eresburg and destroys the pa-
      gan idol tree, Irminsul, at Geismar, where he finds an immense
      treasure. The Saxons are forced to give many peace hostages. On
      their way home the Franks find that all wells and rivers are dry,
      but after three days of prayers miraculous rains fall from a cloud-
      less sky, so that all men and horses may quench their thirst.
        Quatre fils Aymon: [←771] Charlemagne rides to the
      Saxon town of Tremoigne, where the exiled Renaud meets him
      in person to beg his sovereign for peace. The king demands that
      Renaud deliver Maugis to him, which Renaud refuses. A small
      battle takes place in which Renaud and his Saxon allies capture
      Duke Richard of Normandy. Maugis leaves his hermit’s cell and
      arrives at the royal camp. He captures the baby Prince Charlot
      and takes him to the city. Then he leaves for the Holy Land to
      redeem his sins. Renaud pretends to prepare the executions of
      the duke and the baby prince.
        The paladins try to convince Charlemagne to accept
      Renaud’s peace offer. When the king insists on hanging Renaud,
      the paladins temporarily leave court. Finally, Charlemagne
      agrees to make peace, but demands that Bayard be killed to pay
      for his master’s crimes.
        Bayard is thrown into the Meuse River with a mill stone
      around his neck and Renaud goes utterly mad. He breaks his

     Quatre fils Aymon: [←772] Renaud meets the Pope in
  Rome, then embarks on a ship at Brindisi and finally arrives in
  Outremer, where he meets Maugis. They spend many years in
  the service of King Geoffrey of Jerusalem, helping him safeguard
  his kingdom from Saracen attacks. [→795]
     Lombardy: Two Frankish armies, one led by uncle Bernard
  and other by Charlemagne himself, travel to the Alps to come
  to the Pope’s defense against Desiderius of the Lombards. They
  move undetected through the mountains and forest and take the
  garrison of Aosta by surprise. Desiderius refuses to recognize the
  Papal States, even in return for 1,000 pounds of gold. Therefore
  the Frankish army lays siege to the Lombard capital of Pavia.
  Charlemagne sends his paladins ahead.

  king, Ogier defends the city of Pavia against Duke Naymo of
  Bavaria. Charlemagne sends Naymo’s son, Bertrand, to negotiate
  peace and demands that the Lombards hand over Ogier. A furi-
  ous Duke Bero attacks Bertrand, but the young scara kills him
  and flees back to the Frankish camp.

  conditions. He wants to deliver Ogier to Charlemagne, but
  Gerberga warns Ogier of her father’s plans and together they flee

leftColumn:
killed, while Ogier enters the Frankish camp and almost manag-
      es to slay Charlemagne in his tent.
        The Lombard Count Archibaldo and his men present
      themselves at Verona to serve Lord Adalgise. Their secret mis-
      sion is to betray the city into the hands of the Franks. But Ogier
      kills the traitors and places their bodies on the battlements in
      order to make the Franks believe he received reinforcements.
        Ogier and his few remaining men are hungry. One night,
      Ogier sneaks out of his castle and enters the Frankish camp,
      where he attempts to assassinate Charlemagne, but without suc-
      cess. He has to flee across the Alps to Bavaria, where he plans to
      live as an exile.
        At the capture of Verona, Carloman’s widow Gerberga and
      her two sons are taken prisoner. Charlemagne forbids plunder-
      ing and offers reconciliation to the enemy noblemen, but all
      Lombards must shave their beards in sign of submission. This
      merciful and forgiving behavior inspires respect. As trophies, the
      new king takes only books and relics. [→774]
        Winter Court (Rome): Charlemagne and Turpin visit the
      holy city as pilgrims and celebrate Christmas in the company of
      the Pope.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 774
        May Field (Pavia).
        Lombardy: Many Lombards desert their king. After nine-
      teen months of siege, Pavia finally surrenders. Charlemagne
      is crowned King of the Lombards. Desiderius is sent to the
      monastery of Corbie (where he dies some years later). Many
      loyal Lombards flee to Bavaria and Prince Adalgise escapes to
      Constantinople, where he is made a patrician and takes on the
      Greek name Theodotis.
        Charlemagne grants important Lombard domains and
      abbeys to his most loyal vassals. He ratifies the Donation of
      Constantine, by which the Papal States officially become an
      independent territory.
        Queen Hildegard’s baby dies while the king and his wife
      travel back across the Alps.
        Rauph the Coilyear: In Provence, King Charlemagne gets
      separated from his entourage by a storm. He is sheltered by a
      crusty collier, Ralph, who treats him roughly. Charlemagne
      claims to be the queen’s servant and invites Ralph to come and
      sell some charcoal at court.
        Once the king is safe at home, he sends Roland to meet
      Ralph on the road. Ralph refuses to go with Roland, because he
      wants to see his friend (Charlemagne). Roland mocks him, and
      Ralph responds by demanding a duel.
        At court, Ralph is astonished when he sees that the guest
      he manhandled is none other than the Frankish king. The peers
      suggest hanging Ralph for his impudence, but the clement king
      dubs him instead. The new knight wants to duel with Roland,
      but instead becomes embroiled in a combat with a Saracen on

      a camel.

Jehan de Lanson: Charlemagne appoints Roland to carry
  a message to the Visigothic Count Jehan of Lanson, who holds
  Marseille without having done homage to the king. As soon as
  Roland and his companions arrive before Lanson Castle, they
  are attacked by a small army. Roland leads his troops in retreat to
  a tower on a bridge which spans the Huveaune river.
     Jehan makes peace and invites the peers into his castle,
  but the next day he sets an ambush in a nearby hunting forest.
  Viscount Isoré of Marseille betrays his lord’s sinister plot and
  warns Roland. The peers once again take refuge in the tower. In
  a little skirmish, Jehan captures Isoré, while Roland takes Jehan’s
  nephew Alori. The good sorcerer-knight Basin frees Isoré, while
  Alori is hanged.
     Jehan then hires the services of a sorcerer named Malaquin,
  but Basin kills his rival in a magic judicial duel. Nevertheless,
  Jehan continues the siege.
     The paladins send Basin to Charlemagne to ask for help.
  When the king is about to leave, some pilgrims arrive with a
  forged letter pretending that the paladins have already defeated
  Jehan and that royal assistance is no longer needed. Suspecting
  the letter to be false, Naymo orders the pilgrims (all Jehan’s rela-
  tives) to be imprisoned. Charlemagne leaves for Lanson Castle.
     Jehan plans to ambush the king, but his vassal, Berart,
  reports it to Charlemagne. The ambush fails and Jehan flees
  into his castle, to which the king lays siege. Unfortunately,
  Charlemagne is captured by Jehan while out hunting. Basin, in
  disguise, enters Lanson Castle and liberates the king. Jehan is
                                 n
  thrown into a dungeon and his fief is given to the loyal Isoré.
     Saxony: The Saxons once more plunder Hesse, but when
  they want to burn down the church of Fritzlar they are chased
  away by two white angels who protect the relics of St. Boniface.
  The scarae retaliate without mercy and build a second strong-
  hold at Paderborn.
     Chevalerie Ogier: [←773] While sleeping in the Black
  Forest of Bavaria, Ogier is surprised and captured by Duke
  Naymo and brought to Charlemagne’s court in Paris. The king
  wants to hang the Dane at Montfaucon for high treason, but the
  paladins ask the king to forgive Ogier. The king agrees to send the
  Dane to the prison of Boulogne, under the care of Archbishop
  Turpin. Charlemagne orders that Ogier be treated harshly, but
  the archbishop secretly brings his prisoner abundant food and
  drink. The king forbids the name of Ogier to be pronounced at
  court. In a few years, many believe the Dane to be dead. [→780]
     Winter Court (Paris): King Charlemagne swears “to
  overwhelm in war the infidel and faithless Saxon people and to
  continue until they either have been defeated and subjugated to
  Christianity, or are completely annihilated.”
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 775
     May Field (Düren).
     Saxony: The king sends an army of scarae into Saxony. They
  launch a successful attack against the Saxon leader, Widukind,

        The Lombard Count Archibaldo and his men present
      themselves at Verona to serve Lord Adalgise. Their secret mis-
      sion is to betray the city into the hands of the Franks. But Ogier
      kills the traitors and places their bodies on the battlements in
      order to make the Franks believe he received reinforcements.
        Ogier and his few remaining men are hungry. One night,
      Ogier sneaks out of his castle and enters the Frankish camp,
      where he attempts to assassinate Charlemagne, but without suc-
      cess. He has to flee across the Alps to Bavaria, where he plans to
      live as an exile.
        At the capture of Verona, Carloman’s widow Gerberga and
      her two sons are taken prisoner. Charlemagne forbids plunder-
      ing and offers reconciliation to the enemy noblemen, but all
      Lombards must shave their beards in sign of submission. This
      merciful and forgiving behavior inspires respect. As trophies, the
      new king takes only books and relics. [→774]
        Winter Court (Rome): Charlemagne and Turpin visit the
      holy city as pilgrims and celebrate Christmas in the company of
      the Pope.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 774
        May Field (Pavia).
        Lombardy: Many Lombards desert their king. After nine-
      teen months of siege, Pavia finally surrenders. Charlemagne
      is crowned King of the Lombards. Desiderius is sent to the
      monastery of Corbie (where he dies some years later). Many
      loyal Lombards flee to Bavaria and Prince Adalgise escapes to
      Constantinople, where he is made a patrician and takes on the
      Greek name Theodotis.
        Charlemagne grants important Lombard domains and
      abbeys to his most loyal vassals. He ratifies the Donation of
      Constantine, by which the Papal States officially become an
      independent territory.
        Queen Hildegard’s baby dies while the king and his wife
      travel back across the Alps.
        Rauph the Coilyear: In Provence, King Charlemagne gets
      separated from his entourage by a storm. He is sheltered by a
      crusty collier, Ralph, who treats him roughly. Charlemagne
      claims to be the queen’s servant and invites Ralph to come and
      sell some charcoal at court.
        Once the king is safe at home, he sends Roland to meet
      Ralph on the road. Ralph refuses to go with Roland, because he
      wants to see his friend (Charlemagne). Roland mocks him, and
      Ralph responds by demanding a duel.
        At court, Ralph is astonished when he sees that the guest
      he manhandled is none other than the Frankish king. The peers
      suggest hanging Ralph for his impudence, but the clement king
      dubs him instead. The new knight wants to duel with Roland,
      but instead becomes embroiled in a combat with a Saracen on

      a camel.

Jehan de Lanson: Charlemagne appoints Roland to carry
  a message to the Visigothic Count Jehan of Lanson, who holds
  Marseille without having done homage to the king. As soon as
  Roland and his companions arrive before Lanson Castle, they
  are attacked by a small army. Roland leads his troops in retreat to
  a tower on a bridge which spans the Huveaune river.
     Jehan makes peace and invites the peers into his castle,
  but the next day he sets an ambush in a nearby hunting forest.
  Viscount Isoré of Marseille betrays his lord’s sinister plot and
  warns Roland. The peers once again take refuge in the tower. In
  a little skirmish, Jehan captures Isoré, while Roland takes Jehan’s
  nephew Alori. The good sorcerer-knight Basin frees Isoré, while
  Alori is hanged.
     Jehan then hires the services of a sorcerer named Malaquin,
  but Basin kills his rival in a magic judicial duel. Nevertheless,
  Jehan continues the siege.
     The paladins send Basin to Charlemagne to ask for help.
  When the king is about to leave, some pilgrims arrive with a
  forged letter pretending that the paladins have already defeated
  Jehan and that royal assistance is no longer needed. Suspecting
  the letter to be false, Naymo orders the pilgrims (all Jehan’s rela-
  tives) to be imprisoned. Charlemagne leaves for Lanson Castle.
     Jehan plans to ambush the king, but his vassal, Berart,
  reports it to Charlemagne. The ambush fails and Jehan flees
  into his castle, to which the king lays siege. Unfortunately,
  Charlemagne is captured by Jehan while out hunting. Basin, in
  disguise, enters Lanson Castle and liberates the king. Jehan is
                                 n
  thrown into a dungeon and his fief is given to the loyal Isoré.
     Saxony: The Saxons once more plunder Hesse, but when
  they want to burn down the church of Fritzlar they are chased
  away by two white angels who protect the relics of St. Boniface.
  The scarae retaliate without mercy and build a second strong-
  hold at Paderborn.
     Chevalerie Ogier: [←773] While sleeping in the Black
  Forest of Bavaria, Ogier is surprised and captured by Duke
  Naymo and brought to Charlemagne’s court in Paris. The king
  wants to hang the Dane at Montfaucon for high treason, but the
  paladins ask the king to forgive Ogier. The king agrees to send the
  Dane to the prison of Boulogne, under the care of Archbishop
  Turpin. Charlemagne orders that Ogier be treated harshly, but
  the archbishop secretly brings his prisoner abundant food and
  drink. The king forbids the name of Ogier to be pronounced at
  court. In a few years, many believe the Dane to be dead. [→780]

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
taking many hostages and much booty. Many Saxons convert,
      but Widukind escapes to Godfrid of Denmark’s court.
        Lion de Bourges: [←770] Lion helps the king to capture the
      treacherous Gombaut, who has killed Herpin and the Emir of
      Toledo. Lion kills the Saracen enchanter in a duel. [→776]
        Orlando Innamorato, Orlando Furioso: These two stories
      are so complex and tightly interwoven that we’ll simply follow
      the stories of the main characters.
        Angelica: In honor of his foreign visitors, Charlemagne or-
      ganizes a grand tournament. The event is disturbed by the arrival
      of an exotic knight, Argalia, and an extremely beautiful princess,
      Angelica. The mysterious knight challenges all paladins. With
      his magic golden lance he unhorses Astolf and Ferrau but then
      flees into the Ardennes Forest, luring the paladins away from the
      king’s court. Renaud and Roland pursue him, while Astolf picks
      up the golden lance.
        By means of his magic, Maugis discovers the true identi-
      ty and intentions of the visitors. He tries to capture Angelica
      at night, but he is taken prisoner himself and forced to betray
      Renaud into Angelica’s hands. Having drunk from the Fountain
      of Hate, Renaud stubbornly refuses the lady’s advances.
        Zerbin and Isabella: At the tournament of Bayonne, the
      Scottish prince, Zerbin, captures the heart of the Moorish prin-
      cess Isabella, who wishes to convert and marry the valorous Scot.
      Isabella’s father refuses, so Zerbin orders his vassal Oderic to ab-
      duct his lover. However, instead of taking her to Scotland, the
      traitor sells the princess to Moorish slave traders who lock her
      up in a cavern in a forest near the Pyrenees. Fortunately, Roland
      finds her and kills the slavers.
        Isabella and Roland head for Bordeaux, when they meet
      a band of knights from Mayence, led by Anselm, who holds
      Zerbin captive. Anselm claims Zerbin treacherously slew his
      son, Pinabel. Roland charges the knights from Mayence and lib-
      erates Zerbin. To thank the paladin, the Scottish prince follows
      him to the Frankish army.
        Medoro: Khagan Gradasso invades France, wishing to cap-
      ture both Bayard and Durendal. He meets the Franks in the
      battle of Orleans, but is unhorsed by Astolf in a single combat.
      During the battle Renaud kills the courteous Moorish Prince
      Dardinel.
        At night, two of Dardinel’s vassal knights, Cloridan and
      Medoro, enter the Frankish camp in search for their lord’s dead
      body. They are discovered and kill a few guards when Zerbin
      spots them. The Scot kills Cloridan and wounds Medoro.
      Angelica heals the young Medoro, with whom she falls in love.
      She gives him Roland’s golden bracelet as a wedding gift and
      takes him to Cathay.
        Several knights are sent to find Roland, who has traveled
      to the East in pursuit of Angelica. All of them participate in the
      siege of Albracca and the adventure of the Gardens of Fortune.
        Byzantium: Emperor Constantine V is killed while on
      campaign against the Bulgars.
rightColumn:
Les Narbonnais: [←754, Aymeri de Narbonne] Charlemagne
  sends for Aymeri to bring his sons to court to be knighted.
  Before leaving, Aymeri promises Narbonne to his youngest son,
  Gilbert, and puts Lady Ermengard in command over the city.
  Once knighted, Bernard marries the daughter of the Duke of
  Brabant. Bevis (wielding the sword Griebe) and Ernold go to the
  court of Yon of Gascony; Garin serves in Lombardy, William
  (who receives a protective talisman from his mother) enters
  Charlemagne’s court, and Aimer promises not to rest until all of
  Spain has been reconquered from the Moors. [→776]
     Winter Court (Paris).
     Harvests: Good; Stewardship +5.
  aNNo 776
     May Field (Nijmegen).
     Saxony: Saxons murder the “traitors” who accepted the
  Frankish religion. They abandon their hostages, break their
  sworn oaths and attack Frankish settlements. The Franks re-
  sist valiantly and witness a protective miracle at Fritzlar: “They
  saw the likeness of two shields, red in color and flaming and
  moving to and fro over the church. Struck by great terror, the
  Saxons began to flee.”
     Charlemagne sends an army into Saxony. Widukind once
  more flees to the court of King Godfrid of Denmark, but some
  other Saxon leaders are captured and surrender to the Franks at
  the source of the Lippe. They are baptized and their lands given
  to Franks, who build strongholds to secure the borders.
     Ado becomes the Archbishop of Saxony.
     Italy: Adalgise returns to Italy from his exile in
  Constantinople to support the revolt of the Dukes Rodgaud of
  Friuli, Arichis of Benevento, and Hildebrand of Spoleto, allied
  to the Byzantines of southern Italy. The Frankish army crush-
  es the rebellion in Friuli. Rodgaud is killed by his own men
  somewhere in the mountains. Many traitors are exiled or hung,
  though some escape to Bavaria or even Avarland. Charlemagne
  confiscates many estates and gives them to Frankish nobles. He
  stops the Lombard trade of Christian slaves to the lands of the
  Saracens.
     Lion de Bourges: [←775] Lion takes leave of the king and
  travels to Sicily in order to take the sub-kingdom back from
  Garnier. At Sicily, Lion restores the peace. He reconquers the
  entire island, then attacks Calabria, where Garnier is hiding at
  the castle of Monrochier, together with his sister Clarissa (the
  mother of Lion’s bastard child Gerard) and her husband Walter.
  However, when Gerard learns about his father, he joins his fa-
  ther’s side and helps him in the siege of Reggio. [→779]
     Les Narbonnais: [←775] A Saracen spy informs Lord
  Tiebaut of the defenseless position of Narbonne. The Moors
  sail to Septimania to besiege the city. During a Frankish sortie,
  they capture young Gilbert, nail him to a cross and show him
  to his mother.
     On his way to Narbonne, Aymeri meets a band of Saracens
  who have been to Orange to ask Orable’s hand for their lord,

title: Phase 1: Unification
leftColumn:
Tiebaut. In the ensuing fight Aymeri is captured, but rescued
      by his son, William, who takes Baucent, the horse Orable is
      sending as a gift to Tiebaut. William falls in love with Orable,
      to whom he sends a sparrow-hawk and a promise to marry her
      after killing Tiebaut.
        Aymeri returns to his city, defeats the Moors, destroys their
      idols, and liberates his sorely wounded son.
        Back in Orange, Tiebaut marries Orable. In their bed-
      room, the princess gives her husband several frightening vi-
      sions and she puts a magical enchantment on him to keep her
      virginity. The next morning, Tiebaut returns to the siege of
      Narbonne.
        Aymeri and his sons arrive in Paris, where William takes on
      a fierce Breton champion who challenged the court. William
      and his brothers are knighted. A messenger informs the king of
      the siege of Narbonne.
        Aymeri and his sons immediately return to their city, where
      William once more recues his captured father and wounds
      Tiebaut. [→781, Le Couronnement de Louis]
        Orlando Innamorato, Orlando Furioso [←775]
        Roland: Roland dresses in black armor as a sign of his
      mourning over Angelica. He is challenged by Mandricard, who
      wishes to take Durendal and avenge the death of his father,
      Agrican. The fight is interrupted and Roland wanders into the
      forest alone. Here he finds a shepherd who lodged Angelica
      and Medoro, who gave the shepherd the golden bracelet.
      When Roland hears how Angelica married the young Moor,
      his passion drives him mad. He strips off his armor, hangs
      Durendal on a tree and spends the next year as a half-naked
      wild man in the forest.
        Zerbin and Isabella: Zerbin goes to look for Roland and
      finds his horse, sword, and armor, which he leaves hanging in a
      tree. Mandricard kills Zerbin in a duel and captures Durendal.
      When Isabella finds the body of her husband, she almost takes
      her own life. A monk comforts her and convinces her to escort
      him and Zerbin’s body to a monastery where Isabella can retire.
      On the way, the Saracen Rodomonte of Algiers kills the monk
      and forces Isabella to become his future bride. Isabella, howev-
      er, tells him she can make a potion of invulnerability, which she

  hold, but the treacherous Pinabel tries to murder his com-

  stumbles upon Merlin’s Tomb, where she receives the aid of the
  faerie Melissa, who tells her about Brunello’s magic ring and
  Atlante’s hippogriff and blinding shield. First Bradamant cap-

  pretends to be blinded by his shield. But when he wants to take
  her to his castle, she subdues him and forces the enchanter to
  liberate Rogero.

  then he flies off on the hippogriff. He first visits an enchanted
  island where the evil faerie Alcina holds many knights prisoner
  in her castle. She captures Rogero, who spends some months in
  happy idleness. He is saved by Melissa, and finds Angelica’s ring
  and Atlante’s shield.
     Next Rogero ends up in Ireland, where he finds Angelica
  chained to a rock as a living sacrifice to a sea monster. He kills the
  horrendous beast and frees the princess from Cathay, but instead

  cousin, Bradamant.

leftColumn:
a plague of harpies by using the horn of terror (which loses its
      power in the process). Astolf continues to the top of the moun-
      tains where the Nile has its source. He arrives at the terrestrial
      paradise, where he meets some saints who fly him to the moon,
      where he finds a flask containing Roland’s lost wits, a plant to
      restore Sepanus’ sight, and a bag in which the winds can be held.
        Duels at Biserta: Astolf sets the hippogriff free. He then
      leads an army of Christian knights from Senapus’ court to
      Biserta. The Saracens retreat to defend their famous stronghold
      and offer to settle the war by a duel. On the island of Lampedusa,
      Rogero (who still hasn’t had time to convert) fights Renaud.
      Melissa incites the Saracens to break the agreement and attack
      while the two champions are still fighting. Seeing this act of trea-
      son, Rogero refuses to continue his duel with Renaud.
        Roland swims across the sea and arrives at the Frankish
      camp, where he is seized by four paladins. Astolf administers the
      flask containing his wits, and Roland recovers his sanity and no
      longer yearns for Angelica. The Saracens and the Franks agree to

a threefold duel, pitting Roland, Oliver and Brandimart against
  Agramant (on Veillantif), Gradasso (wielding Durendal) and
  Sobrino. In a terrible fight Brandimart is slain by Gradasso, but
  Roland kills Gradasso and Agramant, bringing the Franks victo-
  ry. Rogero and Sobrino are baptized. Having retrieved Durendal,
  Roland gives the sword Balisard to Rogero.
     Winter Court (Herstal): Isembart, son of Warin, saves
  Charlemagne’s life during a dangerous boar hunt in the Ardennes
  Forest.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 777
     May Field (Paderborn): Several Saxon chiefs give hostages
  and are baptized.
     An embassy of Moorish rebels, headed by Ibn-al-Arabi (the
  Wali of Saragossa and a partisan of the Persian caliph), comes
  to ask Charlemagne’s aid in his resistance against the emir of
  Cordoba.
            Italy: The Franks invades Benevento and
         conquer the duchy of Spoleto.
            Rogero and Bradamant: Bradamant’s par-
         ents agree to marry her to the Byzantine Prince
         Leo. Rogero travels to Byzantium in order to defy
         Leo, whom he meets at the siege of the Bulgarian
         capital. With Rogero’s aid the Bulgars push back
         the Byzantine army, but the paladin is betrayed
         into the hands of the Byzantines and imprisoned.
            Bradamant opposes her parents’ will and
         demands that a wedding tournament be held in
         which all contenders must fight the warrior maid-
         en herself in a duel for conquest.
            Leo liberates Rogero, not knowing who he
         is, and in return Rogero vows to assist the prince
         in his next adventure. When news reaches the
         Byzantines of Bradamant’s wedding tournament,
         Leo requires Rogero to win Bradamant for him.
         Rogero, wearing a Byzantine shield and armor,
         presents himself at Montalban to fight Bradamant,
         who cannot defeat him despite her best efforts.
         She is therefore given as a bride to Leo. This turn
         of events plunges Rogero into the deepest despair.
            Marfisa arrives, wishing to defend the rights
         of her brother, who had already received the con-
         sent to marry Bradamant from the maiden herself.
         Prince Leo is surprised to find out about Rogero
         and Bradamant’s love, and when Rogero finally re-
         veals his identity, the courteous Byzantine prince
         grants Rogero the hand of Bradamant, which he
         had himself won by right of arms. Rogero and
         Bradamant finally marry.
            An embassy from Bulgaria arrives and pres-
         ent Rogero the crown. King Rogero and Queen
         Bradamant travel to their kingdom. Prince Leo nat-
         urally offers peace with his neighbors. [→784]
