      their heads back to Frankland.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 778
        May Field (Poitiers).

        Song of Roland, Pseudo-Turpin: Blancandrin, Emir
      Marsile’s councilor, is sent to the Frankish court to negotiate
      a peace treaty. Roland is opposed to this peace, and names his
      stepfather Ganelon as ambassador to Marsile. Ganelon curses
      Roland and together with Blancandrin, who accompanies him
      to Spain, he conceives a plan to get rid of Roland.
        King Charlemagne enters Spain with a mighty army, in-
      cluding troops from all regions, even Bavaria. As the grandson
      of Floris of Asturias he claims the throne of Spain. He wishes to
      avenge the deaths of Basan and Basile, and to pacify the import-
      ant southern trade routes.
        Charlemagne takes Pamplona after a miracle: God lets the
      city walls crumble to dust. He then lays siege to Saragossa (the
      formerly-allied wali has been deposed by Marsile). The Moors
      send horses, silver and gold as a peace tribute.
        When Charlemagne hears the Saxons are raiding
      Westphalia and Hesse (again), he withdraws. He leads his army
      back to Frankland. On Ganelon’s advice, Roland is put in charge
      of the rear-guard.
        With the help of the treacherous Basques, the Moors am-
      bush the baggage and rear-guard in the Roncevaux Pass. At first,
      Roland refuses to blow his horn, Oliphant, but later he chang-
      es his mind. Charlemagne hears Roland’s horn-call and hastens
      back to aid his rear-guard. When he arrives, Emir Marsile has
      already plundered the baggage and his army has melted away
      into the dark mountains, leaving the battlefield covered with the
      bodies of the dead Franks. The entire Frankish force is slain, in-
      cluding Turpin, Roland, Oliver and other paladins.
        To allow Charlemagne to pursue the Saracens, God stops
      the course of the sun. The king catches up with the enemy and
      the Moors are all put to the sword or driven into the River Ebro.
      Then a second Saracen army attacks, led by Sultan Baligant of
      Babylon. With Saint Gabriel’s help, Charlemagne kills Baligant
      in battle and the Franks finally prevail. At the sight of his utter
      defeat, Emir Marsile almost dies of grief.
        Back at Aachen, Count Ganelon is accused of treason. In
      a judicial duel, Thierry of Anjou defeats Ganelon’s champion,
      Pinabel. Ganelon is quartered and his 30 hostages are hanged.
      The Moorish Queen Bramimonde, who was taken prisoner,
      willingly converts. She is baptized Juliana and comes to live at
      Charlemagne’s court.
        Aude la Belle dies of grief after hearing the news of Count
      Roland’s death.

      Byzantine-Lombard alliance, led by the Duke of Naples, invades
      the Papal States. They are defeated by the Pope’s army.

  Customs

  F
      eudalism: Charlemagne confiscates Church lands and
      manors and grants them to his vassals, who pay an annual
      compensation to the previous owner. At the same time he
  grants more and more immunities to abbeys.
     Fiefs become inheritable by right and not just by custom,
  as previously.
     All conquered lands in pagan territories such as Spain,
  Saxony, and Slavonia are granted as allods to their respective
  conquerors.
     Truce of God: Within Frankland, many knights respect
  the peaceful precepts of the Church. Across the borders, the ne-
  cessities of war prevail.
     Bishops and priests are now officially no longer allowed to
  wield arms and shed blood.
     Knighthood: The civilizing influence of knighthood now
  permeates Frisia and Saxony. Only the Slavs, the Danes and the
  Huns hold on to their barbarian warrior traditions.
     Heraldry: A knight’s arms can no longer be borne by any-
  one other than the knight or his immediate family. Commoners,
  such as sergeants, are no longer allowed to carry shields with
  their lord’s coat of arms.
     Tournaments: The sport of chivalry gets more refined.
  Tournaments now often include a jousting competition and a
  grand melee, instead of animal fights and the bohort. Paladins
  are no longer allowed to compete in tournaments, except in the
  regal tournaments at the annual Pentecost court.
     Women: Marriage has now become a religious ritual led
  by the priests. Following in the steps of Dame Bradamant, it
  becomes possible for women to become knights, even if female
  knights remain highly exceptional.

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Chivalry: The code of chivalry is now generally accepted
      not only at court, but in all of Frankland and the British Isles.
        Romance: Romance has previously been a court whimsy,
      but now it gets serious. Many young knights and ladies are tak-
      ing full advantage. Queen Fastrada regularly organizes official
      courts of love during which noble ladies discuss their romantic
      lovers. Abroad, foreign ladies and princesses are becoming very
      interested in the romantic courting of elegant Frankish knights.
        Fashion: The clothing of the nobles gets more extravagant.
      The cotte is shorter, with the sleeves buttoned from cuff to el-
      bow. A short cape and pointed shoes are common.
        For women the cotte is tighter, with a belt worn on the hips.
      Shoes are pointed. Hair dressings more elaborate, perhaps coiled
      on both sides of the head, or held in a jeweled net or with a long
      curl. Circlets are popular.
      Warfare

        Armor: The standard armor is a reinforced chain mail hau-
      berk and chausses (leggings) with a closed helmet (12 points).
        Weapons: New weapons are the war flail, the two-handed
      mace (or morning star) and the two-handed sword. The light
      crossbow is now common, while the medium crossbow comes
      into use half-way through the phase in Lombardy and spreads
      throughout Europe. The weapon is almost entirely used by city
      militia. The crossbow is condemned by the Church as unknight-
      ly and its use against Christians warrants excommunication.
        Horses: Andalusian chargers may be captured in battle
      against the Saracens.
        Some knights protect their horse with a cuirbouilli barding
      (6 points).
        Castles: Square stone keeps with outer works are now stan-
      dard for counts, and even many rich knights have built one on
      their domain. Chimneys greatly improve the standard of life in-
      side manors and castles.
        Levy Troops: Lombard city levies with crossbowmen are
      regularly hired by Frankish lords.
      aNNo 779
        May Field (Düren).
        Saxony: After a victorious battle against the Saxons at
      Detmold, Charlemagne divides the conquered territory among
      bishops, priests and abbots, so that they can baptize and preach.
        Brittany: The new Count of the Breton March, Wido, in-
      vades and ravages Brittany.
        British Isles: In Mercia, Offa defeats Cynewulf of Wessex
      and builds his famous Dyke.
        Spain: King Charlemagne concludes a 10 year truce with
      the Moors. Emir Marsile may keep his title, but he rules under
      the supervision of a Frankish duke, Anseïs of Carthago.
        Anseïs de Carthage: Charlemagne must name a vassal as
      Duke of the newly-created Spanish March. His councilors pro-
      pose the young knight Anseïs, son of the fallen Ripay of Brittany,
rightColumn:
assisted by the experienced Isoré. Charlemagne gives Anseïs one
  of his own swords along with the duchy.
     The new duke installs himself at Moriglane. Soon, Isoré’s
  daughter, Letise, falls hopelessly in love with him, but her father
  is opposed to their union, deeming his daughter unworthy of a
  duke. On the advice of his men, Anseïs decides to ask for the
  hand of Marsile’s beautiful daughter, Gaudissa.
     Anseïs sends Isoré and Raymond of Navarra to the castle
  of Morinda in Cordoba, where the princess lives. Her father
  Marsile agrees to wed his daughter to Anseïs. The problem is that
  Gaudissa had already been promised to a Saracen knight, Agolant
  the Savage, who presents himself at Marsile’s court. Furious, he
  demands a duel with Anseïs’ representative, Raymond. The
  Frankish knight is victorious, so Princess Gaudissa is allowed to
  accompany Isoré and Raymond back to Spain.
     During her father’s absence, Letise managed to slip into
  Anseïs’ bed. When her father hears the news, he is convinced
  that the young duke raped his daughter, so he swears to avenge
  himself on Anseïs. He returns to Morinda, abjures the Christian
  faith and exhorts Emir Marsile to once more take up arms
  against the Franks. Marsile agrees and puts the renegade knight
  in command of his troops. The emir and Isoré sail to Spain and
  rout Anseïs’ army, forcing the young duke to flee despite the help
  of Oliver and the White Knight.
     The beautiful Gaudissa, however, has fallen madly in love
  with her betrothed and sends him a secret message. With her help,
  Anseïs rescues her and takes her back with him to Moriglane,
  where she embraces Christianity and becomes his wife.
     Still, the war isn’t going well for Duke Anseïs, who is obliged
  to call on Charlemagne for help. The king and several paladins
  cross the Pyrenees, and with their support the young duke finally
  manages to chase the Moors from his territory. Emir Marsile, the
  renegade Isoré, and his daughter Letise, are captured and taken back
  to Charlemagne’s court to be tried. Marsile refuses baptism and is
                                n
  beheaded. Isoré is hanged, while his daughter becomes a nun.
     Lion de Bourges: [←776] During a tournament, Lion’s son,
  Oliver, falls in love with a lady named Alexandrine. His fos-
  ter-parents admit not being his true parents, so Oliver travels to
  Spain to look for them. With the help of the White Knight, he
  helps Duke Anseïs resist the Moors. [→780]
     Spain: Hisham, known as Marsile II, succeeds his father as
  Emir of Cordoba.

  and Amaugin, accuse Garnier of treason. In a judicial duel Garnier
  defeats Auboin, who is hanged. But while Garnier is in Spain with
  the King to help Anseïs of Carthago, Amaugin and his cousin
  Samson abduct Aye. Garnier’s nephews Fouquerant and Renier
  try to stop them, but they are besieged in Avignon by Berenger
  and Amaugin, who finally take Aye to the castle of Grailmont.

  teous Ganor, learns that Berenger and Samson are Ganelon’s

      courts of love during which noble ladies discuss their romantic
      lovers. Abroad, foreign ladies and princesses are becoming very
      interested in the romantic courting of elegant Frankish knights.
        Fashion: The clothing of the nobles gets more extravagant.
      The cotte is shorter, with the sleeves buttoned from cuff to el-
      bow. A short cape and pointed shoes are common.
        For women the cotte is tighter, with a belt worn on the hips.
      Shoes are pointed. Hair dressings more elaborate, perhaps coiled
      on both sides of the head, or held in a jeweled net or with a long
      curl. Circlets are popular.
      Warfare

Armor: The standard armor is a reinforced chain mail hau-
      berk and chausses (leggings) with a closed helmet (12 points).
        Weapons: New weapons are the war flail, the two-handed
      mace (or morning star) and the two-handed sword. The light
      crossbow is now common, while the medium crossbow comes
      into use half-way through the phase in Lombardy and spreads
      throughout Europe. The weapon is almost entirely used by city
      militia. The crossbow is condemned by the Church as unknight-
      ly and its use against Christians warrants excommunication.
        Horses: Andalusian chargers may be captured in battle
      against the Saracens.
        Some knights protect their horse with a cuirbouilli barding
      (6 points).
        Castles: Square stone keeps with outer works are now stan-
      dard for counts, and even many rich knights have built one on
      their domain. Chimneys greatly improve the standard of life in-
      side manors and castles.
        Levy Troops: Lombard city levies with crossbowmen are
      regularly hired by Frankish lords.
      aNNo 779
        May Field (Düren).
        Saxony: After a victorious battle against the Saxons at
      Detmold, Charlemagne divides the conquered territory among
      bishops, priests and abbots, so that they can baptize and preach.
        Brittany: The new Count of the Breton March, Wido, in-
      vades and ravages Brittany.
        British Isles: In Mercia, Offa defeats Cynewulf of Wessex
      and builds his famous Dyke.
        Spain: King Charlemagne concludes a 10 year truce with
      the Moors. Emir Marsile may keep his title, but he rules under
      the supervision of a Frankish duke, Anseïs of Carthago.
        Anseïs de Carthage: Charlemagne must name a vassal as
      Duke of the newly-created Spanish March. His councilors pro-
      pose the young knight Anseïs, son of the fallen Ripay of Brittany,

assisted by the experienced Isoré. Charlemagne gives Anseïs one
  of his own swords along with the duchy.
     The new duke installs himself at Moriglane. Soon, Isoré’s
  daughter, Letise, falls hopelessly in love with him, but her father
  is opposed to their union, deeming his daughter unworthy of a
  duke. On the advice of his men, Anseïs decides to ask for the
  hand of Marsile’s beautiful daughter, Gaudissa.
     Anseïs sends Isoré and Raymond of Navarra to the castle
  of Morinda in Cordoba, where the princess lives. Her father
  Marsile agrees to wed his daughter to Anseïs. The problem is that
  Gaudissa had already been promised to a Saracen knight, Agolant
  the Savage, who presents himself at Marsile’s court. Furious, he
  demands a duel with Anseïs’ representative, Raymond. The
  Frankish knight is victorious, so Princess Gaudissa is allowed to
  accompany Isoré and Raymond back to Spain.
     During her father’s absence, Letise managed to slip into
  Anseïs’ bed. When her father hears the news, he is convinced
  that the young duke raped his daughter, so he swears to avenge
  himself on Anseïs. He returns to Morinda, abjures the Christian
  faith and exhorts Emir Marsile to once more take up arms
  against the Franks. Marsile agrees and puts the renegade knight
  in command of his troops. The emir and Isoré sail to Spain and
  rout Anseïs’ army, forcing the young duke to flee despite the help
  of Oliver and the White Knight.
     The beautiful Gaudissa, however, has fallen madly in love
  with her betrothed and sends him a secret message. With her help,
  Anseïs rescues her and takes her back with him to Moriglane,
  where she embraces Christianity and becomes his wife.
     Still, the war isn’t going well for Duke Anseïs, who is obliged
  to call on Charlemagne for help. The king and several paladins
  cross the Pyrenees, and with their support the young duke finally
  manages to chase the Moors from his territory. Emir Marsile, the
  renegade Isoré, and his daughter Letise, are captured and taken back
  to Charlemagne’s court to be tried. Marsile refuses baptism and is
                                n
  beheaded. Isoré is hanged, while his daughter becomes a nun.
     Lion de Bourges: [←776] During a tournament, Lion’s son,
  Oliver, falls in love with a lady named Alexandrine. His fos-
  ter-parents admit not being his true parents, so Oliver travels to
  Spain to look for them. With the help of the White Knight, he
  helps Duke Anseïs resist the Moors. [→780]
     Spain: Hisham, known as Marsile II, succeeds his father as
  Emir of Cordoba.
     Aye d’Avignon: [←764] Berenger’s relatives Milo, Auboin,
  and Amaugin, accuse Garnier of treason. In a judicial duel Garnier
  defeats Auboin, who is hanged. But while Garnier is in Spain with
  the King to help Anseïs of Carthago, Amaugin and his cousin
  Samson abduct Aye. Garnier’s nephews Fouquerant and Renier
  try to stop them, but they are besieged in Avignon by Berenger
  and Amaugin, who finally take Aye to the castle of Grailmont.
     Charlemagne returns from Spain and sends his troops to
  besiege Grailmont. Overtaken by fear, Berenger flees by boat
  to Aigremor, on the isle of Majorca. The local wali, the cour-
  teous Ganor, learns that Berenger and Samson are Ganelon’s
  sons, so he sends them to the emir’s court at Morinde, keeping

title: Phase 2: Expansion
leftColumn:
Aye for himself. At Morinde, Berenger marries the emir’s sister,
      Plumboie, and informs the emir of Aye’s presence at Aigremor.
      The emir orders Ganor to hand Aye over to him, but the wali
      refuses, for he intends to marry the girl himself. He puts her in
      the impregnable tower of Aufalerne. [→780]
        Winter Court (Worms): King Charlemagne officially
      confirms the creation of the missi dominici.
        Harvests: Very bad, famines break out in many regions.
      Stewardship –7.
      aNNo 780
        May Field (Eresburg).
        Saxony, Slavonia: King Charlemagne is determined to
      conquer, colonize and Christianize by the sword. He crosses the
      Elbe and makes first contact with the Slavs. The emphasis is on
      Christianization, so there is much church building and baptism
      in order to establish a missionary organization.
        Byzantium: Emperor Leo IV dies, Empress Irene rules in
      Byzantium in the name of her young son, Constantine VI.
        Religion: The Adoptionist heresy spreads in the Pyrenees.
        Lion de Bourges: [←779] Duke Anseïs of Carthago dies. His
      only daughter, Galienne, agrees to marry Oliver of Bourges. [→781]

        Chevalerie Ogier: [←774] An astrologer informs Bruhier,
      the new Sultan of Babylon, that only Ogier can kill him.
      Believing the Dane to be dead, the sultan raises his army to in-
      vade Frankland. He challenges Charlemagne’s court to a duel of
      himself against ten Franks.
        Carahue is captured by Christian knights, whom he won’t
      fight out of loyalty to Ogier. Meanwhile, a Saracen named
      Rubion accuses Carahue and Gloriande of treason. When the
      Saracens threaten to burn Gloriande, Charlemagne sets Carahue
      free so that he may fight Rubion in a duel. Carahue defeats his
      opponent, who admits his wrongs and is subsequently hanged.
        The unstoppable Sultan Bruhier raids Frankland heavily.
      Charlemagne wishes Roland and Oliver were still alive, because now
      there is no one left who can resist the Saracens. The remaining court
      knights do not dare to suggest that Charlemagne liberate Ogier, but
      Naymo has the clever idea of having children shout the Dane’s name
      at court. Charlemagne relents and orders Ogier brought to him, to
      act as his champion against Bruhier; but Ogier only agrees to the
      duel on the condition that he may first slay Prince Charlot. On his
      courtiers’ advice, Charlemagne grudgingly accepts.
        No horse is strong enough to carry Ogier, until Broiefort is
      brought back from a monastery, where he had been kept all these
      years in his masters’ absence. While Charlemagne is praying in
      a chapel, Ogier seizes Charlot and lifts his sword to cut off the
      prince’s head. At that very moment, an angel appears. It holds
      back Ogier’s arm and orders the Dane to forgive Charlemagne
      and to fight Bruhier in the name of the Christian faith. After
      this miracle, Ogier reconciles with a joyful Charlemagne.
        The next day, Ogier faces Bruhier in the field. The fight
      lasts a long time because the Saracen keeps healing his wounds
      with a magical balm. At one moment, Bruhier pretends to
rightColumn:
surrender and to accept baptism, but when Ogier realizes the
  trick, he cuts off Bruhier’s head. Broiefort is killed in the fight,
  and Ogier takes Bruhier’s horse, Baucent.
     Meanwhile, the Saracen pirate Justamon raids Mercia and
  captures Princess Clarice, heir to the throne. Ogier comes to her
  rescue and the Saracens flee. Ogier marries Clarice and is given
  the fiefs of Hainaut and Brabant. [→781]
     Aye d’Avignon: [←779] A pilgrim tells Garnier where Aye is
  held captive, so he leaves for Aigremor with his companions, all
  disguised. Even so, Aye recognizes Garnier when he passes near
  the tower of Aufalerne, and she throws him her wedding ring.
  Garnier and his men offer their services as mercenary knights to
  Ganor. In a small battle Garnier kills Berenger, who was fighting
  for the Moorish emir, and takes Samson and Amaugin prisoner.
     Ganor leaves on a pilgrimage to Persia. Garnier takes advan-
  tage of his lord’s absence to liberate all Frankish prisoners. He
  returns to Frankland and forgives Samson and Amaugin, who
  he weds to his sisters. Lady Aye gives birth to a boy, Guy. [→781]
     Italy: In the company of Queen Hildegard, Charlemagne
  crosses the Alps and attacks the rebellious Arichis of Benevento.
  In Parma, he meets the learned monk Alcuin, who becomes the
  king’s favorite councilor, creates the Palace Academy, and intro-
  duces the Caroline minuscule script.
     Winter Court (Pavia).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 781
     Le Couronnement de Louis: [← 776, Les Narbonnais]
  William attends the coronation of Prince Louis, future King of
  Aquitaine. The Pope celebrates a mass. Arneïs of Orleans wants
  to become the prince’s tutor, but William opposes this and kills
  Arneïs as a traitor. Charlemagne lets William crown his son and
  he becomes Prince Louis’ tutor until he comes of age.
     William goes on a pilgrimage to Rome. On his way, he has
  a dream in which the city is ravaged by fire. He hurries to Rome,
  only to see the city besieged by the Saracens. They have already
  captured Capua and have taken many prisoners: the duke, his
  wife, their beautiful daughter and many knights. The Pope cele-
  brates a mass for William and asks him to defend Rome by fight-
  ing the Saracen champion, a giant named Corsolt. In a tough
  duel, during which William loses the tip of his nose, he kills the
  pagan giant and captures the magnificent horse Alion.
     The pagans flee and William liberates the prisoners. As a
  reward, he receives the hand of Cunegonde, the Duke of Capua’s
  daughter. Just before the marriage takes place, William receives
  a call for help from young King Louis, so he dashes off back to
  Frankland. He learns that Louis is hiding in a church in Orleans,
  a city held by traitors: old Richard of Normandy and Acelin.
  William kills them and liberates young Louis.
     Back in Italy, William has no time to marry Cunegonde.
  He must come to the aid of the Pope once more, who is besieged
  by a rebel baron named Guy of Alemannia. William defeats the
  traitor and installs young Prince Pepin as regent of Italy. [→782,
  Enfances Vivien]

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
May Field (Rome): The Pope anoints Pepin as King of
      Italy under the tutelage of Charlemagne’s cousin, Adalhard.
        La chanson des Saisnes: [←750] Widukind plunders
      Cologne, kills Duke Milo and takes his daughter, Helissent,
      prisoner. He offers the girl as a servant to his new wife. [→782]
        Aye d’Avignon: [←780] Ganor returns home and finds out
      about Garnier’s treason. He travels to Avignon in disguise, ab-
      ducts little Guy and takes the boy to Aigremor. Before leaving,
      he sends a loving message to Aye. At Aigremor, Ganor raises Guy
      as if he were his own son.
        Back in Frankland, Samson and Amaugin convince
      Charlemagne that Garnier has illegally fortified his city of
      Nanteuil. The traitors besiege Avignon. Garnier once more cap-
      tures Samson and Amaugin, but liberates them to obtain the
      king’s goodwill. However, on his way to court, Garnier is am-
      bushed and killed by Milo. The king grants Garnier’s fief and his
      widow to Milo. Aye demands that the marriage be postponed for
      a year. [→795, Duchesse Parise]
        Lion de Bourges: [←780] Oliver goes back to Palermo to
      help his father. Meanwhile, Lion’s son, Gerard, has captured Duke
      Garnier and the city of Reggio. Lion finds Oliver thanks to his
      shield (a silver angel on a blue field) and for the first time the entire
      family is reunited. Gerard marries the heiress of Calabria, Oliver
      inherits Sicily and William receives Palermo and Bourges. [→785]
        Chevalerie Ogier: [←780] Sir Ogier is ambushed by Bernard
      II, the jealous son of the late Duke Bernard of Brabant. Ogier’s
      nephew, Walter, comes to his rescue and brings him to Denmark.
      At Charlemagne’s court, Bernard tells everyone that Ogier is dead
      and he claims Clarice and the Mercian throne for himself. Queen
      Clarice sends a message to Denmark to ask her husband for help.
        Giants attack Denmark. Ogier leads an army to succor his
      father, but King Godfrid is murdered by one of his own men.
      Ogier refuses the crown of Denmark in favor of his half-brother
      Hemming (his Frankish name is Guyon), whom he installs as the
      new king. He then returns to Charlemagne’s court, where both
      his sons serve as household knights, but an angel orders him
      to go to Byzantium and fight the invading Emir Justamon on
      Rhodes. Ogier heeds the divine message and sends Walter to his
      wife with his ring as a sign that he lives. While Ogier travels to
      Byzantium, Clarice quarrels with Charlemagne for her refusal to
      marry Duke Bernard. Walter brings Clarice the ring, challenges
      Bernard at court and defeats him in a duel. [→782]
        Italy: Charlemagne launches a successful attack against the
      rebellious Arichis of Benevento. The issue of the Donation of
      Constantine is now definitively settled: the pope receives in-

May Field (Rome): The Pope anoints Pepin as King of
      Italy under the tutelage of Charlemagne’s cousin, Adalhard.
        La chanson des Saisnes: [←750] Widukind plunders
      Cologne, kills Duke Milo and takes his daughter, Helissent,
      prisoner. He offers the girl as a servant to his new wife. [→782]
        Aye d’Avignon: [←780] Ganor returns home and finds out
      about Garnier’s treason. He travels to Avignon in disguise, ab-
      ducts little Guy and takes the boy to Aigremor. Before leaving,
      he sends a loving message to Aye. At Aigremor, Ganor raises Guy
      as if he were his own son.
        Back in Frankland, Samson and Amaugin convince
      Charlemagne that Garnier has illegally fortified his city of
      Nanteuil. The traitors besiege Avignon. Garnier once more cap-
      tures Samson and Amaugin, but liberates them to obtain the
      king’s goodwill. However, on his way to court, Garnier is am-
      bushed and killed by Milo. The king grants Garnier’s fief and his
      widow to Milo. Aye demands that the marriage be postponed for
      a year. [→795, Duchesse Parise]
        Lion de Bourges: [←780] Oliver goes back to Palermo to
      help his father. Meanwhile, Lion’s son, Gerard, has captured Duke
      Garnier and the city of Reggio. Lion finds Oliver thanks to his
      shield (a silver angel on a blue field) and for the first time the entire
      family is reunited. Gerard marries the heiress of Calabria, Oliver
      inherits Sicily and William receives Palermo and Bourges. [→785]

      II, the jealous son of the late Duke Bernard of Brabant. Ogier’s
      nephew, Walter, comes to his rescue and brings him to Denmark.
      At Charlemagne’s court, Bernard tells everyone that Ogier is dead
      and he claims Clarice and the Mercian throne for himself. Queen
      Clarice sends a message to Denmark to ask her husband for help.
        Giants attack Denmark. Ogier leads an army to succor his
      father, but King Godfrid is murdered by one of his own men.
      Ogier refuses the crown of Denmark in favor of his half-brother
      Hemming (his Frankish name is Guyon), whom he installs as the
      new king. He then returns to Charlemagne’s court, where both
      his sons serve as household knights, but an angel orders him
      to go to Byzantium and fight the invading Emir Justamon on
      Rhodes. Ogier heeds the divine message and sends Walter to his
      wife with his ring as a sign that he lives. While Ogier travels to
      Byzantium, Clarice quarrels with Charlemagne for her refusal to
      marry Duke Bernard. Walter brings Clarice the ring, challenges
      Bernard at court and defeats him in a duel. [→782]

title: Phase 2: Expansion
leftColumn:
Giant’s Rock. The ladies, servants and squires stay at the camp
      in the Ardennes. Charlemagne cannot cross the Rhine because
      Widukind guards the eastern bank. Both sides observe and in-
      sult each other while fortifying their camps.
        Lady Sebile sees young Baldwin, of whom Helissent has al-
      ready told her, and instantly falls in love with him. She suggests
      to her husband to put the lady’s tents near the river bank, in or-
      der to lure the Franks.
        One day, Lady Sebile spots Baldwin on the other side of the
      Rhine, and orders Helissent to ask him to come over. Charmed
      by Sebile’s gracious forms, Baldwin directs his horse into the
      water and crosses the Rhine. Sebile invites the vigorous Frank
      into her tent, leaving Helissent outside on guard. Unfortunately,
      some Saxons arrive and Baldwin has to fight his way out of the
      Saxon camp.
        Baldwin tells Charlemagne of his exploits, and though the
      king is impressed by his nephew’s valor, he asks him not to repeat
      such a perilous solo expedition. Still, he gives him permission to
      marry Lady Sebile (once the Saxons are conquered).
        News reaches Charlemagne that several wives, left behind
      in Saint Hubert, have accepted the uncourteous advances of ser-
      vants and squires. He sends some knights to investigate, and they
      throw the fornicators into the Meuse.
rightColumn:
Charlemagne knights young Berart of Ardennes, who is anx-
  ious to prove his valor and crosses the Rhine alone. When the king
  hears this, he gathers his knights and goes after young Berart. The
  result is a small battle with the Saxons, in which Charlemagne
  wounds Widukind and Berart kills a Saxon half-giant.
     Back in their fortified camp, Charlemagne receives a message
  from Lady Sebile, who betrays her husband’s plans to cross the Rhine
  the next night. Subsequently, Berart and the Ardennes knights orga-
  nize an ambush on the river bank and defeat the surprised Saxons.
     Baldwin is vexed to not have been able to distinguish him-
  self against the Saxons. He crosses the Rhine alone to go to Lady
  Sebile’s tent, despite the presence of Saxon warriors. After he’s
  killed one of their chiefs, he returns to the Frankish camp. Again,
  Charlemagne tells him not to go out all by himself.
     The Franks gladly welcome reinforcements led by Salomon
  of Brittany, but the Count misunderstands Charlemagne’s in-
  structions and immediately crosses the Rhine to occupy the tents
  on the eastern bank. In a new battle, Salomon’s men rout the
  Saxons and return to their king victorious.
     Berart secretly meets Helissent in Lady Sebile’s tent. The
  Saxon lady gives Berart a hawk as a present for Baldwin, whom
  she reproaches for not coming himself. On his way back, Berart
  kills a Danish knight.

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
Baldwin is slightly offended by lady Sebile’s message. He
      ignores the king’s warnings and once more goes out to visit his
      lady. He kills a guard and puts on the Saxon’s arms. Thus dis-
      guised, he reaches Sebile’s tent. Shortly after, Widukind arrives
      unexpectedly and recognizes Baldwin despite his disguise. The
      young Frank fights his way back to the Rhine and escapes, but
      on the western bank he meets Berart, who mistakes him for a
      Saxon. They fight until Berart knocks off Baldwin’s helmet.
        Charlemagne once more forbids all knights to cross the
      Rhine. As time passes, Lady Sebile begins to worry, thinking
      her Frankish lover has lost interest. Meanwhile, a proud and
      foolhardy Berart disagrees with the interdiction and accuses
      Charlemagne of cowardice.
        The next day, the irate king crosses the Rhine alone, kills
      several Saxon knights, and returns to the camp unharmed. He
      then challenges Baldwin to fetch Lady Sebile’s golden wedding
      ring. His cousin curses the king for he cannot refuse this mission.
      He immediately crosses the Rhine and heads for Sebile’s tent. As
      before, he kills the guard and takes the victim’s armor and horse.
      Disguised as a Saxon knight, he orders some warriors to guard the
      ford. He enters Sebile’s tent and starts courting his lady. Sebile
      agrees to give Baldwin her golden ring and she abandons herself to
      her lover. Helissent warns them of Widukind’s arrival, so Baldwin
      leaves the tent. When Widukind finds his knight’s dead body, he
      pursues Baldwin, who now rides the dead guard’s horse.
        Meanwhile, Baldwin’s horse, Vairon, has returned to the
      Frankish camp alone. A worried Charlemagne goes to the ford,
      where he meets Baldwin, thinking he is a Saxon. The king
      charges, but stops the fight when he recognizes his nephew.
        Charlemagne announces his intention to build a bridge
      across the Rhine in order to facilitate the passage of troops
      into Saxon-controlled territory. After a collective prayer, the
      Franks witness a great deer crossing the Rhine at an unknown
      ford. They accept this as a divine indication of where to build
      the bridge. Since several counts argue about who’s in command
      of the bridge works, Charlemagne appoints Naymo as the chief
      supervisor. When the Saxons see what the Franks are up to,
      they send archers to harry the Frankish workers. In response,
      the Franks use armored boats to protect their laborers, and then
      launch a counter-attack. They kill many archers, but not with-
      out suffering important losses themselves. They establish a forti-
      fied bridgehead on the eastern bank. The Saxons start building
      siege equipment, including a large siege tower, but the Franks
      raid their camp and destroy the material. In the summer, the
      bridge is completed.
        The Frankish troops can now cross the Rhine in safety.
      Widukind pretends to retreat, but suddenly launches an all-
      out attack with his entire army near the Süntel Mountains. The
      Franks are outnumbered and, despite their valiant resistance,
      many are slain. Among the dead are Garin of Anjou; Aldalgis,
      the royal chamberlain; Geilo, the royal stable master; Worad, the
      Count of the Palace; and Engleboeuf, Duke Salomon’s brother.
        The next day the battle continues, and even more Saxons
      join the fray. But the tide turns when Charlemagne and his
rightColumn:
paladins arrive on the field. The king personally wounds
  Widukind (he believes he has killed him) and the Saxons are
  forced to flee.
     Charlemagne orders the decapitation of 4,500 male prison-
  ers at Verden. The remaining prisoners, all ladies, are baptized and
  given to Frankish knights. Entire Saxon clans are deported into
  Frankland as slaves. Lady Sebile is married to Baldwin. Helissent

segments.text:
Baldwin is slightly offended by lady Sebile’s message. He
      ignores the king’s warnings and once more goes out to visit his
      lady. He kills a guard and puts on the Saxon’s arms. Thus dis-
      guised, he reaches Sebile’s tent. Shortly after, Widukind arrives
      unexpectedly and recognizes Baldwin despite his disguise. The
      young Frank fights his way back to the Rhine and escapes, but
      on the western bank he meets Berart, who mistakes him for a
      Saxon. They fight until Berart knocks off Baldwin’s helmet.
        Charlemagne once more forbids all knights to cross the
      Rhine. As time passes, Lady Sebile begins to worry, thinking
      her Frankish lover has lost interest. Meanwhile, a proud and
      foolhardy Berart disagrees with the interdiction and accuses
      Charlemagne of cowardice.
        The next day, the irate king crosses the Rhine alone, kills
      several Saxon knights, and returns to the camp unharmed. He
      then challenges Baldwin to fetch Lady Sebile’s golden wedding
      ring. His cousin curses the king for he cannot refuse this mission.
      He immediately crosses the Rhine and heads for Sebile’s tent. As
      before, he kills the guard and takes the victim’s armor and horse.
      Disguised as a Saxon knight, he orders some warriors to guard the
      ford. He enters Sebile’s tent and starts courting his lady. Sebile
      agrees to give Baldwin her golden ring and she abandons herself to
      her lover. Helissent warns them of Widukind’s arrival, so Baldwin
      leaves the tent. When Widukind finds his knight’s dead body, he
      pursues Baldwin, who now rides the dead guard’s horse.
        Meanwhile, Baldwin’s horse, Vairon, has returned to the
      Frankish camp alone. A worried Charlemagne goes to the ford,
      where he meets Baldwin, thinking he is a Saxon. The king
      charges, but stops the fight when he recognizes his nephew.
        Charlemagne announces his intention to build a bridge
      across the Rhine in order to facilitate the passage of troops
      into Saxon-controlled territory. After a collective prayer, the
      Franks witness a great deer crossing the Rhine at an unknown
      ford. They accept this as a divine indication of where to build
      the bridge. Since several counts argue about who’s in command
      of the bridge works, Charlemagne appoints Naymo as the chief
      supervisor. When the Saxons see what the Franks are up to,
      they send archers to harry the Frankish workers. In response,
      the Franks use armored boats to protect their laborers, and then
      launch a counter-attack. They kill many archers, but not with-
      out suffering important losses themselves. They establish a forti-
      fied bridgehead on the eastern bank. The Saxons start building
      siege equipment, including a large siege tower, but the Franks
      raid their camp and destroy the material. In the summer, the
      bridge is completed.
        The Frankish troops can now cross the Rhine in safety.
      Widukind pretends to retreat, but suddenly launches an all-
      out attack with his entire army near the Süntel Mountains. The
      Franks are outnumbered and, despite their valiant resistance,
      many are slain. Among the dead are Garin of Anjou; Aldalgis,
      the royal chamberlain; Geilo, the royal stable master; Worad, the
      Count of the Palace; and Engleboeuf, Duke Salomon’s brother.
        The next day the battle continues, and even more Saxons
      join the fray. But the tide turns when Charlemagne and his

paladins arrive on the field. The king personally wounds
  Widukind (he believes he has killed him) and the Saxons are
  forced to flee.
     Charlemagne orders the decapitation of 4,500 male prison-
  ers at Verden. The remaining prisoners, all ladies, are baptized and
  given to Frankish knights. Entire Saxon clans are deported into
  Frankland as slaves. Lady Sebile is married to Baldwin. Helissent
  is promised to Berart. The Franks recapture the fortified city of
  Tremoigne. Baldwin is appointed Duke of Saxony. [→783]
     Winter Court (Thionville): Paul the Deacon arrives at court.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

  mother Bertrada dies three months later. She is buried alongside
  her late husband at the chapel of Andenne.
     Charlemagne meets Fastrada, who gives him her magic
  ring. They marry shortly thereafter.

  lious vassals, while the Franks restore the order in the disloyal
  Christian towns of Urgel, Gerone and Vich on the southern side
  of the Pyrenees.

  small army to travel to the East and bring back Ogier. Carahue

leftColumn:
his wife Gloriande and Emir Moisan. Clara marries Walter,
      whom Ogier installs as the new Christian King of Jerusalem. On
      their way back to Frankland, Ogier lands at Rhodes where he
      hangs the traitors Beringer and Godebeuf. He stays on the island
      and becomes an independent vassal of the Byzantine Emperor.
      Carahue and Gloriande go to Cathay where they preach
      Christianity for the rest of their blessed lives. [→789]
        La chanson des Saisnes: [←782] While Charlemagne is
      on his way back to Frankland, Widukind raises another army
      to besiege Tremoigne. Baldwin deems it unnecessary to call on
      the King’s assistance for the city’s defense, contrary to Sebile’s
      advice. The Saxon duchess secretly sends a messenger to ask
      Charlemagne for help.
        Although the Saxons suffer heavy losses and do not succeed
      in reconquering Tremoigne, the Franks know they won’t be able
      to resist them much longer. Baldwin’s vassals advise him to with-
      draw to Cologne, but the impetuous youth refuses. Instead, he
      orders a frontal surprise attack and suffers a bloody defeat. He is
      obliged to retreat to Cologne.
        Meanwhile, Charlemagne receives Sebile’s messenger while
      already on his way back to Tremoigne to succor the duke. The
      Franks catch the besieging Saxons in a pincer. They are, however,
      still largely outnumbered. Berart and Baldwin both die on the
      battlefield and their bodies are brought to the city. Lady Sebile is
      sick with grief, and when Charlemagne hears the sad news, Duke
      Naymo prevents the King from killing himself.
        The Franks withdraw to Cologne. Here, Widukind’s son
      Dyalas challenges Charlemagne to a duel. He accepts and kills his
      opponent’s horse, but not Dyalas himself. Instead, he offers Dyalas
      baptism and the title of Duke of Saxony, which the young prince ac-
      cepts, impressed as he is by Charlemagne’s piety and magnanimity.
        The next day, Duke Naymo receives a challenge from the
      Saxon Colorez. When his opponent is unhorsed, the duke al-
      lows him to climb back into the saddle but the pagan knight
      refuses baptism. Inspired by the presence of the king, Naymo
      eventually kills Colorez.
        Charlemagne founds an abbey on the field where Baldwin
      and Berart died. Sebile retires there as a nun. Upon his return to
      Saint Hubert, Charlemagne delivers Berart’s body to his grieving
          n
      parents.
        Winter Court (Herstal).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 784
        May Field (Thionville).
        Saxony: Once more, Charlemagne launches several cam-
      paigns deep into the Saxon heartlands.
        Religion: Death of Arch-chaplain Fulrad. He is succeeded
      by Angilram, the Bishop of Metz.
        Rogero and Bradamant: [←777] King Rogero of Bulgaria
      is ambushed and slain by men from the House of Mayence.
        Winter Court (Eresburg).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

     May Field (Paderborn).
     Saxony: Famines and floods in Saxony. Widukind is forced
  to surrender and is baptized at Attigny. Many Saxons are deport-
  ed into Frankland as peasant slaves for Frankish nobles. Saxony
  is almost completely controlled by the Franks, and Frisia is of-
  ficially annexed to the kingdom. Willehad is appointed as mis-
  sionary for Saxony and Liutger for Frisia. The Pope requests all
  Christians to give prayers of thanks for the defeat of the Saxons.
     Karel ende Elegast: The Thuringian Count Hardrad and
  his supporters conspire against their king in order to put the sons
  of Carloman on the throne. The conspiracy is discovered by the
  exiled Count Elegast (Basin). All traitors are deprived of their
              n
  eyes and sent into exile.
     Spain: An Asturian-Frankish alliance led by King Louis re-
  captures Gerona from the Moors.
     Lion de Bourges: [←781] Florentine dies and Lion retires to
  a monastery. [→787]
     Brittany: The perfidious Bretons once more revolt against
  the Franks.
     Elie de Saint-Gilles: [←767, Raoul de Cambrai] Count
  Julien of Saint Giles rebukes his son, Elie, for not serving King
  Louis and for his supposed lack of valor. Elie proves his skill
  at arms and leaves his father’s castle. Count Julien orders some
  of his knights to follow and discreetly protect his son. Elie en-
  counters a mortally wounded knight, Amauri, son of the Count
  of Poitiers. He has been attacked by rebelling Bretons. King
  Louis retreats to Angers, after Count William Shortnose saves
  Louis on the field but is taken prisoner himself. Elie pursues
  the Bretons (led by Lord Macabray) and attacks them, giving
  William and the other prisoners a chance to escape. Elie himself,
  however, is taken prisoner.
     William, accompanied by his brothers Ernold and Bernard,
  and his nephew, squire Bertrand, discovers Elie’s identity and
  hurries to Saint Gilles to bring the news and ask for help. He
  slays the troublesome gatekeeper, but Count Julien forgives the
  Narbonnais when he learns the reason of William’s visit.
     Meanwhile, Lord Macabray takes Elie to his castle and offers
  him the hand of his daughter if he will renounce God. Elie refus-
  es, steals a horse, and escapes by crossing a river on horseback.
     In the forest Elie fights some robbers whose food he stole.
  One of them, Galopin, becomes his servant. He claims to be
  Thierry of Ardennes’ son, cursed by evil faeries to forever remain
  a dwarf, and that he was sold to merchants as an unlucky child.
  He helps Elie fight the pursuing Bretons and they become friends.
  The Bretons ambush Elie and capture him again. At Macabray’s
  castle, his daughter heals Elie’s wounds and confesses her love.
  When Macabray’s authority is challenged by his rival, Lord
  Lubien, his cowardly sons refuse to act as their father’s champion.
  For the love of his daughter, Elie accepts to take Macabray’s place.
  He kills Lord Lubien and takes his fabulous horse Prinsaut. He
  then kills Macabray’s worthless son, Caïfas. He takes refuge in one

      sick with grief, and when Charlemagne hears the sad news, Duke
      Naymo prevents the King from killing himself.
        The Franks withdraw to Cologne. Here, Widukind’s son
      Dyalas challenges Charlemagne to a duel. He accepts and kills his
      opponent’s horse, but not Dyalas himself. Instead, he offers Dyalas
      baptism and the title of Duke of Saxony, which the young prince ac-
      cepts, impressed as he is by Charlemagne’s piety and magnanimity.
        The next day, Duke Naymo receives a challenge from the
      Saxon Colorez. When his opponent is unhorsed, the duke al-
      lows him to climb back into the saddle but the pagan knight
      refuses baptism. Inspired by the presence of the king, Naymo
      eventually kills Colorez.
        Charlemagne founds an abbey on the field where Baldwin
      and Berart died. Sebile retires there as a nun. Upon his return to
      Saint Hubert, Charlemagne delivers Berart’s body to his grieving
          n
      parents.
        Winter Court (Herstal).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 784
        May Field (Thionville).
        Saxony: Once more, Charlemagne launches several cam-
      paigns deep into the Saxon heartlands.
        Religion: Death of Arch-chaplain Fulrad. He is succeeded
      by Angilram, the Bishop of Metz.
        Rogero and Bradamant: [←777] King Rogero of Bulgaria
      is ambushed and slain by men from the House of Mayence.
        Winter Court (Eresburg).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

aNNo 785
     May Field (Paderborn).
     Saxony: Famines and floods in Saxony. Widukind is forced
  to surrender and is baptized at Attigny. Many Saxons are deport-
  ed into Frankland as peasant slaves for Frankish nobles. Saxony
  is almost completely controlled by the Franks, and Frisia is of-
  ficially annexed to the kingdom. Willehad is appointed as mis-
  sionary for Saxony and Liutger for Frisia. The Pope requests all
  Christians to give prayers of thanks for the defeat of the Saxons.
     Karel ende Elegast: The Thuringian Count Hardrad and
  his supporters conspire against their king in order to put the sons
  of Carloman on the throne. The conspiracy is discovered by the
  exiled Count Elegast (Basin). All traitors are deprived of their
              n
  eyes and sent into exile.
     Spain: An Asturian-Frankish alliance led by King Louis re-
  captures Gerona from the Moors.
     Lion de Bourges: [←781] Florentine dies and Lion retires to
  a monastery. [→787]
     Brittany: The perfidious Bretons once more revolt against
  the Franks.
     Elie de Saint-Gilles: [←767, Raoul de Cambrai] Count
  Julien of Saint Giles rebukes his son, Elie, for not serving King
  Louis and for his supposed lack of valor. Elie proves his skill
  at arms and leaves his father’s castle. Count Julien orders some
  of his knights to follow and discreetly protect his son. Elie en-
  counters a mortally wounded knight, Amauri, son of the Count
  of Poitiers. He has been attacked by rebelling Bretons. King
  Louis retreats to Angers, after Count William Shortnose saves
  Louis on the field but is taken prisoner himself. Elie pursues
  the Bretons (led by Lord Macabray) and attacks them, giving
  William and the other prisoners a chance to escape. Elie himself,
  however, is taken prisoner.
     William, accompanied by his brothers Ernold and Bernard,
  and his nephew, squire Bertrand, discovers Elie’s identity and
  hurries to Saint Gilles to bring the news and ask for help. He
  slays the troublesome gatekeeper, but Count Julien forgives the
  Narbonnais when he learns the reason of William’s visit.
     Meanwhile, Lord Macabray takes Elie to his castle and offers
  him the hand of his daughter if he will renounce God. Elie refus-
  es, steals a horse, and escapes by crossing a river on horseback.
     In the forest Elie fights some robbers whose food he stole.
  One of them, Galopin, becomes his servant. He claims to be
  Thierry of Ardennes’ son, cursed by evil faeries to forever remain
  a dwarf, and that he was sold to merchants as an unlucky child.
  He helps Elie fight the pursuing Bretons and they become friends.
  The Bretons ambush Elie and capture him again. At Macabray’s
  castle, his daughter heals Elie’s wounds and confesses her love.
  When Macabray’s authority is challenged by his rival, Lord
  Lubien, his cowardly sons refuse to act as their father’s champion.
  For the love of his daughter, Elie accepts to take Macabray’s place.
  He kills Lord Lubien and takes his fabulous horse Prinsaut. He
  then kills Macabray’s worthless son, Caïfas. He takes refuge in one

        Roman d’Aquin: King Charlemagne wants to recapture
      the castles the pagan Bretons captured while he was at war with
      Widukind of the Saxons. Charlemagne and Audulf, the roy-
      al seneschal, lead the Frankish army to the city of Dol, where
      Archbishop Isoré joins the troops.
        Charlemagne sends four counts (Ripay of Dol, Baldwin of
      Nantes, Richard of Le Mans, and Thierry of Vannes) to Quidalet
      with a letter demanding King Aquin’s surrender and baptism.
      The insulted king refuses and wants to attack the messengers.
      Queen Irdisa kisses him to calm him down, and the king lets
      the Franks go. On their way out, they are attacked by vengeful
      pagans. They escape unharmed thanks to a miraculous mist.
      Nevertheless, the pagans pursue the Franks all the way to the
      camp, where the counts inform the king of what has happened.
      Duke Naymo advises the King to lay siege to Quidalet quick-
      ly, but the intrepid pagans attack. Only a few pagans survive
      the skirmish and flee back to Quidalet to warn King Aquin.
      Charlemagne orders Count Thierry of Vannes to go to Aquin
      one last time to ask his surrender and baptism, but to no avail.
        Both sides prepare for battle. Archbishop Isoré absolves all
      knights on the condition they fight valiantly against the pagans.
      At the end of the day, the pagans retreat to Quidalet. They took
      300 prisoners, while the Franks took 1,000. King Charlemagne
      captures a fabulous horse, named Corengne. On the second day
      of battle, Prince Doret is assisted by demons. But the archbishop

title: Phase 2: Expansion
leftColumn:
where he builds his camp. During the night, the pagans sail to the
      island in small, silent boats. They surprise the Franks, set fire to
      their camp and kill all the horses. In the ensuing battle, all Franks
      are killed, except Duke Naymo and Fagon. In the morning at low
      tide, the marshal carries the wounded duke on his shoulders and
      wades through the sea back to the mainland. At Rance’s Ford, he
      is too tired to carry the duke any longer and leaves him behind.
        When Charlemagne hears the terrible news, he rides out
      immediately to the ford, where he finds the nearly-dead duke.
      As the king laments his dear companion and prays for Naymo’s
      soul, a sigh escapes from the duke’s body — he’s not dead after
      all. He is brought to the camp, where a healer restores him to life.
        The next day, Charlemagne wants to take Quidalet quickly to
      avenge the men who died on the Isle of Cesembre. During a prayer
      in Saint Servan’s Chapel, the King asks God for help and asks Him
      to severely punish anyone who breaks an oath taken in the chapel.
      Charlemagne sends out his spies to find out possible weak points
      in the city’s defenses. One spy tells him that the city has no direct
      access to fresh water; it comes to them via an underground chan-
      nel. He suggests using a thirsty horse to locate it. The horse scrapes
      the ground near St. Servan’s Chapel. After some digging, the Franks
      find a stone vault and a subterranean aqueduct. They block it, de-
      priving Quidalet of fresh water. After five days, King Aquin flees
      from his city by boat, together with his most loyal men. He sets
      sail to Carheix. When the Franks attack Quidalet, they encounter
      little resistance. Charlemagne rescues the prisoners in Oreigle and
      captures King Aquin’s treasure, which he shares with his barons. He
      gives the city of Quidalet to Archbishop Isoré. He orders that all
      pagan prisoners be beheaded if they refuse baptism.
        Duke Naymo wants to capture the city of Gardaine, to
      which Prince Doret has retreated. Charlemagne lends him the
      Oriflamme. The Duke arrives at Gardaine, a city defended by a
      large ditch and walls with spikes, on which the heads of Franks
      are set. Among the city’s troops there are lions and even a giant.
      The pagans launch a surprise attack, before the Franks have even
      established their camp, but they are driven off and retreat be-
      hind the city walls. A pagan embassy offers to pay a tribute in ex-
      change for peace: Prince Doret offers gold, weapons and virgins.
      The insulted Franks slaughter the messengers; only two escape.
        The pagans once again ride out to do battle. This time the
      Franks almost lose, but Charlemagne comes to their aid with the
      rest of his army. The pagans retreat.
        The next morning a pagan ballista severely wounds
      Charlemagne, who was inspecting the city’s defenses. As he falls, the
      pagans ride out and try to capture the Frankish king. The most vig-
      ilant Frankish barons come to their king’s aid and deliver him from
      the pagan troops. Charlemagne prays to God to help him capture
      this city. At night, a miraculous storm breaks out and a high tide
      smashes large parts of the city walls. The wild water reaches the
      Frankish camp before it retires back into the sea. In the morning,
      the archbishop arrives with his troops. But another army approaches
      from the north. Duke Naymo weeps, thinking they are pagans. But
      instead of enemies, they are men of Duke Yon of Gascony.
rightColumn:
The Frankish council decides to march on King Aquin in
  Carheix. Charlemagne is still severely wounded and needs to be
  transported on a cart. During the voyage, the king almost dies,
  but Archbishop Isoré’s prayers save his life. The Franks arrive at
  Carhaix and rapidly capture the city. King Aquin flees again, but
  Naymo intercepts Queen Erdisa’s convoy and captures her. He
  encourages her to be baptized, but she refuses for the loyalty to
  her husband and kin. The duke then brings her to Charlemagne,
  who asks her to be baptized. This time, she accepts.
     Aquin has fled to the castle of Menay. When the Frankish
  vanguard arrives, the pagans defeat them, kill Duke Yon, and lib-
  erate Queen Erdisa. Then more Franks arrive and burn the castle
  to the ground with Greek fire. Aquin flees one last time. Along
  the road, he pillages a chapel and attacks the hermit, Corentin,
  living there, but the good man escapes, thanks to a miraculous
  mist. Corentin is found by Frankish knights, who arrest him
  and bring him to their king. After a short prayer, Corentin tells
  Charlemagne that he can lead them to King Aquin and his men.
     In the final battle between the pagans and the Franks, Duke
  Naymo kills King Aquin in a man-to-man fight. Brittany be-
  comes a part of Frankland. Charlemagne gives it to Salomon,
                n
  who becomes its first duke.
     Elie de Saint-Gilles: [←785] Macabray’s daughter converts
  (she is baptized as Rosamund), but the Church won’t allow her
  to marry Elie, for he served as her godfather at her baptism. Elie
  and Galopin leave on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. On their
  return Galopin marries Rosamund and Elie weds Louis’ cousin
  Avissa. [→Aiol, 791]
     Winter Court (Florence).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 787
     May Field (Florence): The engagement between
  Constantine and Rothrud is broken.
     The king is informed of a possible secret alliance between
  Duke Tassilo and the Avars. To ensure his loyalty, the duke is forced
  to give twelve high noblemen and his son Theodo as hostages.
     Italy: Charlemagne travels to Rome, where Duke Arichis
  of Benevento swears fidelity, pays tribute and gives hostages, in-
  cluding his sons, Romuald and Grimoald. A few months later
  Duke Arichis and Romuald both die of illness. Grimoald suc-
  ceeds his father as the Duke of Benevento but Frankish adminis-
  trators control his duchy.
     The king orders all Lombards to shave their beards in the
  manner of the Franks.
     Istria, a former Byzantine province, is annexed to Lombardy
  and given to a Frankish count.
     Gascony, Septimania: Count Odalric the Gascon captures
  his rival, Count Chorson of Toulouse. But Odalric is brought to
  justice and condemned to exile. William Shortnose is appointed
  the new Duke of Toulouse.
     Religion: Benedict of Aniane preaches in Septimania and
  spreads his new rule. A heretical “letter fallen from Heaven”

where he builds his camp. During the night, the pagans sail to the
      island in small, silent boats. They surprise the Franks, set fire to
      their camp and kill all the horses. In the ensuing battle, all Franks
      are killed, except Duke Naymo and Fagon. In the morning at low
      tide, the marshal carries the wounded duke on his shoulders and
      wades through the sea back to the mainland. At Rance’s Ford, he
      is too tired to carry the duke any longer and leaves him behind.
        When Charlemagne hears the terrible news, he rides out
      immediately to the ford, where he finds the nearly-dead duke.
      As the king laments his dear companion and prays for Naymo’s
      soul, a sigh escapes from the duke’s body — he’s not dead after
      all. He is brought to the camp, where a healer restores him to life.
        The next day, Charlemagne wants to take Quidalet quickly to
      avenge the men who died on the Isle of Cesembre. During a prayer
      in Saint Servan’s Chapel, the King asks God for help and asks Him
      to severely punish anyone who breaks an oath taken in the chapel.
      Charlemagne sends out his spies to find out possible weak points
      in the city’s defenses. One spy tells him that the city has no direct
      access to fresh water; it comes to them via an underground chan-
      nel. He suggests using a thirsty horse to locate it. The horse scrapes
      the ground near St. Servan’s Chapel. After some digging, the Franks
      find a stone vault and a subterranean aqueduct. They block it, de-
      priving Quidalet of fresh water. After five days, King Aquin flees
      from his city by boat, together with his most loyal men. He sets
      sail to Carheix. When the Franks attack Quidalet, they encounter
      little resistance. Charlemagne rescues the prisoners in Oreigle and
      captures King Aquin’s treasure, which he shares with his barons. He
      gives the city of Quidalet to Archbishop Isoré. He orders that all
      pagan prisoners be beheaded if they refuse baptism.
        Duke Naymo wants to capture the city of Gardaine, to
      which Prince Doret has retreated. Charlemagne lends him the
      Oriflamme. The Duke arrives at Gardaine, a city defended by a
      large ditch and walls with spikes, on which the heads of Franks
      are set. Among the city’s troops there are lions and even a giant.
      The pagans launch a surprise attack, before the Franks have even
      established their camp, but they are driven off and retreat be-
      hind the city walls. A pagan embassy offers to pay a tribute in ex-
      change for peace: Prince Doret offers gold, weapons and virgins.
      The insulted Franks slaughter the messengers; only two escape.
        The pagans once again ride out to do battle. This time the
      Franks almost lose, but Charlemagne comes to their aid with the
      rest of his army. The pagans retreat.
        The next morning a pagan ballista severely wounds
      Charlemagne, who was inspecting the city’s defenses. As he falls, the
      pagans ride out and try to capture the Frankish king. The most vig-
      ilant Frankish barons come to their king’s aid and deliver him from
      the pagan troops. Charlemagne prays to God to help him capture
      this city. At night, a miraculous storm breaks out and a high tide
      smashes large parts of the city walls. The wild water reaches the
      Frankish camp before it retires back into the sea. In the morning,
      the archbishop arrives with his troops. But another army approaches
      from the north. Duke Naymo weeps, thinking they are pagans. But
      instead of enemies, they are men of Duke Yon of Gascony.

The Frankish council decides to march on King Aquin in
  Carheix. Charlemagne is still severely wounded and needs to be
  transported on a cart. During the voyage, the king almost dies,
  but Archbishop Isoré’s prayers save his life. The Franks arrive at
  Carhaix and rapidly capture the city. King Aquin flees again, but
  Naymo intercepts Queen Erdisa’s convoy and captures her. He
  encourages her to be baptized, but she refuses for the loyalty to
  her husband and kin. The duke then brings her to Charlemagne,
  who asks her to be baptized. This time, she accepts.
     Aquin has fled to the castle of Menay. When the Frankish
  vanguard arrives, the pagans defeat them, kill Duke Yon, and lib-
  erate Queen Erdisa. Then more Franks arrive and burn the castle
  to the ground with Greek fire. Aquin flees one last time. Along
  the road, he pillages a chapel and attacks the hermit, Corentin,
  living there, but the good man escapes, thanks to a miraculous
  mist. Corentin is found by Frankish knights, who arrest him
  and bring him to their king. After a short prayer, Corentin tells
  Charlemagne that he can lead them to King Aquin and his men.
     In the final battle between the pagans and the Franks, Duke
  Naymo kills King Aquin in a man-to-man fight. Brittany be-
  comes a part of Frankland. Charlemagne gives it to Salomon,
                n
  who becomes its first duke.
     Elie de Saint-Gilles: [←785] Macabray’s daughter converts
  (she is baptized as Rosamund), but the Church won’t allow her
  to marry Elie, for he served as her godfather at her baptism. Elie
  and Galopin leave on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. On their
  return Galopin marries Rosamund and Elie weds Louis’ cousin
  Avissa. [→Aiol, 791]
     Winter Court (Florence).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 787
     May Field (Florence): The engagement between
  Constantine and Rothrud is broken.
     The king is informed of a possible secret alliance between
  Duke Tassilo and the Avars. To ensure his loyalty, the duke is forced
  to give twelve high noblemen and his son Theodo as hostages.
     Italy: Charlemagne travels to Rome, where Duke Arichis
  of Benevento swears fidelity, pays tribute and gives hostages, in-
  cluding his sons, Romuald and Grimoald. A few months later
  Duke Arichis and Romuald both die of illness. Grimoald suc-
  ceeds his father as the Duke of Benevento but Frankish adminis-
  trators control his duchy.
     The king orders all Lombards to shave their beards in the
  manner of the Franks.
     Istria, a former Byzantine province, is annexed to Lombardy
  and given to a Frankish count.
     Gascony, Septimania: Count Odalric the Gascon captures
  his rival, Count Chorson of Toulouse. But Odalric is brought to
  justice and condemned to exile. William Shortnose is appointed
  the new Duke of Toulouse.

  spreads his new rule. A heretical “letter fallen from Heaven”

      Land. [→809]
        Bavaria: Duke Tassilo forsakes his oaths and plots treason,
      allying with the Byzantines and the Avars. With the duke’s sup-
      port, the Avars unsuccessfully raid Bavaria and Friuli. The Pope
      condemns Tassilo, while Charlemagne raises an army to punish
      his disloyal vassal and resist an Avar invasion. The Bavarian peo-
      ple prefer to concede the king’s right rather than oppose him,
      so Tassilo comes to Charlemagne and commends himself into
      vassalage. Gerold is appointed as the new Duke of the province,
      renamed Germania. Tassilo is sent to the monastery of Jumieges,
      in Normandy, to do penance for his sins. His relatives are sent to
      various monasteries.
        Italy: Lombards supporting Arichis’ widow, Adalperge
      (a daughter of Desiderius), the exiled Beneventans, and
      the Byzantines try to invade Lombardy, but are defeated by
      Grimoald and his Frankish vassals. The triple alliance between
      the Lombards, Bavarians and Byzantines comes to an end.

      [→789]

      At Charlemagne’s court he learns that Oliver died heroically at

      father’s death on the Moors. The king makes him one of his

aNNo 789
     May Field (Cologne): Charlemagne orders that each mon-
  astery and each bishopric should have a school, where talented
  boys should be taught how to read, write, sing and pray.
     He orders the construction of a great wooden bridge across
  the Rhine.
     Slavonia: A campaign into the land of the Slavs is launched.
  By the guidance of God, Charlemagne is victorious and receives
  submission, hostages and oaths from the Slav King Dragovit.
     Lion de Bourges: [←788] Lion’s son, Oliver, travels to the Holy
  Land and fights for three years to recapture Jerusalem. [→792]
     Queen Sebille/Ogier: Macharias wants to avenge the death
  of his uncle Hardrad, the Thuringian traitor. After King Charlot’s
  wedding, Macharias tries to seduce Charlot’s wife (a Byzantine
  princess). She refuses his advances, but one day, as Charlot goes
  out hunting, he slips an ugly dwarf into the queen’s bed. When the
  queen wakes up, she hits the dwarf on the mouth and he leaves.
     The next day, as Charlot goes to hear morning mass, the
  dwarf tries again and enters the royal bed completely naked. But
  since he’d been waiting all night for the king to leave his bed, he
  instantly falls asleep. Upon his return, Charlot discovers his wife
  in bed with the naked dwarf. He calls his vassals as witnesses to
  the apparent adultery. Among the councilors is Macharias, who
  condemns the queen and demands that she be burned alive. As
  the queen turns out to be pregnant, however, she is spared and
  sent into exile instead.
     Macharias follows her as she leaves court and slays her ac-
  companying knights, but the queen herself escapes into the
  Ardennes Forest. Back at court, the traitor is exposed by the
  queen’s hunting dog, who attacks him three times. Macharias is
  then defeated in a strange judicial combat with the same dog and
  put to the death. The queen is declared innocent, but nobody
  knows where she is and the paladins cannot find her. When the
  Byzantine Emperor hears about his daughter’s misadventure, he
  is furious and threatens to invade Frankland.
     Meanwhile the queen has found refuge with a uncouth
  woodsman, Varocher, who agrees to take her to Byzantium. In
  Avarland, she gives birth to a healthy boy with a royal birth-
  mark. She returns to Frankland and tries to make peace between
  her husband and her furious imperial father, who is besieging
  Paris. She presents Varocher as the Byzantine champion in a tri-
  al by combat, against Ogier. When Ogier learns how the loyal
  Varocher helped the queen, the noble paladin surrenders and is
  allowed to come back to Charlemagne’s court. The Byzantine
  Emperor finally accepts Charlemagne’s excuses and peace of-
  ferings. Varocher is dubbed and allowed to build a castle on his
                  n
  land. His sons become knights.
     Winter Court (Worms): King Offa of Mercia does not
  wish to marry his daughter to Pepin the Hunchback. He would
  prefer to have his son Ecfrith marry Princess Bertha — which
  Charlemagne angrily refuses.
     Prince Charlot becomes Duke of the Breton March.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

title: Phase 3: Consolidation
leftColumn:
Phase   3: Consolidation

      (790–800)

      Customs

      F
         eudalism: Because of marriages, inheritances and con-
         quests, many landholders have multiple lords to whom
         they pay homage. To resolve the problem of primary loy-
      alty, a vassal chooses which lord is his primary lord, whose loyal-
      ty precedes all others. This is his liege lord.
        Charlemagne creates the office of missus dominicus, a
      special envoy whose task it is to check on counts and their
      administration.
        Lords now often prefer to pay mercenaries to fight in the
      royal army in their stead.
        The Church officially declares the war against the pagans as
      a crusade, which absolves knights of all sins committed before or
      during the Holy War.
        Truce of God: Knights who break the divine truce are
      automatically excommunicated by their bishop (meaning they
      can no longer benefit from Prayers, see Prayers & Miracles in
      Chapter 9), unless they are fighting a Holy War.
        Knighthood: Bestowing knighthood is established as a
      royal prerogative, no longer practiced by mere knights or counts.
      Only kings and their direct representatives, such as paladins, may
      make knights. Every now and then Charlemagne himself gives,
      or on very rare occasions even grants, a manor to a commoner
      who distinguished himself by a particularly noble act.
        Heraldry: Heralds develop more elaborated rules of her-
      aldry, including proper methods of handing down a knight’s
      arms to his descendants.
        Tournaments: The rules and ceremonies become more
      sophisticated. Tournaments are now as much a festival for ro-
      mantic ladies as for virile knights. At the same time, since ar-
      mor and horses are more expensive, fewer knights can afford to
      participate.
        Women: Only the woman gives a dowry to the husband;
      the husband no longer gives a bride-gift. The custom of the wid-
      ow’s portion is no longer respected everywhere.
        Chivalry: The path of true nobility starts to be adopted by
      foreign knights as well, in an effort to emulate the splendor of
      the Frankish court.
        Romance: Fin’amor is now widespread among the Britons,
      Lombards, Saracens, Byzantines and even the assimilated Saxons.
        Fashion: Typical men’s clothing is a cotte hanging to the
      ankle (merchants and middle-class men wear it to the calf, peas-
      ants to the knee). A surcoat with long wide sleeves goes over the
      cotte. Dress shoes are slightly pointed, buttoning at the ankle.
        Noblewomen typically wear a cotte (dress) with a belt
      around the waist. Sleeves are tight-fitting from elbow to wrist.
rightColumn:
For head covering, a wimple is worn with a stiffened linen cap on
  top. The woman’s pelisse is a long, outdoor garment.
  Warfare

     Armor: The occasional plating for extra protection at the el-
  bows and knees is now extended to include legs and body. A fair
  amount of chain mail is still used, though, so this armor is called
  partial plate (14 points), worn with a fully-enclosed helmet.

         eudalism: Because of marriages, inheritances and con-
         quests, many landholders have multiple lords to whom
         they pay homage. To resolve the problem of primary loy-
      alty, a vassal chooses which lord is his primary lord, whose loyal-
      ty precedes all others. This is his liege lord.
        Charlemagne creates the office of missus dominicus, a
      special envoy whose task it is to check on counts and their
      administration.
        Lords now often prefer to pay mercenaries to fight in the
      royal army in their stead.
        The Church officially declares the war against the pagans as
      a crusade, which absolves knights of all sins committed before or
      during the Holy War.
        Truce of God: Knights who break the divine truce are
      automatically excommunicated by their bishop (meaning they
      can no longer benefit from Prayers, see Prayers & Miracles in
      Chapter 9), unless they are fighting a Holy War.
        Knighthood: Bestowing knighthood is established as a
      royal prerogative, no longer practiced by mere knights or counts.
      Only kings and their direct representatives, such as paladins, may
      make knights. Every now and then Charlemagne himself gives,
      or on very rare occasions even grants, a manor to a commoner
      who distinguished himself by a particularly noble act.
        Heraldry: Heralds develop more elaborated rules of her-
      aldry, including proper methods of handing down a knight’s
      arms to his descendants.
        Tournaments: The rules and ceremonies become more
      sophisticated. Tournaments are now as much a festival for ro-
      mantic ladies as for virile knights. At the same time, since ar-
      mor and horses are more expensive, fewer knights can afford to
      participate.
        Women: Only the woman gives a dowry to the husband;
      the husband no longer gives a bride-gift. The custom of the wid-
      ow’s portion is no longer respected everywhere.
        Chivalry: The path of true nobility starts to be adopted by
      foreign knights as well, in an effort to emulate the splendor of
      the Frankish court.
        Romance: Fin’amor is now widespread among the Britons,
      Lombards, Saracens, Byzantines and even the assimilated Saxons.
        Fashion: Typical men’s clothing is a cotte hanging to the
      ankle (merchants and middle-class men wear it to the calf, peas-
      ants to the knee). A surcoat with long wide sleeves goes over the
      cotte. Dress shoes are slightly pointed, buttoning at the ankle.
        Noblewomen typically wear a cotte (dress) with a belt
      around the waist. Sleeves are tight-fitting from elbow to wrist.

leftColumn:
pass the city gates. There they don their armor, take their swords
      and, after a short but bloody battle, capture the city from within.
      William personally kills the noble Moors Harpin, Otrant, and
      Synagon. [→791, Prise d’Orange]
        William Shortnose becomes Duke of Septimania.
        Winter Court (Worms): The palace accidentally burns down.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 791

        May Field (Regensburg): King Charlemagne orders the
      construction of a great royal palace at Aachen.
        Avarland: Charlemagne starts a massive campaign to conquer
      the lands of the Avars. Three armies are sent to the east, one led by
      Charlot, another by Duke Thierry of Ardennes and chamberlain
      Meginfred, and the third army under Pepin of Italy. Duke Gerold
      leads a flotilla carrying provisions and reserve troops. Some minor
      fortifications are captured and the Avars retreat into their Ring, but
      the Frankish campaign is halted by an outbreak of pestilence among
      the horses. Many Saxon soldiers in the Frankish ranks desert.
        Aquitaine: Saracens invade Guyenne and beleaguer
      Bordeaux.
        Prise d’Orange: [←790, Charroi de Nîmes] Gilbert escapes
      from jail in Orange and flees to Nîmes. He tells William and
      Bertrand of the defenses of Orange and of the beautiful Lady
      Orable. William, who has been in love with this lady for a long
      time now, swears to capture Orange. Therefore the two brothers
      and their friends swim across the Durance river and enter the
      city disguised as Moors. They are even invited into the white
      marble tower of Gloriette (built on a granite rock foundation),
      where they meet Lady Orable.
        When the black skin paint accidentally comes off, William
      is recognized because of his nose. The Franks quickly grab some
      swords, capture Gloriette and lock themselves up inside. But the
      besieging Moors succeed in entering the tower via a secret vault and
      they capture everybody. The Franks first suspect Orable of betrayal,
      but the lady helps them to get out of their cell by providing them
      food and equipment (including enchanted golden mail and hel-
      met, and Lord Tiebaut’s own sword). Orable agrees to be baptized
      if William promises to marry her, which he does. She then shows
      them another secret tunnel (its entrance is hidden inside a pillar) by
      which they can send a messenger to Nîmes and Narbonne.
        The relief army attacks the city from the outside, while
      William and his men launch a surprise attack from Gloriette,
      slaughtering many Moors. Even though Tiebaut escapes, Orange
      is captured and William marries Orable, who is baptized as
      Guibourc. [→792, Enfances Vivien]
        Aiol: [←786, Elie de Saint Giles] When the loyal Elie los-
      es Bourges to the traitor Macharias of Orleans, he flees to the
      forests south of Bordeaux with his wife Avissa, Charlemagne’s
      niece. In this wilderness she gives birth to a son, Aiol (the name
      means “snake”). [→809]
        Winter Court (Regensburg).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
