aNNo 792
     May Field (Regensburg): A conspiracy of Franks (among
  them many surviving supporters of Carloman II) and Pepin the
  Hunchback (pretending to be ill while his father is away fighting the
  Avars) is discovered by Abbot Fardulf. Some nobles are executed by
  the sword for high treason, some are hanged on the gallows by order
  of the cruel Queen Fastrada. Pepin is sent to the monastery of Prüm.
  All Franks must swear an oath of allegiance to the king.
     Lion de Bourges: [←789] Lady Joieuse gives birth to twins:
  a boy and a girl. Garnier tries to kill them all, but is thrown into
  a fire by Lion’s loyal vassals. [→793]
     The Lay of Hildebrand: [←788] During the Frankish
  Avar campaign, Hadubrand meets his father in battle without
  recognizing him. Both knights start boasting and the exiled
  Hildebrand soon realizes he is facing his own son. He tries to
  convince his son of his true identity, but Hadubrand believes
  his father to be dead. They do battle against one another and
                          n
  Hadubrand unknowingly kills his own father.
     Enfances Vivien: [←Prise d’Orange, 791] When Vivien comes
  of age, he refuses to become a merchant. Instead, he gathers a band
  of mercenaries and captures Luiserna. The Saracens besiege him,
  but Vivien vows never to retreat from pagans. When one of his
  mercenaries laments their precarious situation, Vivien throws him
  off the battlements. Vivien’s foster-mother arranges for his kins-
  men to help him in the battle. When William first meets Vivien
  on the field he attacks him, thinking that he must be a Saracen gi-
  ant. Their duel ends when William recognizes his nephew. Finally
  the Franks defeat the Moors, set fire to Luiserna and take Vivien
  back to Narbonne. [→793, Aliscans/Chevalerie Vivien]
     Winter Court (Aachen): Charlemagne spends most re-
  maining winters in his new palace until his death.
     Harvests: Great famine. Cannibalism in some remote vil-
  lages! Charlemagne orders all bishops to distribute food to the
  hungry. Stewardship –15.
  aNNo 793
     May Field (Regensburg).
     Saxony, Frisia: The Frisians and Saxons revolt, again. They
  kill Duke Thierry of Ardennes in an ambush near the mouth of
  the River Weser. Bishop Liudger performs a miracle by healing
  the blind Frisian skald, Bernlef, and the rebellious Frisians per-
  manently convert to Christianity.
     British Isles: Danes sack the Abbey of Lindisfarne on the
  Northumbrian coast.
     Italy: King Pepin of Italy faces a rebellion led by the Duke
  of Benevento.
     Lion de Bourges: [←792] The Saracen princess Gracienne
  liberates her lover, William, from her father’s prison. Shortly
  after, she accepts baptism and they marry. William then travels
  to Bourges with Oliver, where they demand to blow the magic
  horn of the city. Since the horn is false, they both fail and are
  imprisoned. [→794]

  convince his son of his true identity, but Hadubrand believes
  his father to be dead. They do battle against one another and
                          n
  Hadubrand unknowingly kills his own father.
     Enfances Vivien: [←Prise d’Orange, 791] When Vivien comes
  of age, he refuses to become a merchant. Instead, he gathers a band
  of mercenaries and captures Luiserna. The Saracens besiege him,
  but Vivien vows never to retreat from pagans. When one of his
  mercenaries laments their precarious situation, Vivien throws him
  off the battlements. Vivien’s foster-mother arranges for his kins-
  men to help him in the battle. When William first meets Vivien
  on the field he attacks him, thinking that he must be a Saracen gi-
  ant. Their duel ends when William recognizes his nephew. Finally
  the Franks defeat the Moors, set fire to Luiserna and take Vivien
  back to Narbonne. [→793, Aliscans/Chevalerie Vivien]
     Winter Court (Aachen): Charlemagne spends most re-
  maining winters in his new palace until his death.
     Harvests: Great famine. Cannibalism in some remote vil-
  lages! Charlemagne orders all bishops to distribute food to the
  hungry. Stewardship –15.
  aNNo 793
     May Field (Regensburg).
     Saxony, Frisia: The Frisians and Saxons revolt, again. They
  kill Duke Thierry of Ardennes in an ambush near the mouth of
  the River Weser. Bishop Liudger performs a miracle by healing
  the blind Frisian skald, Bernlef, and the rebellious Frisians per-
  manently convert to Christianity.
     British Isles: Danes sack the Abbey of Lindisfarne on the
  Northumbrian coast.
     Italy: King Pepin of Italy faces a rebellion led by the Duke
  of Benevento.
     Lion de Bourges: [←792] The Saracen princess Gracienne
  liberates her lover, William, from her father’s prison. Shortly
  after, she accepts baptism and they marry. William then travels
  to Bourges with Oliver, where they demand to blow the magic
  horn of the city. Since the horn is false, they both fail and are
  imprisoned. [→794]

title: Phase 3: Consolidation
leftColumn:
Aliscans/Chevalerie Vivien: [←792, Enfances Vivien]
      Vivien leads an army into Spain for plunder. He sacks Barcelona
      and captures the cities of Tortosa and Portpaillart. Many
      Moorish warriors are slain or have their eyes cut out. Deramay,
      who briefly imprisons Emir Hisham and usurps the title of Emir
      of Cordoba, decides to counter-attack: he sails to Septimania,
      where he offers to do battle with Vivien and his young compan-
      ions. Uncle Gerard of Commarchis advises the youth to retire,
      but Vivien refuses because of his oath never to flee from the
      Saracens. He even disdains to send a messenger to call for help.
        Only in the middle of the Battle of the Archant, which is
      clearly turning to the advantage of the Moors, does Vivien call on
      his uncles. When William (wielding Joyeuse, which Charlemagne
      gave him) and his brothers finally arrive, Vivien is lying on the
      field in a pool of blood. William gives his nephew absolution be-
      fore he dies in his arms. Bertrand does not survive the battle either,
      and all the other Frankish counts have been taken prisoner by the
      Moors. William captures the horse Folatil and sets Beaucent free
      to prevent him from falling into Moorish hands.
        To avert a complete disaster, William rides to Orange to
      muster reinforcements. Guibourc first refuses to let him in, as
      she doesn’t recognize him and she is not used to seeing William
      flee from the enemy. The count then travels to Laon, where he
      meets Louis and Ernold, the royal seneschal.
        William is scorned for his shabby appearance, and, initially,
      the king refuses to send any troops. The Count is furious, and he
      openly insults and threatens King Louis and Queen Blancheflour.
      Princess Aelis offers herself as a hostage and William reconciles
      with her royal parents. Louis gives in and the Count is allowed
      to recruit as many knights as he can. He sees Rainouart, a rather
      oafish, but very strong, kitchen knave whom he takes with him.
        Back in Orange, Guibourc recognizes Rainouart as her own
      brother. The Franks avenge Vivien and the others in a second
      battle at the Archant. Some of the Franks desert, but Rainouart
      rallies them and leads them back to William’s army. Rainouart,
      who fights with a huge club, kills many pagans, including his own
      giant brothers, Jambu and Valegrape. He liberates the Frankish
      prisoners held captive on the Moorish galleys.
        Afterwards, William feasts in Orange, but forgets to thank
      Rainouart. He sends some knights to calm down his angry
      brother-in-law and bring him back to Orange. Rainouart is bap-
      tized and married to Aelis. He converts his cousin, Baudus, who
      comes to Orange where he is baptized at Rainouart’s marriage.
      [→793, La Bataille Loquifer]
        La Bataille Loquifer: [←793, Aliscans/Chevalerie Vivien]
      Deramay wants to spirit Rainouart and Aelis away on his ships,
      but after a short fight he abandons his plan and returns to
      his city of Loquiferne. Shortly after, Aelis dies giving birth to
      Maillefer. The Moors again attack, and Rainouart accepts a duel
      with the giant Loquifer, who, like Rainouart, fights with a large
      iron club. Both combatants try to convert each other, but in the
      end Rainouart slays Loquifer. To avenge themselves, the Moors
      send a thief-sorcerer, Picolet, who abducts Maillefer and takes
      him to Spain. The furious Rainouart kills Deramay in a duel.
rightColumn:
Rainouart falls asleep on the beach, where he is abducted
  by faeries who take him to the magic island of the dead. Morgan
  le Fay welcomes him. Rainouart has to fight an invulnerable
  giant cat, Chapalu, who is in fact a cursed knight who must
  drink Rainouart’s blood in order to be restored to his true form.
  During his stay on the island, Rainouart sleeps with Morgan,
  who later gives birth to a son named Corbon. He finally leaves
  on a boat together with Chapalu, but this cursed knight has been
  ordered to drown Rainouart, because Morgan wishes Corbon
  to inherit his domains. Some friendly sirens, whom Rainouart
  had spared earlier, take him on their back and depose him on
  the shores near his native city of Portpaillart in Spain. [→794,
  Moniage Rainouart]
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 794
     May Field (Frankfurt): Following the death of Queen
  Fastrada, Charlemagne marries the noble Liutgarde.
     The king orders a canal to be dug in order to link the Rhine
  to the Danube (the Fossa Carolina), but after a few months of
  fruitless labor, the project is abandoned due to heavy rains and
  dangerous mudslides.
     The Franks condemn the Byzantine use of religious icons
  (the Iconoclast Controversy) and the theological views called
  Adoptionism. Angilbert sends embassies to Constantinople and
  Jerusalem.
     Saxony: The king sends two armies into Saxony and
  the Saxons, seeing they are surrounded, promise to become
  Christians and be loyal to the king, but they have no intention
  of keeping their oaths.
     Lion de Bourges: [←793] After a vision telling him to help
  his sons, Lion comes to Bourges and receives the support of the
  White Knight, King Louis, and William Shortnose and his rela-
  tives. The Franks capture many Saracens. One of them indicates
  where the magic horn is buried. This time Lion and his sons suc-
  ceed in blowing it. [→798]
     Moniage Rainouart: [←793, Bataille Loquifer] Mad with
  grief over the loss of his wife, Rainouart attempts to enter the
  monastery of Brioude, despite being utterly unsuited to the con-
  templative life. When a Saracen army arrives, Rainouart briefly
  takes up arms again and defeats the pagans. He baptizes his baby
  son, Maillefer, and returns to the cloister.
     The monks are not happy with him and they even buy leop-
  ards to kill Rainouart, but their plan fails. The abbot renounc-
  es Christianity and finds a pretext to embark on a ship with all
  his monks, including Rainouart. The abbot has betrayed them
  to Moorish pirates who attack them. Rainouart is miraculous-
  ly saved, gets ashore, and takes possession of the tower of Aiète
  where Tiebaut’s treasure is hidden.
     The Moors challenge Rainouart to a duel with a monstrous
  knight named Gadifer, who rides a demonic war horse and uses
  a sort of golden armored chariot (called Travail) in which he is
  almost invulnerable. From Travail he shoots arrows at Rainouart

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
but, with God’s help, Rainouart succeeds in killing his oppo-
      nent. He returns to the monastery safely.
        A few months later, Rainouart dies of sadness. This is the
      sign for Tiebaut to plan another attack against the lands of the
      Narbonnais. [→801, La Mort Aymeri/Guibert d’Andrenas]
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 795

        May Field (Mayence).
        Saxony: The king campaigns in Saxony. Once the Saxons
      have been soundly beaten, their country laid waste and their hos-
      tages received, the king returns to his palace at Aachen.
        Quatre fils Aymon: [←773] Renaud and Maugis return
      to Frankland, where they present themselves as pilgrims at
      Charlemagne’s court. Renaud’s sons, Aymonnet and Yon, have
      grown up to become royal pages, as have Fulco’s sons Constant
      and Rohart. Fulco’s sons start a fight and end up accusing Renaud
      of having murdered their father by treason. Aymonnet (wielding
      Froberge), and his brother Yon (wielding Courtain) fight a judi-
      cial duel against the two traitor sons. The opposing factions both
      hide troops in the woods surrounding the field. When the fight
      turns to the advantage of Renaud’s sons, Grifo of Hautefeuille ad-
      vances his troops, but Renaud intercepts them and forces them to
      retreat. Aymonnet and Yon kill their adversaries. [→796]
        Duchesse Parise: [←781, Aye d’Avignon] Garnier’s daughter,
      Parise, marries Raymond of St. Gilles. When she gets pregnant,
      the traitors Berengier, Amaugin, Milo, Alori, and Hardrad send
      her poisoned apples to kill her, but her brother-in-law, Bevis, eats
      them instead and dies. The traitors then accuse Parise of hav-
      ing killed Bevis. Milo pretends to defend her honor, but loses
      on purpose, so Parise is condemned and sent into exile. She is
      accompanied by some loyal knights. [→796]
        British Isles: A commercial and military treaty is signed
      with Offa of Mercia. In return, he pays a poll-tax of one denier
      per house to Charlemagne, who collects the money and sends it
      to the pope.
        Rome: On Christmas day, Pope Hadrian dies and is re-
      placed by Leo III. The new Pope is elected without the consul-
      tation of the Roman aristocracy. He favors talented clerks over
      the local nobles’ sons, which does not make him very popular.
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 796
        May Field (Paderborn).
        Avarland: Assisted by the paladin Eric of Friuli and the
      Slav chieftain Vojnomir, King Pepin forces his way through the
      Ring of the Avars. The Franks capture a large booty and send
      fifteen wagons filled with treasure to Aachen. The Avar Tudun
      surrenders and is baptized Theodore. Avarland is Christianized
      by the Archbishopric of Salzburg.
        Religion: Alcuin becomes Abbot of St. Martin’s in Tours.
rightColumn:
Duchesse Parise: [←795] In Asturias, Parise gives birth to a
  boy, Hugo, who gets stolen by brigands and sold to the king, who
  raises him as his own son. Despairing, Parise travels to Cologne.
  [→796, Guy de Nanteuil]
     Guy de Nanteuil: [←796, Duchesse Parise] Guy vows to
  avenge his father’s death. He promises his mother’s hand to his
  Moorish foster-father, Ganor, in return for aid. Ganor and Guy
  lead an army to Avignon, where Guy kills Milo in battle. Ganor
  is baptized and marries Aye. She gives him two sons, Anthony
  and Richier. [→804]
     British Isles: The death of King Offa of Mercia unleashes
  revolt among the kingdom’s tributary regions. Offa’s son, Ecfrid,
  succeeds as king. In Northumberland, Offa’s brother-in-law is
  murdered. Eardwulf becomes King of Northumbria.
     Quatre fils Aymon: [←795] Renaud leaves his family and re-
  tires as a simple, anonymous worker at the cathedral of Cologne
  to repent for his sins. [→797]
     Gormond and Isembart: While Sir Isembart is away from
  home, fighting for King Louis, the monks of Saint Riquier seize
  legal control of his holdings and castle. When he returns home,
  he is denied access to his domains. He calls on the king for help,
  but Louis ignores his vassal. [→797]
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 797
     May Field (Aachen).
     Saxony: After a short but violent campaign, Charlemagne
  receives the submission of the whole Saxon people. He contin-
  ues the deportation of Saxons into Frankland and the distribu-
  tion of Saxon domains to his loyal followers.
     Italy, Avarland: Eric of Friuli crushes Avar raiders.
  Charlemagne appoints his loyal friend Arno as the Archbishop
  of Salzburg.
     Byzantium: Palace revolution in Constantinople: Irene has
  her own son blinded and is crowned Empress of Byzantium. The
  Franks judge that there is no emperor in the East, and that the
  throne lays vacant.
     Religion: Datheus of Milan founds the first known or-
  phanage, wishing to stop parents from killing children whose
  birth they want to conceal.
     Spain: Emir Hisham, fearing rumors about traitors, slaugh-
  ters thousands at Toledo, in an event called the “Day of the Ditch.”
     Quatre fils Aymon: [←796] The other workers at the cathedral
  of Cologne become jealous of Renaud. They kill him and throw his
  body into the Rhine. His body is found and brought to the Bishop,
  who sanctifies Renaud and displays his relics inside the cathedral.
                              n
  The tomb of Saint Renaud rapidly attracts many pilgrims.
     Gormond and Isembart: [←796] The furious Isembart
  goes into exile to Cornwall, where he renounces Christ and joins
  the pagan lord, Gormond. He helps to capture a city by means of
  birds which transport flaming oil and urges Gormond to invade
  his rich Frankish homeland. [→798]

title: Phase 4: Empire & Decline
leftColumn:
Winter Court (Aachen): Charlemagne receives many am-
      bassadors: Moorish rebels led by Bahaluc, the Wali of Barcelona;
      an envoy from the governor of Sicily; a delegation from the new
      Khan of the Avars; and some Saxon princes. Isaac the Jew re-
      turns from his embassy with many wonderful presents from the
      Persian caliph, including a white elephant.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 798
        May Field (Detmold).
        Denmark: Frankish ambassadors sent to the Danish King
      Sigfrid are ambushed and killed.
        Saxony: Charlemagne lays waste to the whole of Saxony
      and takes many hostages, including some of the most treacher-
      ous Saxon nobles.
        Lion de Bourges: [←794] In a fight pitting William and
      Gerard against the jealous Henry of Palermo, the latter slays his
      rivals and flees to Cathay with his new wife Suzanne (formerly
                                     n
      Margalie, Synagon’s wife). Oliver pursues Henry but is slain.
        Gormond and Isembart: [←797] Pagans from Cornwall
      meet the Franks in battle near the abbey of St. Riquier, where
      King Louis kills Gormond. The pagans start retreating, but
      stand their ground when Isembart takes command. He un-
      horses his own father, Bernard, without recognizing him, but
      Isembart is finally killed. Just before he dies, the apostate returns
             n
      to Christianity.
        Winter Court (Aachen): Froia, the Asturian legate, offers
      a magnificent pavilion as a gift to Charlemagne. King Alfonso of
      Asturias plunders Luiserna.
        The bishops Theodulf of Orleans and Leidrad of Lyon are
      sent as missi dominici to inspect Provence and Septimania.
        Charlemagne receives an embassy of peace from Empress
      Irene of Byzantium, who offers Charlemagne the Crown of
      Thorns and the imperial title.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 799
        May Field (Aachen).
        Septimania, Provence, Aquitaine: Saracen pirates at-
      tack merchants in the western Mediterranean. Vikings raid the
      Aquitainian coast.
        Rome: Pope Leo III is brutally assaulted during a religious
      procession in Rome. The Romans capture the Pope, blind him,
      tear his tongue out, and cast him into a prison at the Greek
      monastery of Saint Erasmus (indicating the Byzantines were in-
      volved). But the Pope miraculously heals.
        “By His work and the intercession of the blessed apostle
      Peter, that the aforesaid Pope both regained his sight and had
      his tongue restored to him for speaking.” Life of Leo III
        The Pope manages to escape and, escorted by Duke Winichis
      of Spoleto, travels to Paderborn where he meets Charlemagne.
      He goes back to Rome accompanied by many bishops, a guard of
      scarae and some missi to investigate the conspiracy.
rightColumn:
Avarland: The Avars revolt once more and they treacher-
  ously kill Gerold II of Bavaria and Eric of Friuli in an ambush.
  The Lombard Aio becomes the new Duke of Friuli, while
  Gerold is replaced by a pair of governors. A Bulgar-Frankish alli-
  ance finally annihilates the rebellious Avars.
     Brittany: Count Wido, commander of the Breton March,
  conquers the whole of Brittany.
     Winter Court (Aachen): The emperor receives envoys
  from Harun al-Rashid. In return, Charlemagne sends Isaac the
  Jew to Byzantium, the Holy Land and Persia.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 800
     May Field (Mayence): Queen Liutgard dies.
     Rome: Charlemagne decides that the papal situation in
  Rome needs his personal attention: he travels to Rome with
  almost his entire court. On his way, he stops to check the
  coastal defenses and to visit Abbot Alcuin at the tomb of St.
  Martin at Tours.
     After arriving in Rome, Charlemagne liberates the city
  with the help of the Frisian leader Sir Magnus. He then im-
  mediately organizes a trial for Pope Leo, who takes an oath of
  innocence. His opponents, Campulus and Paschalis, are sent
  into exile in Frankland.
     On Christmas Day, Pope Leo celebrates mass in St. Peter’s.
  He bows to Charlemagne and presents the Frankish king with
  a golden crown: Charlemagne crowns himself as Holy Roman
  Emperor. He lets his beard grow long as a sign of imperial dig-
  nity. King Charlot is crowned co-emperor of the Franks.
     Charlemagne travels back to Aachen via Lombardy, taking
  with him a giant bronze statue of Theodoric the Great.
     Italy: King Pepin conducts raids into Benevento.
     Spain: Against the advice of Sancho the Gascon, King
  Louis and William Shortnose lead an army into Spain. They
  take Lerida and lay siege to Barcelona.
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

  Phase    4: Empire   &  Decline

  (801–814)

  Customs

  F
      eudalism: The practice of “scutage” comes into use,
      where a lord pays a simple “shield fee” instead of showing
      up himself or providing troops for the king.
     Truce of God: Even converted Saxons and Slavs learn to
  respect the sacred days of peace.
     Knighthood: Some opulently wealthy merchants and re-
  nowned artisans try to buy titles and even land from impover-
  ished nobles, as do particularly greedy abbots.

title: Warfare
leftColumn:
Heraldry: Commoners in the household of a knight wear
      colored badges for prestige and identification.
        Tournaments: The extravagance of tournaments reaches its
      peak. They become more theatrical, with associated pageantry in
      parades and feasting. Knights are now obliged to stake their equip-
      ment for all events, including the jousting competition and the
      melee. This results in the advent of professional “tourney-knights”
      who specialize in fighting in tourneys for themselves or in the ser-
      vice of a rich lord. Such a tourney-lord shares the gains and creates
      a personal treasury of horses and armor to pay for possible losses.
        Women: The values of dowries rises.
        Chivalry: This most noble code of conduct has become the
      international standard for knights and ladies of honor.
        Romance: Now a common practice around the feudalized
      world.
        Fashion: Clothes become even more stylish and expen-
      sive than before. Men’s sleeves are wide and full, gathered at the
      wrist. The tabard (a loose tunic with wide sleeves) is the favored
      clothing over armor.
        Women’s capes are so long they often drag on the ground.
      Frivolous hats come into fashion, such as tall, pointy cones with a vel-
      vet roll around the head and a veil of muslin over the face and neck.
      Warfare

        Armor: Full plate armor (16 points) comes into use during this
      phase, fully covering the body and limbs. At first it is possessed only
      by the wealthiest of lords, but it fairly quickly becomes common-
      place among knights of all rank. Helms are lighter than previously;
      closed with a detachable visor, often with a pointed “dog-face.”
        Weapons: Halberds complete the panoply of available op-
      tions for warriors in a melee. They are especially appreciated by
      militiamen, foot soldiers and garrisons. Lastly, the Britons intro-
      duce the longbow at the end of Charlemagne’s reign.
        Horses: Destriers rapidly replace chargers as the standard
      mount for all those who can afford it. Rich knights are willing to
      pay even more for the Frisian destrier, though they remain rare.
        Partial plate horse barding (12 points) is used to protect
      destriers capable of bearing it along with a rider.
        Attack-trained horses, capable of fighting along with their rid-
      er, become available. Such training doubles the cost of the horse.
        Castles: The new fashion is the concentric castle with rings
      of strong defensive works built in such a way that the inner walls
      are close to the outer, effectively adding both defensive values.
      Extra strength is built on the outer defenses of the gates as bar-
      bicans. The great cost of these is due to the skill needed, which
      generally only a few scholars from the Palace Academy possess.
        Levy Troops: Chivalrous or Christian knights from out-
      side Frankland occasionally join the Frankish forces with the
      aim to conquer pagan lands.
      aNNo 801
        May Field (Aachen): The Basques of Pamplona and
      Navarra pay a tribute to the Franks.

La Mort Aymeri/Guibert d’Andrenas: [←794, Moniage
  Rainouart] As Aymeri lies ill in his bed, he dreams that he will
  die gloriously in battle. He refuses to give his fief to one of his
  sons, urging them instead to conquer lands for themselves.
  Aymeri leaves Narbonne to his adoptive son, Aymeriet. He pro-
  poses to capture the Moorish city of Andrenas for his youngest
  son, Gilbert, where he can marry the beautiful Princess Augaiete.
     The Narbonnais assemble their army and leave for Spain. They
  lay siege to the city of Balaguer, whose Wali, Baudu, they take prison-
  er. The Moor agrees to convert, but when the Franks slaughter the
  citizens of Balaguer, he renounces his oath and travels to Andrenas
  to warn the wali of the city of the coming of the Narbonnais.
     The Franks besiege the city and a great battle ensues in which
  Count Aymeri is captured but protected by Princess Augaiete, who
  wishes to marry Gilbert. After a last full scale attack, the victorious
  Franks kill or convert all the Moors, but Count Aymeri is killed in
  battle by centaurs. Baudu accepts baptism and receives Balaguer as a
  fief from Gilbert, who marries the pretty Augaiete. Gilbert is made
  the new Count of the city of Andrenas, which he defends with
  Huon of Floriville and their men. [→802, Siège de Barbastre]
     Spain: King Louis and Count William capture Barcelona.
  They install Bera as the new Count of the city.
     Gascony: During King Louis’ absence, several Gascon no-
  bles revolt.
     Simon de Pouilles: A Saracen embassy perishes at sea. The
  Sultan suspects that the Franks killed them. He raises an army and
  invades the Holy Land. When Charlemagne hears this, he sends
  twelve counts to Jerusalem. Unfortunately, the Frankish counts ar-
  rive on the same day as the Saracen army and are all taken prisoner.
  They pretend to be simple merchants, so the Saracens put them
  to the test by making them ride a horse or joust. The counts take
  advantage of the available equipment and horses to escape. They
  encounter the Saracen seneschal, Synados, and defeat his men in
  combat. Synados wishes to convert and invites the Franks into
  his coastal castle of Abilant. When Synados’ nephew, Cristamant,
  learns of his uncle’s intention to abandon the pagan gods, he be-
  trays his uncle to the Sultan. The Persians attack Castle Abilant and
  capture Synados, who is sent to prison. The Franks find out about
  Cristamant’s treason and throw him off a tower. The Sultan asks
  his daughter, Licorinde, to bring him Synados. But the princess
  falls in love with Synados and promises to help him and to convert
  as well. The court enchanter, Hunaut, tells his Sultan of a way to
  capture the Franks. Licorinde overhears his plan. She sets Synados
  free and together they follow the enchanter to Abilant, where
  Synados slays him. The Franks welcome the convert back into his
  own castle. One night during the siege, the Frankish Count Simon
  goes to the harbor to buy food supplies from a Saracen merchant,
  Sorbaré, but they get caught by the Saracens, who bring them to
  the Sultan. The court priest tries to convert Simon to their pagan
  worship, but Simon kills the man and smashes his idols. He sets
  Sorbaré free and together they escape. Disguised as Saracens, they
  return to Castle Abilant with Princess Licorinde. [→802]
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.

title: Phase 4: Empire
leftColumn:
aNNo 802
        May Field (Aachen): A Byzantine embassy arrives with a
      marriage proposal from Empress Irene, but she is exiled before
      Charlemagne’s ambassadors return to Constantinople with an
      answer.
        Avarland: The Avars revolt and kill the Frankish counts
      Cadaloc and Gothelam. Charlemagne sends an army and all re-
      bellious Avar princes are either captured and baptized, or killed.
        Italy: King Pepin of Italy conquers Apulia. Duke Winigise
      of Spoleto becomes Duke of Apulia.
        Spain: King Louis defeats the Moors at Tortosa.
        Le Siège de Barbastre: [←801, Guibert d’Andrenas] Guy is
      about to be knighted when the Saracens, led by Corsolt, attack
      Gascoigne and Narbonne, where they capture Bevis and his sons.
      The Franks are taken to Barbastro (south of the Pyrenees), where
      they are thrown into a prison overrun by a giant fire-breathing
      serpent. A disgruntled pagan named Clairon of Valdoine helps
      the Christian prisoners. They baptize him, and in return he gives
      them weapons and armor, so they can seize control of Barbastro.
      The local population is baptized and pledges their fealty to
      Clairon. The Franks send a message to King Louis. The king
      and William, Ernold of Beaulande, Aimer the Puny, Gilbert
      of Andrenas, Garin of Anjou and Walter of Toulouse travel
      to Barbastro. Libanor, a noble Saracen, unsuccessfully tries to
      convert Gerard. Later Gerard rescues Libanor from drowning.
      With the help of four enamored Moorish princesses (Malatrie,
      Almarinde, Blancandine and Alfanie) the Franks eventually
      manage to defeat the besieging Saracens, but Gerard of Amiens
      is killed in battle. The Franks plunder Cordoba and slaughter
      its population. Some Moorish princes agree to convert: Fabur is
      baptized William and Libanor as Louis. Young Gerard marries
      the converted Malatrie, formerly Libanor’s fiancée. All noble
      converts are rewarded: Clarion becomes the Lord of Barbastro,
      Libanor is given Lerida and Morinde, while Fabur receives the
      city of Pamplona. [→807, Prise de Cordres et de Sebille]
        Simon de Pouilles: [←801] Sorbaré sails to Frankland and in-
      forms Charlemagne about the counts’ situation. He converts and
      is baptized as Simon the Convert. He sails back to Abilant, but is
      betrayed by his men, who warn the Saracens. The Sultan’s men
      assail the castle and capture Synados and Licorinde. Count Simon
      disguises himself as a Saracen and presents himself at the sultan’s
      court, where he learns of their next ambush. Finally, the Franks
      send Simon the Convert and two counts to Jerusalem and Aachen
      to ask for military assistance. The united Christian forces defeat
      the Saracens and kill the Sultan. Back in Frankland, Synados and
      Licorinde are baptized and married. Together with Simon the
                                  n
      Convert they enter Count Simon of Apulia’s household.
        British Isles: Egbert is crowned King of Wessex.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 803
        May Field (Mayence): Envoys from Byzantium arrive with
      peace proposals, but Charlemagne declines their offer.
        Religion: Bishops are forbidden to bear arms in battle.
rightColumn:
The emperor sends missi to Mantua to investigate the verity of
  a relic containing the blood of Christ, venerated by the local popu-
  lation. Even the Pope travels to Lombardy to see what’s going on.
     Bulgaria: Krum is crowned Khan of Bulgaria (803–814).
  He welcomes many Avar refugees who fled Frankish dominion.
     Winter Court (Aachen): An earthquake shakes the palace.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 804

     May Field (Paderborn): Slav leaders present gifts and
  pledge fealty.
     Saxony: Charlemagne campaigns in Saxony against the last
  rebellious tribes. He founds the town of Hamburg.
     Brittany: The Bretons revolt. Again.
     Denmark: King Godfrid II of Denmark builds the
  Danevirke, a great rampart to protect his lands from
  Charlemagne’s approaching army.
     Guy de Nanteuil: [←796] Floriant and Hervieu of Lyon false-
  ly accuse Guy of having murdered Milo at the siege of Avignon.
  Guy is ambushed, but kills Floriant and escapes unharmed.
  Charlemagne orders the two feuding parties to make peace.
     Ayglentine of Gascony arrives at court and falls in love
  with Guy, but Charlemagne wants to marry her to Hervieu. The
  Gascon princess refuses, so Hervieu challenges Guy to a duel.
  Guy defeats his opponent, but the combat degenerates into a
  small but bloody battle between the opposing factions.
     Charlemagne still wants to marry off Ayglentine to Hervieu,
  despite her refusal, so two of Guy’s vassals abduct her and bring
  her to Nanteuil. Ignoring the advice of Ogier and Naymo,
  Charlemagne decides to attack Guy. Even though his small army
  is defeated, he still captures Ayglentine. [→805]
     Winter Court (Aachen): Death of Alcuin.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 805
     May Field (Aachen): The emperor gives his time to hunt-
  ing in several of his palaces, then settles for the winter in his pal-
  ace at Thionville, where he is joined by his sons Pepin and Louis
  for Christmas.
     Slavonia: Charlemagne sends an army under Charlot into the
  country of the Slavs, whose leader, Lecho, is killed in battle. Young
  Charlot conquers Bohemia and Carinthia, and then quashes the rem-
  nants of the Avar rebellion, started in 799. The new khagan of the
  Avars is baptized Abraham. The newly conquered region becomes
  the Eastern Mark (Ostmark), defended by the fortress of Magdeburg.
     Guy de Nanteuil: [←804] During a short period of peace,
  Charlemagne prepares a siege of Nanteuil. However, Guy
  launches his troops, together with those of Ganor, who has come
  to aid him, against the royal army. The captive Ayglentine en-
  courages her beloved Guy, who slays his rival Hervieu. Samson
  and Amaugin are killed. Charlemagne makes peace with Guy,
  who is finally allowed to marry Ayglentine. Ganor returns to
  Aigremor. [→813, Duchesse Parise]

segments.text:
aNNo 802
        May Field (Aachen): A Byzantine embassy arrives with a
      marriage proposal from Empress Irene, but she is exiled before
      Charlemagne’s ambassadors return to Constantinople with an
      answer.
        Avarland: The Avars revolt and kill the Frankish counts
      Cadaloc and Gothelam. Charlemagne sends an army and all re-
      bellious Avar princes are either captured and baptized, or killed.
        Italy: King Pepin of Italy conquers Apulia. Duke Winigise
      of Spoleto becomes Duke of Apulia.
        Spain: King Louis defeats the Moors at Tortosa.
        Le Siège de Barbastre: [←801, Guibert d’Andrenas] Guy is
      about to be knighted when the Saracens, led by Corsolt, attack
      Gascoigne and Narbonne, where they capture Bevis and his sons.
      The Franks are taken to Barbastro (south of the Pyrenees), where
      they are thrown into a prison overrun by a giant fire-breathing
      serpent. A disgruntled pagan named Clairon of Valdoine helps
      the Christian prisoners. They baptize him, and in return he gives
      them weapons and armor, so they can seize control of Barbastro.
      The local population is baptized and pledges their fealty to
      Clairon. The Franks send a message to King Louis. The king
      and William, Ernold of Beaulande, Aimer the Puny, Gilbert
      of Andrenas, Garin of Anjou and Walter of Toulouse travel
      to Barbastro. Libanor, a noble Saracen, unsuccessfully tries to
      convert Gerard. Later Gerard rescues Libanor from drowning.
      With the help of four enamored Moorish princesses (Malatrie,
      Almarinde, Blancandine and Alfanie) the Franks eventually
      manage to defeat the besieging Saracens, but Gerard of Amiens
      is killed in battle. The Franks plunder Cordoba and slaughter
      its population. Some Moorish princes agree to convert: Fabur is
      baptized William and Libanor as Louis. Young Gerard marries
      the converted Malatrie, formerly Libanor’s fiancée. All noble
      converts are rewarded: Clarion becomes the Lord of Barbastro,
      Libanor is given Lerida and Morinde, while Fabur receives the
      city of Pamplona. [→807, Prise de Cordres et de Sebille]
        Simon de Pouilles: [←801] Sorbaré sails to Frankland and in-
      forms Charlemagne about the counts’ situation. He converts and
      is baptized as Simon the Convert. He sails back to Abilant, but is
      betrayed by his men, who warn the Saracens. The Sultan’s men
      assail the castle and capture Synados and Licorinde. Count Simon
      disguises himself as a Saracen and presents himself at the sultan’s
      court, where he learns of their next ambush. Finally, the Franks
      send Simon the Convert and two counts to Jerusalem and Aachen
      to ask for military assistance. The united Christian forces defeat
      the Saracens and kill the Sultan. Back in Frankland, Synados and
      Licorinde are baptized and married. Together with Simon the
                                  n
      Convert they enter Count Simon of Apulia’s household.
        British Isles: Egbert is crowned King of Wessex.
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 803
        May Field (Mayence): Envoys from Byzantium arrive with
      peace proposals, but Charlemagne declines their offer.
        Religion: Bishops are forbidden to bear arms in battle.

The emperor sends missi to Mantua to investigate the verity of
  a relic containing the blood of Christ, venerated by the local popu-
  lation. Even the Pope travels to Lombardy to see what’s going on.
     Bulgaria: Krum is crowned Khan of Bulgaria (803–814).
  He welcomes many Avar refugees who fled Frankish dominion.
     Winter Court (Aachen): An earthquake shakes the palace.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 804

May Field (Paderborn): Slav leaders present gifts and
  pledge fealty.
     Saxony: Charlemagne campaigns in Saxony against the last
  rebellious tribes. He founds the town of Hamburg.
     Brittany: The Bretons revolt. Again.
     Denmark: King Godfrid II of Denmark builds the
  Danevirke, a great rampart to protect his lands from
  Charlemagne’s approaching army.
     Guy de Nanteuil: [←796] Floriant and Hervieu of Lyon false-
  ly accuse Guy of having murdered Milo at the siege of Avignon.
  Guy is ambushed, but kills Floriant and escapes unharmed.
  Charlemagne orders the two feuding parties to make peace.
     Ayglentine of Gascony arrives at court and falls in love
  with Guy, but Charlemagne wants to marry her to Hervieu. The
  Gascon princess refuses, so Hervieu challenges Guy to a duel.
  Guy defeats his opponent, but the combat degenerates into a
  small but bloody battle between the opposing factions.
     Charlemagne still wants to marry off Ayglentine to Hervieu,
  despite her refusal, so two of Guy’s vassals abduct her and bring
  her to Nanteuil. Ignoring the advice of Ogier and Naymo,
  Charlemagne decides to attack Guy. Even though his small army
  is defeated, he still captures Ayglentine. [→805]
     Winter Court (Aachen): Death of Alcuin.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 805
     May Field (Aachen): The emperor gives his time to hunt-
  ing in several of his palaces, then settles for the winter in his pal-
  ace at Thionville, where he is joined by his sons Pepin and Louis
  for Christmas.
     Slavonia: Charlemagne sends an army under Charlot into the
  country of the Slavs, whose leader, Lecho, is killed in battle. Young
  Charlot conquers Bohemia and Carinthia, and then quashes the rem-
  nants of the Avar rebellion, started in 799. The new khagan of the
  Avars is baptized Abraham. The newly conquered region becomes
  the Eastern Mark (Ostmark), defended by the fortress of Magdeburg.
     Guy de Nanteuil: [←804] During a short period of peace,
  Charlemagne prepares a siege of Nanteuil. However, Guy
  launches his troops, together with those of Ganor, who has come
  to aid him, against the royal army. The captive Ayglentine en-
  courages her beloved Guy, who slays his rival Hervieu. Samson
  and Amaugin are killed. Charlemagne makes peace with Guy,
  who is finally allowed to marry Ayglentine. Ganor returns to
  Aigremor. [→813, Duchesse Parise]

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
Spain: Emir Hisham of Cordoba crucifies 72 Moorish
      conspirators. In response, rebellions break out all over his lands,
      lasting until 815.
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Famine. The Emperor orders fixed prices for all
      foodstuffs, and forbids their exportation. Stewardship –10.
      aNNo 806
        May Field (Aachen): The emperor makes arrangements
      for the division of his empire among his sons (the “divisio regno-
      rum”): Louis will reign over the western empire, Pepin over Italy,
      and Charlot in the east.
        Slavonia: Armies are sent into the lands of the Slavs along
      the Elbe River and in Bohemia. The Slav leader Miliduoch is
      killed in battle.
        Italy: The Byzantines defeat the Franks and capture Venice.
        Corsica: The coast is defended against Moorish pirates, who
      nevertheless raid some monasteries and sell the monks as slaves.

        Spanish March: Navarra and Pamplona in northeastern
      Spain are once again placed under the Emperor’s authority after
      a Basque revolt.
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 807
        May Field (Aachen): Charlemagne receives an envoy from
      Harun al-Rashid, who brings him many fine gifts, including a
      marvelous water clock.
        Patriarch Thomas of Jerusalem sends an embassy of monks.
        King Pepin of Italy makes peace with Byzantium.

        Spain, Italy: The Moors on Sardinia and Corsica are de-
      feated and put to flight.
        Prise de Cordres et de Sebille: [←802, Siège de Barbastre]
      William’s nephew, Bertrand, is freed from a Saracen prison in
      Cordoba by Nubie, the daughter of the local wali. Together they
      escape, and while the Saracens chase them, the Franks briefly
      take the city of Cordoba. They free Gilbert of Andrenas, who
      was imprisoned there. Bertrand marries the converted Nubie.
      [→810, Enfances Renier]
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Bad; Stewardship –5.
      aNNo 808
        May Field (Aachen).
        Slavonia: The emperor and Prince Charlot defeat a Danish-
      Slav alliance at the River Elbe. The Danish Prince Reginald is
      killed in battle.
        British Isles: Eardwulf, King of the Northumbrians, is de-
      posed from his throne and driven from his country. Eardwulf
      meets with the emperor and proceeds on to Rome. On his re-
      turn, Charlemagne sends Eardwulf back to Northumbria with
      envoys of the Pope.
rightColumn:
Spain: Louis the Pious lays siege to Tortosa, which is de-
  fended by Prince Abdul Rahman II.
     Winter Court (Aachen): A comet is seen in the sky.
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 809

     May Field (Aachen).
     Italy: A fleet from Byzantium skirmishes with the forces of
  King Pepin of Italy.
     Corsica: The Saracens invade and conquer the island.
     Spain: King Louis continues the siege of Tortosa.
     Saxony: Charlemagne raises a defensive fortification on the
  Elbe River.
     Persia: Death of Harun al-Rashid. Al-Amin becomes the
  new caliph of Persia. Civil war breaks out.
     Huon de Bordeaux: At the Pentecost court, Amaury ac-
  cuses Huon (one of the twelve peers) and his brother Gerard
  of treason: that they haven’t pledged fealty for their fief since
  their father died seven years ago. So Charlemagne orders the
  two brothers to come to his court to do homage. On the way
  to Paris, Huon and Gerard are ambushed by an anonymous
  knight. Gerard is heavily wounded, while Huon kills his as-
  sailant. Shortly after Huon arrives in Paris, Amaury the traitor
  brings the lifeless body of Charlot to court and accuses Huon of
  murder. While the young paladin doesn’t deny he killed Charlot,
  he claims it was in self-defense and that he wasn’t aware of the
  identity of his opponent. Charlemagne wants to kill Huon,
  but finally follows the council of the peers and accepts a duel
  between Amaury and Huon, stating that he will accept the out-
  come only if one of the combatants admits his wrongs. Huon
  kills Amaury in the fight, but unfortunately the emperor doesn’t
  hear Amaury when he confesses his treason with his last breath
  (it was he who convinced Charlot to attack Huon and Gerard).
  Charlemagne therefore banishes Huon, sending him to Babylon
  where he must kill a Saracen at Sultan Gaudisso’s court, kiss the
  Sultan’s daughter, and bring back the Sultan’s mustache and four
  teeth. He cannot return to Bordeaux before having completed
  this mission, on the penalty of death. [→810]
     Aiol: [←791] Aiol sets out to reconquer his father’s lands
  as a young impoverished knight, wearing his father’s armor and
  riding his father’s steed, Marchegai. In his search for adventure,
  he proves his valor against the Saracens, chases some thieves
  pillaging an abbey, slays a lion which terrorized the countryside
  around Poitiers for months, and makes friends with a rich pil-
  grim — Duke Renier of Gascony. Everywhere he goes people
  mock him for his rusty and old-fashioned equipment, but he
  remains stoic. One day he arrives at Blois, where he is lodged
  by his aunt, Isabelle. Her daughter, Lusiane, immediately falls in
  love with the young knight, but Aiol ignores her even after she
  openly declares her feelings. [→810]
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Bad. Heavy rains cause floods which destroy har-
  vests all over Frankland. Stewardship –5.

title: Phase 4: Empire
leftColumn:
aNNo 810
        May Field (Aachen): Charlemagne orders a collection for
      the churches of Jerusalem.
        The Emperor orders the construction of defensive fleets in
      both the north and the south of his empire.
        Italy: King Pepin recaptures Venice from the Byzantines
      and raids the shores of Dalmatia.
        The Moors raid Sardinia.
        Denmark: King Godfrid II and his Danes invade Frisia and
      take great tributes of silver from the vanquished Frisians. The
      Emperor raises his army to do battle with Godfrid, but the army
      of the Danes returns home and Godfrid is murdered by one of
      his retainers during a hunt. Hemming II, Godfrid’s son, succeeds
      his father and makes peace with the Emperor after Charlemagne
      threatens to massacre all Danish boys and men taller than a
      sword (the Treaty of Heiligen).
        Aiol: [←809] At Orleans King Louis, Aiol’s cousin, is wag-
      ing war against Macharias, the false Count of Bourges. Aiol is
      unaware of this, and challenges the King’s knights for glory. He
      defeats four of them, but then the Count of Bourges launches an
      attack against the King’s men. In the ensuing battle, Aiol man-
      ages to capture the rebel Count and hands him over to the King.
      When he learns his relation to the king, he reconciles Louis and
      Elie. Aiol, who still hasn’t revealed his true identity to the king,
      becomes a respected member of Louis’ court. The king gives
      him many gifts, which the young knight distributes among his
      friends and followers. [→811]
        Spain: Light Frankish troops advance secretly during the
      night. They take boats to cross the Ebro, but the horse dung
      alerts the Saracens in Tortosa, which can no longer be taken
      by surprise. The Franks accept peace negotiations with Emir
      Tiebaut.
        Enfances Renier: [←807, Prise de Cordres et de Sebille] At
      the birth of Renier, Maillefer decides to conquer Loquiferne for
      his son. Unfortunately, Grymbert steals the infant from the cas-
      tle of Portpaillart and sells him to the local wali, who wants to
      feed the child to the lions, but the beasts refuse. After this mira-
      cle, the Moor decides to let his daughter raise the boy.
        Maillefer and William conquer Loquiferne, while Emir
      Tiebaut flees to Candie.
        Guibourc dies of old age and illness. [→810, Foulque de
      Candie]
        Foulque de Candie: [←810, Enfances Renier] Emir Tiebaut
      besieges Orange, his former fief, and takes some prisoners, in-
      cluding Vivien’s brother Guy and both of Bevis of Commarchis’
      sons. Tiebaut’s sister, Anfelise, has come with him, for she is se-
      cretly in love with Fulco, whom she sees for the first time when
      he arrives with his troops.
        In a sea battle, Fulco rescues the Frankish prisoners. Anfelise
      sends Fulco a love message and a golden ring. They meet secretly
      and Fulco promises to marry her soon.
        Bertrand and Bernard come to William’s aid (of all Aymeri’s
      sons, only Bevis de Commarchis, William, and Bertrand are still
rightColumn:
alive). While Tiebaut plunders a nearby abbey, William con-
  ducts a successful sortie and kills many Moors.
     The Franks call on King Louis for help. The royal army
  forces the Moors to break the siege and retreat to Spain. The
  Franks pursue them to the castle of Arrabloi, where they besiege
  Tiebaut. Anfelise is captured, baptized and married to Fulco.
  Povreveu, who was raised at Tiebaut’s court, wounds Fulco in
  battle. He is recognized by his father, Guy, who wishes to con-
  vert his estranged son. When the cruel Corsuble of Algiers at-
  tacks Guy, Povreveu saves his father and joins his family. He is
  baptized.
     In the next battle, Povreveu kills Corsuble and captures
  three Moorish princesses, who are baptized and married:
  Povreveu weds Ganite, Bertrand receives the hand of Ayglente,
  and Guy, son of Bevis Cornebut, marries Amanevie. All pagan
  prisoners are baptized and set free. King Louis grants a truce to
  the Saracens and gives Spain to Fulco. [→810, Moniage William]
     Moniage William: [←810, Foulque de Candie] Now that the
  Franks are at peace with Emir Tiebaut, William leaves Orange to
  his godson, Maillefer, and retires to a monastery to pay for his
  sins. At the monastery, his warrior habits annoy the monks, who
  plot his death. They send him on an errand, unarmed, through a
  forest infested with brigands. William kills or chases them using
  the leg of his horse as a weapon, and God miraculously heals the
  loyal animal afterward. During a Saracen raid, William briefly
  takes up arms again to defend his homeland.
     Back in the monastery, he decides to become a hermit in
  the deserted rocky plains north of Montpellier. There he finds
  an abandoned manor and the ruins of a tower, which he makes
  his new home. God clears the site of snakes and other vermin.
  His presence attracts a cannibalistic giant, which he fights and
  kills. He then tries to resume his harsh but peaceful life, but
  Saracen raiders find him. He is overwhelmed by their numbers,
  captured, and taken to Palermo where he is thrown into a se-
  cret, foul prison filled with serpents. Charlemagne sends many
  knights to search for him, but no one can find him. [→811]
     Huon de Bordeaux: [←809] Together with eleven of his
  most loyal knights, Huon travels first to Rome to meet the Pope,
  a relative of his, to get absolution for his sins. He continues his
  voyage to Brindisi, an Italian harbor, where he meets Garin the
  sailor (another relative), who accompanies him to the Holy
  Land. Here, they meet a hermit named Jerome (Sherasmin),
  who turns out to be one of Huon’s late father’s loyal knights, who
  agrees to be their guide across the East. While passing through
  an enchanted forest, they meet Oberon, the faerie king. He gives
  Huon two valuable magical objects to help him: a golden goblet
  which fills itself automatically with any desired drink as long as
  the man who holds it is virtuous, and an ivory horn which oblig-
  es all who hear it to dance, and to which Oberon will respond if
  Huon is in dire need of help, as long as he doesn’t utter any lie.
  The group arrives at Tormont, a town ruled by Huon’s renegade
  uncle, Odo. Huon kills the felon and captures the city. [→811]
     Winter Court (Aachen): Charlemagne’s elephant Abul
  Abbas dies.

aNNo 810
        May Field (Aachen): Charlemagne orders a collection for
      the churches of Jerusalem.
        The Emperor orders the construction of defensive fleets in
      both the north and the south of his empire.
        Italy: King Pepin recaptures Venice from the Byzantines
      and raids the shores of Dalmatia.
        The Moors raid Sardinia.
        Denmark: King Godfrid II and his Danes invade Frisia and
      take great tributes of silver from the vanquished Frisians. The
      Emperor raises his army to do battle with Godfrid, but the army
      of the Danes returns home and Godfrid is murdered by one of
      his retainers during a hunt. Hemming II, Godfrid’s son, succeeds
      his father and makes peace with the Emperor after Charlemagne
      threatens to massacre all Danish boys and men taller than a
      sword (the Treaty of Heiligen).
        Aiol: [←809] At Orleans King Louis, Aiol’s cousin, is wag-
      ing war against Macharias, the false Count of Bourges. Aiol is
      unaware of this, and challenges the King’s knights for glory. He
      defeats four of them, but then the Count of Bourges launches an
      attack against the King’s men. In the ensuing battle, Aiol man-
      ages to capture the rebel Count and hands him over to the King.
      When he learns his relation to the king, he reconciles Louis and
      Elie. Aiol, who still hasn’t revealed his true identity to the king,
      becomes a respected member of Louis’ court. The king gives
      him many gifts, which the young knight distributes among his
      friends and followers. [→811]
        Spain: Light Frankish troops advance secretly during the
      night. They take boats to cross the Ebro, but the horse dung
      alerts the Saracens in Tortosa, which can no longer be taken
      by surprise. The Franks accept peace negotiations with Emir
      Tiebaut.
        Enfances Renier: [←807, Prise de Cordres et de Sebille] At
      the birth of Renier, Maillefer decides to conquer Loquiferne for
      his son. Unfortunately, Grymbert steals the infant from the cas-
      tle of Portpaillart and sells him to the local wali, who wants to
      feed the child to the lions, but the beasts refuse. After this mira-
      cle, the Moor decides to let his daughter raise the boy.
        Maillefer and William conquer Loquiferne, while Emir
      Tiebaut flees to Candie.
        Guibourc dies of old age and illness. [→810, Foulque de
      Candie]
        Foulque de Candie: [←810, Enfances Renier] Emir Tiebaut
      besieges Orange, his former fief, and takes some prisoners, in-
      cluding Vivien’s brother Guy and both of Bevis of Commarchis’
      sons. Tiebaut’s sister, Anfelise, has come with him, for she is se-
      cretly in love with Fulco, whom she sees for the first time when
      he arrives with his troops.
        In a sea battle, Fulco rescues the Frankish prisoners. Anfelise
      sends Fulco a love message and a golden ring. They meet secretly
      and Fulco promises to marry her soon.
        Bertrand and Bernard come to William’s aid (of all Aymeri’s
      sons, only Bevis de Commarchis, William, and Bertrand are still

alive). While Tiebaut plunders a nearby abbey, William con-
  ducts a successful sortie and kills many Moors.

  forces the Moors to break the siege and retreat to Spain. The
  Franks pursue them to the castle of Arrabloi, where they besiege
  Tiebaut. Anfelise is captured, baptized and married to Fulco.

  battle. He is recognized by his father, Guy, who wishes to con-
  vert his estranged son. When the cruel Corsuble of Algiers at-

  baptized.
     In the next battle, Povreveu kills Corsuble and captures
  three Moorish princesses, who are baptized and married:
  Povreveu weds Ganite, Bertrand receives the hand of Ayglente,
  and Guy, son of Bevis Cornebut, marries Amanevie. All pagan
  prisoners are baptized and set free. King Louis grants a truce to
  the Saracens and gives Spain to Fulco. [→810, Moniage William]
     Moniage William: [←810, Foulque de Candie] Now that the
  Franks are at peace with Emir Tiebaut, William leaves Orange to
  his godson, Maillefer, and retires to a monastery to pay for his
  sins. At the monastery, his warrior habits annoy the monks, who
  plot his death. They send him on an errand, unarmed, through a
  forest infested with brigands. William kills or chases them using
  the leg of his horse as a weapon, and God miraculously heals the
  loyal animal afterward. During a Saracen raid, William briefly
  takes up arms again to defend his homeland.
     Back in the monastery, he decides to become a hermit in
  the deserted rocky plains north of Montpellier. There he finds
  an abandoned manor and the ruins of a tower, which he makes
  his new home. God clears the site of snakes and other vermin.
  His presence attracts a cannibalistic giant, which he fights and
  kills. He then tries to resume his harsh but peaceful life, but
  Saracen raiders find him. He is overwhelmed by their numbers,
  captured, and taken to Palermo where he is thrown into a se-
  cret, foul prison filled with serpents. Charlemagne sends many
  knights to search for him, but no one can find him. [→811]
     Huon de Bordeaux: [←809] Together with eleven of his
  most loyal knights, Huon travels first to Rome to meet the Pope,
  a relative of his, to get absolution for his sins. He continues his
  voyage to Brindisi, an Italian harbor, where he meets Garin the
  sailor (another relative), who accompanies him to the Holy
  Land. Here, they meet a hermit named Jerome (Sherasmin),
  who turns out to be one of Huon’s late father’s loyal knights, who
  agrees to be their guide across the East. While passing through
  an enchanted forest, they meet Oberon, the faerie king. He gives
  Huon two valuable magical objects to help him: a golden goblet
  which fills itself automatically with any desired drink as long as
  the man who holds it is virtuous, and an ivory horn which oblig-
  es all who hear it to dance, and to which Oberon will respond if
  Huon is in dire need of help, as long as he doesn’t utter any lie.
  The group arrives at Tormont, a town ruled by Huon’s renegade
  uncle, Odo. Huon kills the felon and captures the city. [→811]

  Abbas dies.

title: Chapter Fifteen: The Future
leftColumn:
Emperor Nicephorus of Byzantium and Emir Tiebaut of
      Cordoba sign peace treaties with Emperor Charlemagne.
        Death of Pepin, King of Italy.
        Harvests: Bad. A mysterious illness weakens cattle all over
      Frankland. Rumor has it that Beneventan merchants deposited
      some mysterious poison in the fields and wells. Stewardship –5.
      aNNo 811
        May Field (Aachen): Charlemagne orders the organiza-
      tion of coastal defenses against Viking raids. The northern har-
      bors are fortified and equipped with war machines.
        Mysterious death of Pepin the Hunchback at the monastery
      of Prüm.
        Slavonia, Brittany: Three armies are raised and sent into
      different parts of the empire: the first army against the Slavs
      across the River Elbe, the second army into Pannonia against
      the Slavs and Huns, and the third army under Count Wido into
      Brittany. They all return home unharmed after carrying out the
      Emperor’s orders successfully.
        Aiol: [←810] King Louis receives a challenge from the Wadi
      of Pamplona, so he sends Aiol to Spain as a messenger. The
      young knight kidnaps Princess Mirabel and takes her back to
      Frankland, pursued all the way by Macharias’ knights and the
      Wali’s men. Aiol’s jealous cousin, Lusiane, refuses to help them,
      as she sees Mirabel as her rival for Aiol’s love. Later, when she re-
      alizes Aiol is her relative, she retires to a nunnery. Back at Louis’
      court, Aiol makes himself known, successfully claims his father’s
      lands, and marries the beautiful convert, Mirabel. [→812]
        Moniage William: [←810] While he is undertaking a pil-
      grimage to Jerusalem, Landri the Helmsman, a distant cousin
      of William, is taken prisoner by Lord Synagon of Palermo. The
      Saracen sets Landri free on condition that he convinces King
      Louis to do battle with Synagon’s army. The Franks and the pa-
      gans meet near William’s prison. The veteran paladin escapes
      and helps the Franks obtain victory.
        William returns to his retreat, but his peace is once more
      disturbed when Synagon’s nephew, Isoré, invades Septimania
      and Provence with a huge army. King Louis sends a messenger
      to ask for William’s help. William obeys his king and reaches the
      Aquitainian capital just in time to defeat Isoré in a duel. One of
      Ganelon’s nephews vainly tries to claim this victory as his own,
      until Bernard shows the giant’s head at court and reveals the
      truth.
        Back in his hermitage, William wants to build a bridge over
      the rapids, but every night a demon undoes his work. William
      fights him and plunges the creature into the water below, creat-
      ing a whirlpool. [→812]
        Huon de Bordeaux: [←810] Huon’s next obstacle is the
      citadel of Dunostre, protected by copper automatons wielding
      flails and inhabited by the terrifying giant Orgueilleux, a per-
      sonal enemy of Oberon. Huon frees a Frankish maiden held cap-
      tive in a tower, wins an impenetrable coat of mail, and manages
      to kill the giant and take his ring, which was given to him as a
      sign of the Sultan’s submission. To cross the sea, Huon receives
rightColumn:
the help of Malabron, a water genie in Oberon’s service. On the
  road to Babylon, he helps a Saracen prince who is fighting a fe-
  rocious lion. Instead of thanking Huon, the vile prince rides off
  on Huon’s best horse.
     In Babylon, Huon crosses the three bridges to the sul-
  tan’s palace with the aid of the giant’s ring, but tells a lie to
  the porters. At court, Huon kills the Saracen prince who stole
  his horse, presents himself to the Sultan and kisses his daugh-
  ter, Clarimunda, on the mouth (and she instantly falls in love
  with the young hero). When the Sultan sends his guards after
  the impetuous Frank, Oberon refuses to come to Huon’s aid
  (he lied, after all) and the paladin is captured and thrown into
  prison. Thanks to Princess Clarimunda’s tender care, prison for
  Huon isn’t that bad.
     One day, the giant Agrapard (Orgueilleux’s brother) comes
  to wage war on the sultan. Since all the Saracen knights refuse to
  duel, Huon is liberated from prison to act as the Sultan’s cham-
  pion. After a hard fight, the young paladin kills the giant. As the
  Sultan refuses to convert to Christianity, Huon kills him as well
  — with Oberon’s help, this time — and takes the Sultan’s teeth
  and beard. [→812]
     Byzantium: Emperor Nikephorus leads an expedition
  into Bulgaria and sacks Pliska, but is killed while retreating to
  Thrace. His son, Staurakios, is also wounded and survives only a
  few month before succumbing as well.
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 812
     May Field (Aachen): Peace is made with the Emir of Spain,
  and with Duke Grimoald of the Beneventans, who pays a tribute
  of 25,000 gold solidi.
     Denmark: King Hemming II of the Danes passes away, and
  many Danes die fighting over the succession to the throne.
     Byzantium: Emperor Nicephorus dies in battle against the
  Bulgars after many remarkable victories. His son-in-law, Michael,
  becomes emperor and sends envoys to acclaim Charlemagne as
  “brother emperor” and “basileus.”
     Italy: Bernard, son of Pepin, is crowned King of Italy, while
  Louis is crowned co-emperor of the Frankish empire. Wala and
  Adalhard act as their respective tutors.
     Basque Country: The Basques rebel, but the Franks cap-
  ture Pamplona. After a second Battle of Roncevaux, the Basques
  finally surrender.

  with King Louis, Elie comes to lay siege to Macharias’ cas-
  tle, but the traitor escapes with Mirabel, taking the lady back
  to her father’s court. Aiol convinces King Louis to besiege

      different parts of the empire: the first army against the Slavs
      across the River Elbe, the second army into Pannonia against
      the Slavs and Huns, and the third army under Count Wido into
      Brittany. They all return home unharmed after carrying out the
      Emperor’s orders successfully.
        Aiol: [←810] King Louis receives a challenge from the Wadi
      of Pamplona, so he sends Aiol to Spain as a messenger. The
      young knight kidnaps Princess Mirabel and takes her back to
      Frankland, pursued all the way by Macharias’ knights and the
      Wali’s men. Aiol’s jealous cousin, Lusiane, refuses to help them,
      as she sees Mirabel as her rival for Aiol’s love. Later, when she re-
      alizes Aiol is her relative, she retires to a nunnery. Back at Louis’
      court, Aiol makes himself known, successfully claims his father’s
      lands, and marries the beautiful convert, Mirabel. [→812]
        Moniage William: [←810] While he is undertaking a pil-
      grimage to Jerusalem, Landri the Helmsman, a distant cousin
      of William, is taken prisoner by Lord Synagon of Palermo. The
      Saracen sets Landri free on condition that he convinces King
      Louis to do battle with Synagon’s army. The Franks and the pa-
      gans meet near William’s prison. The veteran paladin escapes
      and helps the Franks obtain victory.
        William returns to his retreat, but his peace is once more
      disturbed when Synagon’s nephew, Isoré, invades Septimania
      and Provence with a huge army. King Louis sends a messenger
      to ask for William’s help. William obeys his king and reaches the
      Aquitainian capital just in time to defeat Isoré in a duel. One of
      Ganelon’s nephews vainly tries to claim this victory as his own,
      until Bernard shows the giant’s head at court and reveals the
      truth.
        Back in his hermitage, William wants to build a bridge over
      the rapids, but every night a demon undoes his work. William
      fights him and plunges the creature into the water below, creat-
      ing a whirlpool. [→812]
        Huon de Bordeaux: [←810] Huon’s next obstacle is the
      citadel of Dunostre, protected by copper automatons wielding
      flails and inhabited by the terrifying giant Orgueilleux, a per-
      sonal enemy of Oberon. Huon frees a Frankish maiden held cap-
      tive in a tower, wins an impenetrable coat of mail, and manages
      to kill the giant and take his ring, which was given to him as a
      sign of the Sultan’s submission. To cross the sea, Huon receives

the help of Malabron, a water genie in Oberon’s service. On the
  road to Babylon, he helps a Saracen prince who is fighting a fe-
  rocious lion. Instead of thanking Huon, the vile prince rides off
  on Huon’s best horse.
     In Babylon, Huon crosses the three bridges to the sul-
  tan’s palace with the aid of the giant’s ring, but tells a lie to
  the porters. At court, Huon kills the Saracen prince who stole
  his horse, presents himself to the Sultan and kisses his daugh-
  ter, Clarimunda, on the mouth (and she instantly falls in love
  with the young hero). When the Sultan sends his guards after
  the impetuous Frank, Oberon refuses to come to Huon’s aid
  (he lied, after all) and the paladin is captured and thrown into
  prison. Thanks to Princess Clarimunda’s tender care, prison for
  Huon isn’t that bad.
     One day, the giant Agrapard (Orgueilleux’s brother) comes
  to wage war on the sultan. Since all the Saracen knights refuse to
  duel, Huon is liberated from prison to act as the Sultan’s cham-
  pion. After a hard fight, the young paladin kills the giant. As the
  Sultan refuses to convert to Christianity, Huon kills him as well
  — with Oberon’s help, this time — and takes the Sultan’s teeth
  and beard. [→812]
     Byzantium: Emperor Nikephorus leads an expedition
  into Bulgaria and sacks Pliska, but is killed while retreating to
  Thrace. His son, Staurakios, is also wounded and survives only a
  few month before succumbing as well.
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 812
     May Field (Aachen): Peace is made with the Emir of Spain,
  and with Duke Grimoald of the Beneventans, who pays a tribute
  of 25,000 gold solidi.
     Denmark: King Hemming II of the Danes passes away, and
  many Danes die fighting over the succession to the throne.
     Byzantium: Emperor Nicephorus dies in battle against the
  Bulgars after many remarkable victories. His son-in-law, Michael,
  becomes emperor and sends envoys to acclaim Charlemagne as
  “brother emperor” and “basileus.”
     Italy: Bernard, son of Pepin, is crowned King of Italy, while
  Louis is crowned co-emperor of the Frankish empire. Wala and
  Adalhard act as their respective tutors.
     Basque Country: The Basques rebel, but the Franks cap-
  ture Pamplona. After a second Battle of Roncevaux, the Basques
  finally surrender.
     Aiol: [←811] Macharias flees from court and plans his
  vengeance. He attacks the newly-wedded couple and takes
  them prisoner. In prison, Mirabel gives birth to twins. The
  foul Macharias throws the babies into a wild river, but the wa-
  ter becomes miraculously calm, allowing a fisherman to save
  them. He takes the babies to a priest to be baptized. Together
  with King Louis, Elie comes to lay siege to Macharias’ cas-
  tle, but the traitor escapes with Mirabel, taking the lady back
  to her father’s court. Aiol convinces King Louis to besiege

             n
      put to death.
        Moniage William: [←811] Death of William. He is sancti-

      fied as Saint Guilhem-du-Desert (Saint William of the Desert).
        Huon de Bordeaux: [←811] On their way back to France,
      Huon makes love to the Saracen princess before being married to
      her, despite Oberon’s warning not to do so. Their boat is caught
      in a terrible storm and the two lovers end up shipwrecked on an
      island, separated from their companions. Clarimunda is caught
      by Galafre of Aufalerne, while Huon has found Malabron, who
      agrees to help Huon if he returns the horn, goblet and coat of
      mail to Oberon. Huon enters into the service of a Saracen min-
      strel at the court of Yvorin, brother of the late Gaudisso. Here,
      Huon (who has taken on a false name) must win a game of chess
      from Yvorin’s daughter to be spared. The princess loses on pur-
      pose, in the vain hope of winning the young hero’s love.
        Huon enters into Yvorin’s service and participates in the
      siege of Aufalerne. The city is besieged because Galafre refuses
      to hand Clarimunda over to her uncle, Yvorin. To end the siege,
      the two sides agree to a duel between champions. Huon kills
      Galafre’s son before encountering Jerome. As soon as they rec-
      ognize each other, Huon surrenders and is led into the city of
      Aufalerne, where he is reunited with his beloved Clarimunda.
      Outside, the two Saracen armies continue their battle, while
      Huon and his men massacre the remaining garrison and take
      control of the city. Unfortunately, Garin the sailor is killed in
      the battle. When the Saracens realize the trick the Franks played
      on them, they make peace and lay siege to Aufalerne. Luckily for
      Huon, a Frankish ship sails by to save them and take them back
      to Frankland. [→813]
        Winter Court (Aachen).
        Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
      aNNo 813
        May Field (Aachen).
        Byzantium: After an unsuccessful siege, the Bulgars raid
      the lands around Constantinople.
        Duchesse Parise: [←805, Guy de Nanteuil] The King of
      Asturias wishes to marry his daughter Sorplante to Hugo, but
      Gontagle of Lausanne (of the Mayence clan) advises against this
      and proposes a test of morality: Hugo is obliged to accompany
      three thieves who steal from the royal treasury, but Hugo him-
      self refuses to steal anything. When the King makes it known
      that he has been robbed of some of his gold, Hugo turns himself
      in and accepts the blame. This conduct very much pleases the
      King, who is convinced of Hugo’s noble birth. During a feast,
      the jealous Gontagle starts a fight with Hugo, who kills the trai-
      tor with a chess board. He then flees to Cologne where he meets
      his mother.
        Meanwhile, Raymond marries a daughter of the late
      Berenger, but his vassals rebel and chase his wife from her castle.
      Hugo has to do battle with his father, who finally recognizes him
      as his son. The remaining traitors of the Mayence clan are pun-
      ished. Raymond invalidates his second marriage and reconciles
rightColumn:
with Parise. Hugo marries Sorplante and succeeds his father-in-
                n
  law as the King of Asturias.
     Huon de Bordeaux: [→812] In Brindisi, Huon and his
  companions mourn Garin’s death with his family. In Rome,
  Clarimunda is baptized and becomes Huon’s wife. Since Huon
  cannot enter Bordeaux, they stop at the monastery of Saint
  Maurice, where they are welcomed. The good news of Huon’s
  return is sent to Gerard. But Huon’s brother has married the
  daughter of Amaury and has switched his allegiance. The thank-
  less traitor ambushes Huon’s men, kills most of them and cap-
  tures his brother, Clarimunda, and Jerome, whom he imprisons
  in Bordeaux. He then rides off to Charlemagne’s court and accus-
  es Huon of felony. After a long court session, the emperor agrees
  to come to Bordeaux to hear Huon’s plea. The young paladin
  tells all of his adventures and explains his brother’s treason, but
  he is incapable of producing the Sultan’s teeth and beard, since
  Gerard took these from him. Charlemagne wants to put Huon
  to the death, but the remaining eleven paladins and Oberon in-
  tervene in Huon’s favor, and manage to get Gerard to admit his
  treason. Gerard and his accomplices are hanged, despite Huon’s
  plea for mercy. Peace is restored, but the end of Charlemagne’s
  reign is announced by Oberon, who invites Huon and the last
                                  n
  surviving paladins to join him at the Eternal Island of Avalon.
     Frankland: Portents announce the emperor’s imminent
  death: “There occurred repeatedly eclipses of both the sun and
  the moon. The wooden bridge across the Rhine near Mayence
  which he had built over a period of ten years, with such im-
  mense skill and labor that it seemed likely to last forever,
  caught fire by accident and was burnt out in three hours.
  There were earth-tremors at the palace of Aachen. And one
  day, as Charlemagne was setting out from his camp and was
  beginning the day’s march, he suddenly saw a meteor flash
  down from the heavens and pass across a clear sky in a great
  blaze of light.” — Einhard
     Winter Court (Aachen).
     Harvests: Normal; Stewardship +0.
  aNNo 814
     Death of Charlemagne (January 28). History retakes its
  normal course.
     At the Emperor’s death, an anonymous monk from Bobbio
  expresses his grief in this poem:
    From the rising sun to the sea-shores where it sets,
    people are now crying and lamenting.
     Alas for miserable me.
    The young and old, glorious nobles,
    bishops and matrons, all lament the loss of their Emperor.
     Alas for miserable me.
    Frankland has endured awful wounds before,
    but never had suffered such a great sorrow as now.
     Alas for miserable me.
